Polo, in the middle of all this, shows up at Cayetana's with a grand gesture: he's gotten her back into school, gotten her mother's job back, and hands over enough money to cover their immediate expenses, all under the idea that everyone deserves a second chance.

Then the show finally pulls back the curtain on where Samuel's been. In flashback, Guzman reaches out and tells Samuel he actually believes his story, and Samuel asks to meet somewhere quiet. On his way there, he's chased down a deserted road by men in a car, barely making it to Guzman, who hides him until the danger passes. That close call becomes the seed of a plan: Samuel disappears into Guzman's grandparents' country house, and Guzman plants the bloody jacket to make it look like something worse happened. The whole point is to pressure Carla into cracking under the guilt of thinking she got him killed.

It works almost too well. The Inspector eventually gets a warrant for the property, and while searching it, finds Samuel very much alive in the boiler room. Instead of blowing the whole thing open, she walks out and claims she saw nothing, which turns out to be because she's in on it too, using the fake disappearance to manipulate Carla into confessing. And Carla does. She goes to the police and tells them everything. Samuel comes out of hiding with a flimsy story about a rave, and the truth about the staged disappearance stays buried, at least for now.

Right before the police can move on Polo, he finally admits the murder to Cayetana but she doesn't flinch. She repeats his line about second chances back to him, and it's clear from how she says it that she's already thinking about how to make the evidence disappear. Polo gets arrested at school not long after, and the fallout splits the group even further: Guzman finds out Ander knew the truth the entire time and cuts him off completely. Cayetana, true to her word, is shown hiding the murder weapon in her closet. In custody, Polo denies everything.

Omar's packing to leave Ander for good, done with months of watching him shut down and go apathetic with no explanation, when he finally learns the real reason: Ander's been carrying Polo's secret this whole time. It reframes everything Omar's been angry about, and instead of walking away, he forgives him.

By the time school resumes after New Year's, Guzman and Samuel seem to have made peace, at least on the surface. Then Polo walks back into school like nothing happened, released from custody with no explanation given. Only Cayetana looks happy to see him. Behind him, a new student is already talking to the principal, and the season ends on that note, one door quietly closing while another one opens.

Where we left everyone:

  • Polo: Free again. Cayetana hid the evidence that would've kept him locked up.

  • Carla: She confessed to the police and it meant absolutely nothing. That has to be its own kind of devastating.

  • Nano: Cleared, but a wrongful arrest doesn't just evaporate. He packs his bags and disappears in the rain, gone before the season even ends.

  • Samuel: Got his brother out, but the method cost him more than he expected, including whatever he and Carla actually became to each other.

  • Ander: Spent the whole season hollowed out by Polo's secret, but Omar finally learns the truth and forgives him. They end the season back together.

  • Cayetana: Burned her integrity to belong somewhere.

  • Valerio: Still here. Still underdressed for an academic institution. Still somehow everyone's problem.

What worked and what didn't

The real backbone of Season 2 is Samuel going after Carla, and it was the best thing the show had going. It just works.

Christian just vanishing from the show partway through bugged me while I was watching. He gets shipped off to Switzerland after one episode and the show barely mentions him again, which felt like a character just getting dropped. Turns out that's real world scheduling catching up with the story: Miguel Herrán, who plays Christian, was juggling this with Money Heist at the same time, and the show clearly wrote him out to make room for it. Doesn't fully excuse how abrupt it feels on screen, but it explains it.

The Valerio and Lu thing was rough to watch. They're half siblings, they kiss more than once, and the show treats it like messy sibling chemistry. There's no real reckoning with how wrong it is, just a "we promised we wouldn't do this again" line and then more scenes of them being pulled toward each other anyway. I get that the show loves pushing boundaries, but this one was unnecessary.

The show does a solid job of showing how guilt with nowhere to go just starts rotting everything around the person carrying it. When Polo finally breaks and confesses to Ander, it feels like relief for about five seconds before you realize what a massive disaster he just created. Because now Ander knows. And that secret's too heavy to carry and too dangerous to pass on, especially to Omar. Watching it hollow Ander out across the season was just painful. The warmth just drains out of him completely. And the biggest casualty of all of it is his relationship with Omar, taken apart piece by piece by something Omar isn't even allowed to know about.

Cayetana, the girl who spent the entire season desperately performing like she belonged at Las Encinas, finally crossed the line into actually becoming one of them: through covering up a murder. That's either brilliant writing or a coincidence that happened to work out perfectly.

Overall thoughts

Season 2 was actually decent. It's faster and a little messier than Season 1, but it works more often than it has any right to. You just have to accept upfront that none of these people behave like actual teenagers. Make your peace with that and it's a gripping watch.

The real question heading into Season 3 is whether the show can hold this kind of tension now that Polo's the known quantity rather than the hidden one. A secret's only dangerous while it's still a secret. Now everyone knows. What does the show do with that?

My Rating: 8.5

Did Cayetana destroying that evidence also made you furious?

Drop your take in the comments. And if you somehow feel bad for Polo after all of this, I want to understand your reasoning.

← Prev: Season 1 Next: Season 3 →

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: New students, old secrets, and a cover-up that goes too far. My look at why Elite Season 2 is a masterclass in tension and messy drama.

entry.title: RECAP: Primal Season 1
entry.content:
I randomly saw the trailer for Season 3 and decided to give the show a shot. Ended up binging the first season in one day.

No dialogue anywhere in it, not a single word, and somehow I understood everything. I felt every single thing these characters felt. That is how you know a show is doing something right.

This post contains spoilers for Primal Season 1.

How A Massacre Turned Into A Friendship

Primal opens on a caveman named Spear, just trying to get home with food for his family. He survives a crocodile and a pterosaur on the way back, which already tells you what kind of world this is. Then he gets home and his mate and two kids are being torn apart by a pack of horned Tyrannosaurus. He is too late to save them. The alpha calls the pack off before Spear can even fight back, and he is left standing in the wreckage of his entire life.

What happens next is the part that actually sets the tone for the whole season. Spear walks to the edge of a cliff and tries to end his life. He does not go through with it, but the show does not flinch from showing him get there. The sun comes up, he sees a vision of his family in the light, and that is the thing that keeps him moving.

Not long after, he comes across a Tyrannosaurus eating fish and assumes, wrongly, that it is one of the pack that killed his family. He follows it planning to kill it, only to find out it is a hornless female with two babies. Before he can do anything, the same horned pack shows up to wipe her family out too. Spear steps in. They fight together, and for a second it looks like they have both won something back.

Then the alpha arrives and eats the babies in one bite.

Spear and the mother dinosaur, now Fang, take the alpha down together. Spear gets the killing blow, driving his spear through its brain. It is revenge for his family and hers, but revenge does not bring anyone back. Fang is left with nothing. Later, on a beach, she finds Spear again. Neither of them has anyone left. They decide to stay together, and that is the whole show in one image: two creatures who should be enemies, walking off into the unknown because they have nothing left to lose and somehow that is the thing that saves them.

Earning Trust One Fight At A Time

If episode one is the tragedy, episode two is the part where you realize this relationship is not going to be easy or sweet. Fang steals Spear's kills. Repeatedly. She eats his fruit even though she is a carnivore. She keeps Spear up at night with her breathing. He throws rocks at her face out of sheer frustration. It is funny, but it is also real: two creatures from completely different worlds trying to figure out how to exist side by side, and constantly failing at it.

It boils over during a deer hunt. Fang steals the kill one too many times and Spear finally snaps, and the two actually fight each other and draw blood. This is the moment the show needed to earn everything that comes after it. They cannot just decide to trust each other because the plot needs them to. They have to fight for it. The standoff gets interrupted by something even scarier: a flash flood carrying hundreds of snakes straight at them. They survive it by working together, and Fang ends up tending to a head injury Spear gets along the way. By the time the water clears, they have actually earned each other.

From there the show starts widening its world fast. There is the mammoth episode, where Spear and Fang kill an old, weakened mammoth separated from its herd and take its tusk as a trophy. The herd tracks them down for it, ready to kill, until Spear realizes they are not after revenge. They just want the tusk back. He hands it over, and the herd carries it to a graveyard of their own dead, where they perform a quiet, almost ceremonial goodbye. For a show this violent, it is one of the gentlest, saddest scenes in the whole season.

Then things go fully feral. A blood moon turns the sky red and a pack of raptors chases Spear and Fang across an open field. They stumble onto another group of humans being hunted by giant red bat creatures that share a den with a massive prehistoric spider. Spear gets captured and cocooned in spider silk. Fang plays dead to get smuggled into the den, fights the spider, frees Spear, and the two of them escape by luring the bats into the raptor pack and letting the two predators wipe each other out. It is chaos from start to finish, and it does not pretend to be anything else.

Every episode Trying To Break Them, And Failing

Episode five is where the season goes for the throat. Spear and Fang stumble into a peaceful oasis, and for a few minutes the show lets them just exist: fishing, eating, resting, being something close to happy. Then they are ambushed by a tribe of ape-men who run brutal gladiator fights for entertainment. Fang gets thrown into the arena against their reigning champion, who drinks some kind of black ooze that turns him into a hulking, mutated monster. He nearly kills her.

Spear climbs up, throws the shaman to their death, and drinks the entire bowl of ooze himself. He turns into something massive and nearly unrecognizable, and he does not stop until every single ape-man in that arena is dead. It is the most violent stretch of the season by a wide margin, and it works because by this point you understand exactly what Fang means to him. When he wakes up the next morning back to normal, covered in blood, and finds Fang lying motionless where the fight ended, the silence in that scene says more than dialogue ever could.

She is not dead, just badly hurt, and the next episode is the long, quiet process of Spear getting her somewhere safe. He drags her on a makeshift stretcher, fights off scavenging dogs and flesh eating insects, and basically runs himself into the ground keeping her alive. By the time she is strong enough to fight again, the two of them clear out a pack of wild dogs together, and it feels like a genuine turning point. Whatever they were to each other before, they are something else now.

The back half of the season keeps raising the stakes. There is a rotting, infected Argentinosaurus that wipes out its entire herd and chases Spear and Fang through a volcanic lava field, finally burning apart after it cannot escape the molten rock. There is a coven of witches who capture and mind-control Fang, complete with a side story about a witch named Lula mourning her own dead daughter, which gives the show a strange, sad humanity in the middle of all the monster stuff. There is an unseen, screeching predator that picks off a Smilodon and an entire Triceratops herd before Spear and Fang figure out fire is the only thing that scares it, and burn it alive in a forest clearing.

And Then Mira Happened

And then the season ends on a gut punch that has nothing to do with monsters at all. Spear and Fang come across an enslaved woman named Mira fighting off a sea creature in a lagoon. They free her from her shackles, travel with her, and slowly build something close to a found family. She teaches Spear how to make a bow. She prays to the moon every night. He starts to actually care what she is trying to say to him even though he cannot understand her language. Then a group of monkey-men ambush their camp and drag her away, and by the time Spear and Fang reach the coast, she is already being shipped off by the same people who enslaved her in the first place. The season ends with Spear saying his first word in the entire show, her name, while Fang roars in grief beside him.

Where We Left Everyone

  • Spear: Lost his entire first family in episode one, found something with Fang and almost lost her too, and ends the season screaming Mira's name as she disappears over the horizon.

  • Fang: Lost her own children the same day Spear lost his family, nearly died in the ape-men arena, and spends the finale roaring in helpless grief right alongside him.

  • Mira: Escaped slavery only to get recaptured in the final minutes of the season, taken away on a ship before Spear and Fang can reach her.

Final Verdict & Overall Thoughts

This is a must watch. If you love drama that is pure, intense, and a little unhinged, this is exactly that, stripped down to its rawest form. No dialogue to hide behind, no exposition to lean on, just pure visual storytelling that hits you right in the chest every single episode. I went in expecting a cool concept and came out completely wrecked by a show that never says a single word.

My Rating: 9.3

Has anyone else seen this show?

Next: Season 2 →

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A full spoiler recap of Primal Season 1, the dialogue-free Adult Swim show about a caveman and a T-Rex bonded by tragedy and survival.

entry.title: REVIEW: FROM Season 2
entry.content:
The story itself still holds up, but this is where a few of the show's habits started to wear on me.

This season picks up right where season 1 left the town, still trapped, still surrounded by whatever is out in those woods, and still refusing to give anyone a straight answer. This season adds a wave of new residents to the mix, and honestly, it is a mixed bag. Some of them earn their place fast, others feel like they are still auditioning for relevance.

This post contains spoilers for season 2.

The Plot

The season opens with Boyd missing, which throws Donna and Kenny straight into crisis mode as a busload of new arrivals shows up with no idea what they just drove into. At the same time, Victor and Tabitha go digging through the tunnels underneath the town, and that whole thread sets the tone for how disorienting this season gets early on. From there, the show spends its first couple of episodes just trying to survive one long night in the diner, with Jim and Tom stuck trying to keep a terrified bus passenger from getting everyone killed.

Once the newcomers settle in, the season shifts into the stuff that actually matters long term. Kenny and Ellis stumble onto something gruesome out in the forest, and Boyd starts dealing with a condition that only gets worse as the episodes go on, something the show takes its time revealing instead of rushing. Sara's return puts Boyd in an impossible spot, Jim starts putting together a theory about the town that nobody wants to hear, and Victor and Jade end up striking a bargain that tells you a lot about how far people are willing to go just to get by in this place.

The back half of the season is where things get genuinely tense. Colony House starts cracking under the pressure of a coming food shortage, the clinic turns into the site of one of the season's scarier nights, and Boyd and Kristi try to make something useful out of what looks like the death of the Nightmare Creature. Jim's alliance with Randall becomes a bigger and bigger problem, building toward a plan that puts the whole town at risk, and by the time the finale rolls around, Boyd is out of answers and the residents are bracing for what feels like the end. Tabitha, meanwhile, holds onto the idea that the children might be the key to getting everyone out, which is one of the more interesting threads the show leaves hanging going into season 3.

What worked:

The cliffhanger. If you thought season 1 ended rough, season 2 is going to knock you upside your head. The show clearly knows how to close out a season on a gut punch, and it did not hold back this time. That alone tells me the writers understand pacing at the macro level even when the week to week pacing gets shaky, which I will get into.

The new characters are a mixed bag, but the ones that land, land well. Randall in particular adds a volatility to the show that it did not really have before, he is the kind of character who makes you nervous every time he is on screen because you genuinely do not know what he is going to do next, and that unpredictability is good for a show that can sometimes feel too controlled. Some of the other new faces will probably need another season to fully click, they are set up but not fully used yet, so I am reserving judgment there rather than writing them off.

Victor and Jade's storyline also stood out to me this season. Watching Victor navigate a bargain with someone outside his usual circle added a new layer to a character I already loved from season 1, and it is a good reminder that the show still knows how to use him well even when the plot around him gets busy.

What didn't:

My biggest annoyance this season is the lack of communication among these residents, and it is honestly baffling at this point. You are in a town you cannot leave. Monsters come out at night. The radio works with no batteries in it. Strange things keep happening constantly. And people still will not tell each other what they know because they are worried nobody will believe them. That is one of the dumbest things I have seen a group of adults do on screen, and Boyd is the worst offender. He can tell Donna things, she has proven herself trustworthy over and over, but he keeps choosing to sit on information instead, and it makes an otherwise smart character look reckless for no good reason.

The story also drags in stretches this season. More questions keep piling up, but the answers are not coming at the same rate, and at some point that stops feeling like intentional mystery building and starts feeling like the writers do not actually know where they are going yet. I am willing to be patient with a slow burn, but a slow burn needs to feel like it is heading somewhere, and a few episodes in the middle of this season felt like they were just killing time until the next big reveal.

The acting issues from season 1 are still around too. I have mostly made peace with it at this point, some performances just are not going to hit as hard as others, but it is worth noting that it has not really improved.

Rating

8.0 out of 10.

Season 2 still has everything that made me fall for this show in the first place, the dread, the mystery, characters like Victor who keep giving me a reason to care. But the communication problem among the residents genuinely frustrates me at this point, and the pacing in the middle stretch drags in a way season 1 never did. It is still a strong season, just not as tight as the one before it.

Am I the only one yelling at Boyd to just talk to Donna already, or does the silence bother you too?

Tell me I'm not alone on this one.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Season 2 of From raises the stakes and the body count, but nobody in this town can communicate. My honest take, spoilers included.

entry.title: REVIEW: FROM Season 1
entry.content:
I kept seeing this show pop up everywhere and I finally sat down to watch it.

From was created by John Griffin and produced by AGBO (the Russo brothers' company), and it premiered on Epix back in February 2022, ten episodes for season 1, and it wastes no time pulling you into a town that should not exist. From sits in that sci-fi horror space where the scares come at night and the questions pile up during the day, that combination is exactly the kind of thing that gets me.

This post contains minor spoilers for season 1.

The Plot

The setup is simple to explain and horrible to live through. Families and individuals from all over end up driving into a small town they never meant to visit, and once they arrive, they cannot leave. Every road out just loops them back in. The town, referred to as the Township by the people stuck there, looks like a normal slice of small town America in daylight. At night it turns into something else entirely, because creatures come out of the surrounding woods and hunt whoever is left outside.

The story follows Sheriff Boyd Stevens, played by Harold Perrineau, who has appointed himself the person responsible for keeping order and keeping people alive. He is not equipped for the job in any official sense, there is no manual for running a town that traps its residents, but he tries anyway, and season 1 spends a lot of time showing what that responsibility costs him personally, especially with his estranged son Ellis living apart from him at Colony House.

Beyond Boyd, the season builds out its cast through the newest arrivals, the Matthews family, who crash into the town in the opening episode and have to learn the rules the hard way. Their arrival gives the show a way to explain the town to the audience without it feeling like exposition, we learn as they learn, and that includes the town's stricter, more paranoid residents who have their own theories about how to survive and who is to blame when someone does not.

What season 1 does well is resist giving you answers. It plants questions about the creatures, about the tree that seems to matter more than it should, about a voice on the radio that nobody can quite explain, and it lets those questions sit instead of rushing to wrap them up. By the finale you are not any closer to knowing what the town actually is, but you are fully invested in the people trying to survive it.

What worked:

The premise alone got me. I am a sucker for mystery and eerie stories, and the show leans all the way into that without over explaining itself. A town that traps people, creatures that only come out at night, a tree that seems to matter for reasons nobody can name, all of it works because the show trusts you to sit in the unease instead of handing you a neat explanation in episode 3. That's quite rare because a lot of horror shows panic and start explaining too early, but this one just does not, and the season works so well because of it.

The characters carried the season for me, and my favorite by far was Victor Kavanaugh, played by Scott McCord. Victor is a Colony House resident who has been trapped in the town since he was a child, and that detail changes everything about how you watch him. He is not just another adult surviving a nightmare, he grew up inside the nightmare, and it shows in how he behaves. There is a stunted quality to him, a kind of arrested development that makes sense once you understand what he has been through, and it is so harrowing to watch once it clicks. You are not just watching a strange character, you are watching what years of being trapped as a child does to a person. The show does not spell this out with a monologue either, it lets his behavior speak for itself, and that kind of trust in the audience is what made me root for him more than almost anyone else in the town.

The rest of the ensemble holds up around him too. Boyd's storyline with his son gives the show an emotional core that is separate from the horror elements, and it means the season is not just running on scares, there is an actual family falling apart and trying to piece itself back together in the middle of all this.

What didn't:

My one real issue was the acting, and it was not consistent across the board. Some performances carried real weight, Perrineau in particular does a lot with Boyd, but a few of the supporting cast members pulled me out of scenes that should have hit harder. It is not that anyone was bad exactly, it is more that some of the delivery felt a little stiff in moments that needed more from the actor, and when a show is built around dread and tension, one flat line reading can break the mood the scene worked so hard to build.

It is a small complaint in the scheme of things, the writing and premise are strong enough to carry the season through it, but it is the one thing that kept season 1 from being flawless for me.

Rating

8.6 out of 10.

Season 1 of From earned that number by building a genuinely unsettling premise and backing it up with characters worth caring about, especially Victor, whose arc is the emotional gut punch of the whole season. The acting inconsistency knocked a little off, but not enough to change how much I enjoyed sitting with this show. I went in expecting jump scares and left thinking about a kid who grew up trapped in a town with no way out, and that is exactly the kind of horror I want more of.

PS: if you have not seen it yet and you like your horror mixed with a genuine mystery you have to think about, this is worth the watch.

Who was your favorite character in season 1, and did the town's mystery pull you in the way it pulled me in?

Drop your thoughts below, I want to know if Victor got to you too.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A town nobody can leave, creatures that hunt after dark, and a kid trapped since childhood. My honest review of From season 1.

entry.title: REVIEW: Takopi's Original Sin
entry.content:
Takopi's Original Sin looks like a cheerful slice of life about a lonely kid, but it isn't.

It is a six episode anime that premiered in Japan on June 28, 2025, adapted from Taizan5's web manga of the same name, produced by Studio Enishiya, and directed by Shinya Iino, known for Dr. Stone. Genre wise, it's in psychological drama territory.

This post contains minor spoilers.

The Plot

Takopi's Original Sin follows a small, cheerful alien named Takopi who lands on Earth with one job, spread happiness, and ends up attaching himself to Shizuka, a quiet fourth grader. She's dealing with relentless bullying at school, led by a classmate named Marina, and a home life that offers her almost nothing. The only real comfort in her world is her dog, Chappy.

What starts as a soft, almost comedic premise, an alien learning to cheer up a sad kid, doesn't stay that way for long. Takopi's good intentions end up making things worse, and the show shifts hard once he's forced to use his tech to try to undo a mistake he never saw coming. From there, it turns into something far heavier, following Takopi as he keeps trying to fix a situation over and over again.

As the story unfolds, it pulls back the curtain on everyone involved, including Marina, who turns out to be dealing with just as much pain at home as Shizuka is, and Azuma, a classmate quietly trying to help in his own way while carrying his own family pressure. Nobody in this show stays a simple hero or villain for long. By the end, Takopi has to accept that some things can't be undone no matter how many times he tries, and the story trades its early shock value for something quieter, sadder, and ultimately more hopeful.

It's a short watch, but it doesn't waste a single episode.

What worked:

Most anime that touch on bullying keep some distance from the real weight of it, but this one goes all the way there, and a few moments, like Takopi finding Shizuka's body, are hard to sit through. The show also plays a clever trick early on, using that intro to make you think the story is headed toward a simple, happy resolution before pulling the rug out completely.

The back half does a lot of work to humanize characters who could have stayed one-note. Azuma ends up being one of the most relatable people in the whole show, not because his situation is normal, but because the pressure he feels from his mother and the shadow of his brother is the kind of pain a lot of people recognize. Watching him break down in a quiet, believable way instead of some dramatic spiral says a lot about how grounded his arc is. Takopi's own guilt does similar work for Marina, letting the show reveal her as someone shaped by her own suffering rather than a flat villain.

What didn't:

A few things did not land as well for me. There is a stretch where nearly every character, including the adults who should be paying attention, treats Shizuka badly with no real pushback, and it starts to feel like the story is piling on just to prove a point it already made.

Azuma being kind to her helps, but not quite enough to balance it out.

Later on, once Shizuka's own darker side starts coming through, the show never really lets us into her head the way it does for Marina and Azuma, and those moments end up carrying less weight than they should have.

The reconciliation between Marina and Shizuka in the finale also could have used a bit more room to breathe.

Rating

8.6 out of 10.

Even with those gaps, the ending pulls everything together. Takopi's sacrifice, backed by his narration over those final scenes, is the moment that stays with me the most, and choosing empathy over another shock for the final note was the right call.

PS: the parents in this show are awful. I've never seen anything like it.

If you were in Marina's position, do you think you'd have turned out any different?

Drop your honest answer below, no judgment.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A review on the six episode anime that turned a cute premise into one of the most gutting watches I've had in a while.

entry.title: KDRAMA RECOMMENDATIONS: (May 27, 2026)
entry.content:
I did not plan to become a K-drama person. It happened quietly, the way most obsessions do.

One show, then another, and suddenly you are eight episodes deep with absolutely no intention of stopping. What I have noticed over time is that the KDramas that actually stick with me are rarely the ones making the most noise. The massive titles get recommended endlessly, and some of them deserve it. But there is a whole tier of shows sitting just below the mainstream conversation that are doing things just as interesting, sometimes even more interesting, and they almost never get their due. This list is for those. Well, mostly those. I am making one deliberate exception, and I will get to that.

These are not ranked. They are just the shows that earned a permanent spot in my memory, and here is why.

Evilive (2023)

This is the show where Kim Young-Kwang absolutely broke my brain. I had seen him before in lighter roles, the kind of romantic lead you enjoy and then quickly forget. Evilive is where I realized what he is actually capable of.

He plays Seo Do-Young, a gangster who is calculating, cold, and completely in control, and he carries the role without ever tipping into cartoonish villainy. Not once. The show is a noir-soaked crime thriller about a disgraced lawyer who gets pulled into the world of online gambling and slowly loses himself to it. The push and pull between the two leads is what makes it work: you watch the lawyer become monstrous while the gangster becomes someone you reluctantly start to understand. It is an uncomfortable trade-off, and the show knows exactly what it is doing with it. Since watching this, I have tracked down nearly everything Kim Young-Kwang has ever been in. That should tell you everything.

What could have been better: The pacing drags in the middle, and the plot occasionally leans on coincidence to move things forward when it should not need to. The performances carry you through every single one of those gaps, but the structural issues are still there.

Quick highlights:

  • Career-best performance. Kim Young-Kwang is a revelation here. If you have only seen him in rom-coms, this role will completely reframe what you think he is capable of.
  • Moral inversion. The show flips your sympathies slowly and deliberately, until you realize you are rooting for exactly the kind of person you probably should not be.
  • Noir atmosphere done right. The tone is grim and stylish without ever feeling try-hard. It earns its darkness.

Strangers from Hell (2019)

"Eerie" does not even begin to cover it. This show is genuinely unsettling in a way that is hard to describe without spoiling it. The atmosphere does all the heavy lifting before anything explicit even happens.

A young man moves into a dirt-cheap apartment building in Seoul, and his neighbors are just wrong. Not wrong in a way you can immediately put your finger on. Just wrong. The dread builds slowly and consistently, and by the time the show starts delivering on what it has been hinting at, you are already too deep to look away. Im Siwan and Lee Dong-Wook both turn in some of the best work of their careers here, moving in completely opposite directions: one is completely unraveling while the other is disturbingly composed. The contrast between them is what makes the whole thing so hard to shake.

What could have been better: Ten episodes feels a bit short. Some of the psychological groundwork needed more room to breathe, and the ending divides people for a reason. I get why it frustrates some viewers.

Quick highlights:

  • Atmosphere over jump scares. The horror here is slow and psychological. Nothing is cheap. The dread is earned through sustained unease, not cheap shocks.
  • Lee Dong-Wook against type. If you know him from his lighter work, this performance will genuinely disturb you, and that is meant as the highest compliment.
  • Nothing else like it in KDrama. As an exercise in sustained atmospheric dread, this stands completely alone in the space.

A Killer Paradox (2024)

The premise is simple, but the execution is far smarter than it has any right to be. A broke, directionless college student accidentally kills a man in self-defense, only to discover the guy was actually a serial killer. Then it happens again.

The show does not rush you toward any easy moral conclusions. Instead it holds the question open the entire time: is he doing something wrong, or is he accidentally doing something right? It sits comfortably with that discomfort for all eight episodes and never blinks. Choi Woo-Shik plays a bewildered, guilt-ridden spiral better than anyone working in Korean drama right now, and Son Suk-Ku brings a fantastic world-weary energy to the detective hunting him. Every scene they share feels like a slow-motion collision.

What could have been better: A few supporting plot threads are left dangling in a way that feels less like intentional ambiguity and more like the writers ran out of runway. The finale raises questions it does not quite answer, and not all of them read as deliberate.

Quick highlights:

  • Eight tight episodes. No filler, no bloat. It gets in, makes its point, and gets out. That kind of discipline is rarer than it should be.
  • Genuinely fresh premise. The accidental vigilante angle is not something you have seen handled quite like this before in Korean drama.
  • Two stellar leads. Choi Woo-Shik and Son Suk-Ku are doing completely different things in every scene, and both of them are right.

The Kidnapping Day (2023)

Nobody talks about this show, and it completely baffles me. It is a brilliant black comedy thriller about a clumsy, desperate dad who kidnaps an eleven-year-old genius girl to pay for his own daughter's medical bills.

The twist? The girl is way sharper than he is, and the situation immediately spirals out of control in every possible direction. It is funny in a way KDramas rarely allow themselves to be. Not sitcom-funny. Darkly, uncomfortably funny, where you catch yourself laughing at things you probably should not be laughing at. When it works, and it works more often than not, it is the most purely entertaining thing I watched all year.

What could have been better: The tonal shifts are not always seamless. The show tries to be both tense and comedic, and occasionally it lands awkwardly between the two instead of nailing either one.

Quick highlights:

  • Dark comedy done with care. The humor never punches down. It finds laughs in the chaos of a situation, not at the expense of any one character.
  • The kid steals every scene. The young actress playing the kidnapped girl is the most entertaining character in the whole show, and it is not particularly close.
  • Wildly underrated. This deserved a far bigger conversation than it got. If you like your thrillers with a twisted sense of humor, this is exactly your show.

Moving (2023)

Moving is the best thing the superhero genre has produced in years, and I say that as someone who has watched the genre exhaust itself on increasingly joyless Hollywood spectacles. What this show understands, and what most Western superhero properties have completely forgotten, is that the power is never the point. The people are the point.

The adults in this show are desperately hiding their abilities to protect their kids. Meanwhile the teenagers are discovering their own powers with no idea that their parents know exactly how terrifying that shift feels. That generational tension is the engine of the whole series, and it runs for twenty episodes without ever losing steam. The final stretch is some of the best television I have ever seen. Not best KDrama. Best television. Full stop.

What could have been better: The first few episodes are a deliberate slow-burn, and some viewers tap out early. If you are three episodes in and feel like nothing is happening, please trust the process. A few of the villain-focused backstory episodes also run a little long.

Quick highlights:

  • Superhero storytelling with actual heart. The action sequences are spectacular, but the emotional core is what makes you care about all of it. That balance is almost impossible to pull off, and Moving nails it.
  • The parental storyline. The backstories of the adult characters are devastating in the best possible way. Some of the most affecting work in the whole show happens before the main plot even kicks in.
  • Twenty episodes that earn every minute. This is not a show that overstays its welcome. Every episode adds something.

Flower of Evil (2020)

A detective slowly realizes that her husband is not even close to who she thought he was. That is the setup, but what the show does with it is something else entirely.

Lee Joon-Gi plays a man who has suppressed his true identity so completely that he has become a near-perfect copy of a loving husband. The performance is precise and deeply unsettling, because you are watching someone work incredibly hard to mimic feelings they do not actually possess, until occasionally, almost by accident, something real slips through. The chemistry between the two leads is extraordinary. They are one of the best screen pairs in recent memory, and the show earns its emotional finale in a way most thrillers do not even bother to attempt.

What could have been better: The show leans on its central mystery a little too long, and there are a few episodes in the back half where the plot is clearly just marking time. A tighter edit would have made it a flawless masterpiece instead of just an exceptional one.

Quick highlights:

  • Lee Joon-Gi at his peak. The precision of his performance in this role is almost unsettling to watch. Every micro-expression is doing work.
  • One of the best lead pairings in KDrama. The two leads have chemistry that feels genuinely rare, and the show is built around making that matter.
  • An emotional payoff that actually lands. Most thrillers sacrifice the emotional resolution to keep the plot moving. This one refuses to, and it is better for it.

The Worst of Evil (2023)

An undercover cop drama about a detective who infiltrates a massive criminal organization running the drug trade between Korea, China, and Japan. Ji Chang-Wook plays a man who goes so deep undercover that the line between who he is pretending to be and who he is actually becoming starts to blur in ways that feel genuinely dangerous.

Wi Ha-Joon is fantastic as his criminal counterpart, and every single scene they share crackles with the kind of tension that makes you forget to breathe. The fact that this show barely gets mentioned anywhere is a genuine mystery. The earlier episodes lean beautifully into the moral complexity, and the central performances are strong enough to carry you through anything the script throws at you.

What could have been better: The show loses its nerve slightly in the final few episodes. The earlier parts handle the moral ambiguity with real confidence, but the ending pulls too hard toward a cleaner resolution than the story actually earned. You can feel the compromise, and that is a shame, because everything before it is so good.

Quick highlights:

  • Ji Chang-Wook's best dramatic work. He has always been watchable, but this role demands something heavier, and he delivers it fully.
  • The identity erosion angle. Watching a character slowly lose track of where the performance ends and the reality begins is handled with more nuance here than in most undercover narratives.
  • Wi Ha-Joon as the counterweight. He brings a quiet menace to his role that keeps the dynamic between the two leads interesting right to the end.

Twinkling Watermelon (2023)

This one caught me completely off guard, because it has no business being this emotionally precise. It is the tonal outlier on the list. Not a gritty thriller. A time-travel, coming-of-age story centered around music, and it is warmer, stranger, and more quietly devastating than you would ever expect.

A teenager accidentally travels back in time to 1995 and meets his parents when they were just teenagers themselves, before adult life hit them, and before they became the versions of themselves he grew up with. The show handles the mechanics of time travel with more care than most sci-fi stories manage, and the emotional payoff it builds toward is genuinely beautiful. One minute you are watching a fun time-travel story, and then suddenly you are crying in episode fourteen, genuinely unsure when that happened.

What could have been better: The romance subplot runs a little longer than necessary, and a few episodes in the middle meander. The young cast is so committed that it more than compensates, but the pacing dips are noticeable.

Quick highlights:

  • The concept is handled with real intelligence. Time-travel stories often collapse under their own logic. This one keeps its rules consistent and uses them emotionally, not just mechanically.
  • The music is a genuine part of the story. It is not just set dressing. The role that music plays in connecting the characters across timelines is genuinely moving.
  • It sneaks up on you. You will not see the emotional gut-punch coming, and that is exactly the point.

The Glory (2022)

This is my one deliberate exception, because The Glory is definitely not underrated. It was one of the most talked-about dramas of the last few years. I am including it anyway because I think the mainstream conversation flattened it into a standard revenge thriller, when it is actually doing something much more precise.

Song Hye-Kyo plays a woman who spent years methodically constructing a life designed to ruin the people who brutally bullied her in high school. The drama is in the meticulous planning, not just the execution. Watching her operate like a grandmaster, completely calm and completely in control, is one of the most satisfying experiences I have had watching a protagonist who is clearly the villain to her targets but absolutely the hero to us. Part 1 alone is close to flawless. If you have not watched it yet, close this tab and go fix that right now. I will still be here when you get back.

What could have been better: Part 2 does not land the ending with the same surgical precision that Part 1 established. The final episodes are not bad, they just do not match the incredible heights of what came before, and you can feel the drop.

Quick highlights:

  • Song Hye-Kyo redefines herself completely. This is a career-redefining performance. The restraint she brings to a role that could have easily tipped into melodrama is extraordinary.
  • The planning is the payoff. This show understands that watching a brilliant mind build something over years is far more satisfying than watching it detonate in one episode.
  • The villain ensemble is genuinely hateable. You will not struggle to stay invested. The antagonists are written with just enough dimension to feel real, and just enough cruelty to make you desperate to watch them fall.

What KDrama has had you in a chokehold lately?

I know I am not the only one who has fallen down this particular rabbit hole. If you have seen any of these and want to talk about them, the comments are right there. And if you have a hidden gem I missed, especially in the crime thriller space, drop it below because I want to know about it.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: From noir crime thrillers to heart-wrenching time-travel stories, here are the KDramas that earned a permanent spot in my memory.

entry.title: VEEP Is The Greatest Comedy Show
entry.content:
Veep is not a show about politics. It is a show about people, deeply catastrophically flawed people, who just happen to work in politics.

The moment you stop expecting anyone on screen to do the right thing, you relax into what this show actually is: the most ruthlessly funny, brilliantly written, endlessly rewatchable comedy in the history of television.

Veep ran for seven seasons on HBO, from April 2012 to May 2019. It was created by Armando Iannucci, the Scottish writer behind The Thick of It and the film In the Loop, and it accumulated 59 Primetime Emmy nominations across its run, winning 17 of them. Julia Louis-Dreyfus won six consecutive Emmy Awards for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series for this role. Six. In a row. That tells you something happened here that television does not usually get to do.

This post contains spoilers for HBO's Veep

The Plot (In a Nutshell)

Selina Meyer is the Vice President of the United States, a position she finds both beneath her and completely out of her control. She and her staff spend every episode trying to manage crisis of their own making, advance an agenda nobody can clearly define, and avoid being blamed for any of it. They fail, constantly and spectacularly, and that is the entire show.

My Take

Every storyline runs on someone making the worst possible decision for the most selfish possible reason. These people have no moral compass, zero, and that is the entire engine of the show. Veep's argument, made with absolute consistency across seven seasons, is that political systems do not attract principled people. They attract the ambitious, the vain, and the deeply insecure, people who confuse the pursuit of power with the desire to do good, because it is easier than admitting the truth about themselves. Nobody on this show is lying to the audience. They are lying to themselves, which is funnier and more disturbing at the same time.

Veep also does not wait for you. The dialogue moves at a pace most comedies would consider reckless, and the rewatch value is extraordinary because of it. You will catch things on your third viewing that flew completely past you the first two times.

The Characters: A Beautiful Disaster Zone

L to R: Sue, Mike, Jonah, Amy, Gary, Selina, Dan.

The ensemble works because nobody is good. Not one person. And yet you cannot take your eyes off any of them.

Selina Meyer: Julia Louis-Dreyfus plays her as the rotten little sun this entire solar system orbits. Selina is vain, delusional, intellectually dishonest, and absolutely convinced the universe owes her everything. She will throw anyone under the bus without blinking: her staff, her allies, her own daughter Catherine, it does not matter. You should hate her, yet you can't help but root for her anyway.

Gary Walsh: Selina's body man and personal aide, and Gary is the most unsettling person in the show. His loyalty to Selina is not rational. It is devotional, and almost uncomfortable to watch in the best possible way. He carries her bag, monitors her moods, pre-empts her needs before she has voiced them, and absorbs her cruelty without complaint or apparent damage. She cannot function without him and he cannot exist without her.

Dan Egan: He is what happens when a Ken doll sells his soul. Dan is amoral in a way that is almost aspirational. He has no loyalty, no ideology, no attachment to outcomes beyond what they mean for him personally, and he delivers all of this with the confidence of someone who has never once experienced a consequence. He is terrible. He is magnetic. He is the character the show uses to show you what pure ambition looks like with the ethics surgically removed.

Amy Brookheimer: Amy is the most competent person in the room in almost every scene she is in, and she gets punished for it every single episode. She works harder, thinks faster, and cares more than anyone around her, and the show uses her competence as a punchline because in the world Veep is depicting, being good at your job is not enough and might actually be a disadvantage.

Mike McLintock: The press secretary who seems genuinely confused by reality at all times. Mike is not stupid exactly, he is just operating at a slight delay from the world around him, perpetually one beat behind whatever is happening, and perpetually confident that he has it under control.

Sue Wilson: Sue is the office gatekeeper who has seen everything, feels nothing, and is somehow the most powerful person in the building. She delivers information and stonewalls requests with the exact same flat expression regardless of what the information is or how urgent the request.

Honorable Mentions: Jonah Ryan and Richard Splett

Jonah Ryan: Timothy Simons plays him as a White House staffer who is tall, oblivious, self-aggrandizing, and disliked by literally everyone who has ever met him including foreign politicians. He is a punching bag, a canvas, a target the writers use to show just how creative human cruelty can get when properly motivated.

The nicknames alone deserve an academic paper. In Season 4 Episode 9, an entire list of nicknames the staff keep in a shared document called the Jonad Files gets read out loud in a congressional hearing by a solemn legislator, and it is among the funniest sequences in the entire series. The list includes: Jack and the Giant Jackoff, The Pointless Giant, The 60-Foot Virgin, Hagrid's Nutsack, and The Cloud Botherer. The show's writer David Mandel described the process of writing Jonah insults as "the most math-y of the insults we write", because each one has to be both an insult and a reference to how tall he is.

What makes Jonah a monument rather than just a punchline is where he ends up. He starts as a low-level White House staffer. By the end of the series he has been a Congressman, run for President, and formed his own caucus in the House. The show turns him into a vehicle for something darker as the seasons go on, a portrait of how a specific kind of oblivious, self-righteous, populist uselessness can still find an audience in politics.

And then there is Richard Splett, played by Sam Richardson, who first appeared as a temp in Season 3 and became one of the most beloved characters in the show. Richard is the only good person in the entire Veep universe. He is cheerful, well-meaning, occasionally incompetent in the sweetest possible way, and completely immune to the cynicism that surrounds him. He has been described as "a bunny rabbit in a viper pit", which is accurate. He eventually becomes Selina's Chief of Staff, a sperm donor for Catherine and Marjorie's baby, and the single source of warmth in a show that otherwise has none.

Why It Works

Veep did something that should not be possible: it turned profanity into poetry. The insults are constructed, layered, and have actual rhythm. The writers understood that a great insult needs specificity. Generic abuse is lazy. But when you target someone so precisely, so surgically aimed at their exact brand of failure, it stops being an insult and starts being craft.

The show also has a thesis beneath all the chaos. Iannucci built Veep on the same foundation he used for The Thick of It: the idea that political power does not corrupt people so much as it selects for people who are already compromised, and then gives them a stage. These characters did not become awful because of Washington. Washington chose them because they were already like this.

Final Verdict

If you love sharp writing, flawless performances, and comedy that respects your intelligence enough to never slow down and explain the joke, Veep is the only show you need. It is the greatest comedy ever made, and I do not say that lightly. Seven seasons, no weak links, and an ending that actually earns the finale it gives itself. Go watch it.

What do you think, does Veep earn the Hall of Fame label?

Who was your favorite character, and which insult do you think should go down as the greatest of all time? Let me know in the comments.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: From Selina's vanity to Jonah's ridiculous nicknames, I break down why the disastrous cast of Veep makes it an all-time Hall of Fame comedy.

entry.title: REVIEW: Ready Or Not 2 (2026)
entry.content:
I walked out of Ready or Not 2 thinking one thing: Samara Weaving deserves a raise.

This post contains minor spoilers.

This is the sequel to Ready or Not, the 2019 horror comedy where Grace married into a family that turned her wedding night into a game of hide and seek with her as the prey. This one picks up seconds after that ends. Grace survives the Le Domas massacre, only to find out her nightmare has a bigger, richer, more organized sequel of its own. Turns out the Le Domas family answered to a whole council of elite bloodlines who worship the same guy, Mr. Le Bail, and now every one of those families wants a shot at the power Grace accidentally unlocked by surviving. She gets kidnapped along with her estranged sister Faith and dragged into round two.

What worked:

  • Samara Weaving. She plays Grace as someone who is running on fumes and pure spite at this point, and you feel every bit of that exhaustion. She doesn't play this like a franchise victory lap but like a woman who genuinely cannot believe she's back here again, and that grounds the film even when the plot gets ridiculous.
  • The kills are still creative as hell. Someone gets taken out in an industrial washing machine. A katana accident sets off a whole chain reaction of explosions because the rules of this cult are stricter than most workplaces. Elijah Wood, playing a lawyer who works for Le Bail himself, gets to just stand there watching people combust with this dry, barely amused look on his face, and that's one of the funniest running bits in the movie.

What didn't:

  • Kathryn Newton feels a bit stiff next to Weaving. Faith is supposed to be the emotional counterweight here, the sister with history and baggage, but Newton's delivery doesn't always match the intensity the scene needs. Standing next to someone as committed as Weaving makes that gap more obvious than it would be on its own.
  • Sarah Michelle Gellar deserved so much more. Ursula had real potential as a rival with her own fears about her twin brother, and there's a scene late in the film where she actually opens up about it. Then the script kills her off almost immediately after, before that thread gets to go anywhere. Feels like a waste of a good actor and a good setup.

Final rating and overall thoughts

My Rating: 7.7

This sequel had no business working as well as it does. Taking a tight, one-location premise and blowing it up into a whole council of families with ancestral rules and a "High Seat" could have collapsed into nonsense fast, but it mostly holds together, mainly because Weaving refuses to let it fall apart. Worth it if you loved the chaos and dark comedy of the first one and don't mind the world getting bigger and messier.

Did the bigger cult mythology work for you, or did you want something closer to the first film's scale?

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Grace is back, and she is angrier than ever. My quick take on Ready or Not 2 and why Samara Weaving is the only reason you need to watch.

entry.title: Michael Bay Hurt My Brain: A Transformers Breakdown
entry.content:
I posted how big things break my brain on the blog. Then someone asked about Transformers.

I realized that in all these years, I'd only ever watched the first movie from 2007. Just that one. So I told myself, let me sit down, watch all five Michael Bay films back to back, and see whether the giant robot thing would finally click for me the way the MonsterVerse did.

Verdict before I even start breaking it down: it didn't click the same way. But the marathon wasn't useless either. Let me get into it.

Transformers (2007): The one that actually works.

This one takes the crown, no argument. The story actually makes sense from start to finish, which sounds like a low bar until you watch the other four and realize how rare that is in this franchise.

Shia LaBeouf is the reason this film holds together. Sam Witwicky isn't some chiseled action hero pretending he's built for this. He's sweating, he's panicking, he's confused as hell, and that's exactly correct. If somebody told me my car could turn into a 15 foot alien robot and there's a whole war coming to wipe out the planet because of it, I wouldn't be calm either. I'd be shouting "what do you mean my car is alive" the whole movie too. LaBeouf grounds the chaos around him because he plays a normal person reacting like a normal person, and that's something the other films lost almost completely.

Megan Fox as Mikaela was fine. Not the deepest character ever written, but she wasn't a problem either. The film doesn't lean on her for much beyond "love interest who can also fix engines", and honestly that's enough for what the story needed.

The action and the CGI holds up too. You can see that, especially in the Mission City battle where the robots actually look like they're interacting with the environment around them instead of just smashing through it.

The film made over 700 million dollars worldwide on a budget of 150 million, which tells you it wasn't just me who thought this thing worked. People showed up, and people kept showing up for the sequels, even after the quality dropped off a cliff. We'll get to that.

Plot: 7.6. CGI: 9. This is the one Transformers movie I'd actually rewatch without rolling my eyes.

Revenge of the fallen (2009): Where the wheels came off.

This one is weak. Genuinely weak.

The plot is a mess. Too many threads pulling in too many directions, too much shouting, too many characters competing for screen time without earning any of it. You can tell the writers had a deadline and not a clear story. Even the action, which should be the one reliable thing in a Michael Bay movie, gets buried under the noise of everything else happening at once.

And then there's Skids and Mudflap. These two robots talk in exaggerated slang, can't read, and one of them has a gold tooth. The comic relief just lands as lazy and a little embarrassing.

The cast tried. The returning leads gave what they could, but a good cast can't save a script that doesn't know what it wants to be. The jokes are hit or miss at best, the pacing drags despite all the chaos on screen, and somehow this is also the longest film in the franchise up to that point.

What's wild is despite all that, the box office went up. This one made over 836 million dollars worldwide against a 200 million dollar budget, comfortably outgrossing the first film. Numbers don't always tell you about quality. Sometimes they just tell you people trusted the brand enough to show up anyway.

Plot: 4. CGI: 8.7, because even when the story fails the robots themselves, the effects team didn't slack.

Dark of the moon (2011): The three day watch.

This film took me three days to finish. Not because it's long, though it is, but because my brain kept tapping out halfway through.

Megan Fox is gone here, and the reason behind it is more interesting than anything in the actual movie. In a 2009 interview with Wonderland magazine, she compared Bay to Hitler, saying he wanted that kind of reputation on set and calling him a nightmare to work for. Bay later told GQ that it was actually Spielberg, the franchise's executive producer, who told him to fire her over those comments. Spielberg has since denied that this happened at all. Fox's side always maintained she chose to leave on her own. Either way, she was out, and Rosie Huntington-Whiteley stepped in to play the love interest this time around.

I'll be honest, the new girl can't act well. She's not given much to work with either, but even accounting for that, she doesn't bring the same grounding presence LaBeouf had paired with Fox in the first film.

The story itself is actually a step up from Revenge of the Fallen. There's a clearer through line involving a hidden Cybertronian ship on the moon, and the stakes feel more coherent. But the action sequences ask you to turn your brain off completely. These humans survive damage that should kill anyone several times over, falling buildings, explosions at point blank range, vehicles flipping through debris, and they just walk it off. At some point I genuinely started laughing at the movie.

The film made over 1.1 billion dollars worldwide, making it the highest grossing entry in the entire series. The CGI, as always with this franchise, holds up. Smooth, detailed, impressive in motion.

Plot: 5.9. CGI: 8.8.

Age of extinction (2014): New cast, same problems.

Total reset on the human side. New lead, new daughter, new businessman villain figure. None of the original human cast returns for this one, fresh start across the board.

Mark Wahlberg doesn't work for me here. He's trying a little too hard to be the cool, capable lead, and it just doesn't click. He feels like he's performing confidence rather than actually carrying it.

Then there's the storyline with his daughter Tessa and her secret boyfriend Shane. When Wahlberg's character finds out about the relationship and threatens to call the police, Shane pulls out an actual citation, claiming the relationship is protected under what the film calls a Romeo and Juliet law, since Tessa was 17 when it started and he was barely over the line himself. It's framed as a joke between him and the dad but I found it deeply uncomfortable, and the actor for Shane, Jack Reynor, later told the Hollywood Reporter that looking back, especially in the years since the Me Too movement gained ground, it's definitely a problematic joke, even though he wasn't the one who wrote it. That's not me being overly sensitive, that's the actor himself looking back and going "Yeah, that wasn't great."

By this point in the marathon I had fully stopped trying to find logic in the bigger plot too. Why is there suddenly a tech company building its own Transformers from scratch. Why are the Dinobots a thing now, dinosaur robots locked away by a bounty hunter from space. None of it connects to anything that came before in any satisfying way, it just exists because the franchise needed something new to sell.

That said, the story does feel more deliberate than Dark of the Moon, even if it's introducing concepts with no real foundation. This one also crossed 1.1 billion dollars worldwide, so clearly none of my complaints mattered to the box office.

Plot: 6.4. CGI: 9, still rock solid.

The last knight (2017): Whatever this was.

By this film, it felt like the team just did whatever they wanted with no real plan to tie it together. We've got King Arthur, Merlin, ancient Transformer knights, and a Cybertronian goddess who brainwashes Optimus Prime into an actual villain. There's also a historian character who apparently knows the secret history connecting all of it.

I'm typing this and I'm already struggling to remember the actual plot mechanics, and I watched it days ago. That tells you something. I was just relieved when it ended.

The CGI though, is excellent here. Whatever else this film gets wrong, the visual craft on the robots themselves is some of the best in the series. The final battle, unfortunately, is exactly where my biggest complaint about the whole franchise comes into full focus, I'll get into that soon.

This was also the point where the box office finally cracked. The film opened to a franchise low domestic debut and finished around 600 million dollars worldwide, well below Age of Extinction's billion dollar haul. A sign that audiences were getting tired of the formula.

Plot: 5.8. CGI: 8.9.

The action problem nobody talks about enough.

Here's my real issue across all five films, and it's not really about plot. Michael Bay's editing style, his lighting choices, and the overcomplicated robot designs combine to make the action hard to follow. The robots have so many moving panels and overlapping metal pieces that during a fight, you can lose track of which limb belongs to which character. Add in Bay's fast cuts and his preference for tight, chaotic framing during big battles, and a lot of these sequences become a blur of metal and sparks rather than something you can actually track beat by beat. It's less about whether you can technically see the screen and more about whether your brain can process what's happening on it fast enough.

The first film handles this slightly better just because the pacing gives you more room to register what's going on. The sequels speed everything up and throw more robots into frame at once, and that clarity gets harder to hold onto.

Overall: Did this finally make me a Transformers person.

Short answer, no. Not the way the MonsterVerse movies did, not the way Attack on Titan did. These films did their job as blockbuster entertainment, and I don't regret the marathon, but I never reached that point of being fully invested.

Part of it is scale. I like Optimus Prime, I like Bumblebee, there's a real charm to these robots across the series. But size wise, they just don't hit the level I want from giant robot media. I'm talking Pacific Rim kaiju scale, Attack on Titan colossal titan scale. Transformers robots don't feel big in a "this thing could swallow a city block" way, and that difference matters more to my enjoyment than I expected going in.

Still, not a bad watch overall. The first film earns its reputation. The rest range from fine to forgettable, with Revenge of the Fallen being the clear low point for reasons that go beyond just plot quality.

What about you, have you sat through all five of these, and did any of them actually convert you into a fan?

Or did you also stop at one and never look back. Drop your verdict in the comments.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Watched all five Michael Bay Transformers movies back to back. Here's a full breakdown of what works, what doesn't, and why it never fully clicked.

entry.title: The Tropes That Make Me Turn Off the TV.
entry.content:
We all have a list of movies we love, but I think the list of movies we refuse to watch is just as revealing.

I think of entertainment as an escape. When I sit down to watch something, I am choosing to step outside of the real world for a while. So the last thing I want is to spend hours inside a story that mirrors the worst and most exhausting parts of reality, just packaged with better cinematography and a soundtrack.

There are themes and genres I avoid completely, no matter how many people tell me I am missing out. Awards, critical praise, word-of-mouth recommendations, none of that is enough to make me sit through something that I know will leave me feeling worse than before I pressed play. That applies to movies and TV shows equally.

Protecting My Peace

There is a category of film and television that some people call important and I understand the argument. Representation matters, telling difficult stories has value, but there is a difference between a story that challenges you and a story that just grinds you down. Some content exists almost entirely to immerse you in suffering, often the suffering of people who look like me, with very little payoff beyond the reminder that the world can be brutal. I have heard that described as trauma porn and I think that label fits.

That is why I stay away from anything centered on slavery or heavy, systemic racism. A film like 12 Years a Slave is exactly what I will never watch. I've heard it is considered a masterpiece. But I also know what it will cost me emotionally to sit through it, and I have made a deliberate choice not to pay that price. The same goes for stories about systemic violence, police brutality, racially motivated killings, and that whole world.

What bothers me most about this category is how it gets framed as a civic duty. People will tell you that you owe it to yourself to watch these things, as if choosing not to relive horror in your leisure time is the same as being ignorant of it. That logic does not hold up for me. I am already aware of what these stories depict. I live in a world where those realities exist. Watching a two-hour dramatization of them does not make me more informed or more empathetic.

Given the choice between a supernatural thriller and a historically grounded story about oppression and dehumanization, I will take the supernatural thriller every single time. Give me something strange, clever, something that takes me somewhere I have never been. That is what I am sitting down for.

Grit vs. Intellectual Stakes

Gang violence and the drug trade fall into the same category for me. These are stories I actively avoid, no matter how well they are made. People tell me constantly to watch Top Boy. They tell me Snowfall is one of the best shows on television. I believe them. I also have no plans to watch either. We Own This City is on that same list. The reason is simple: corrupt cops are just another gang. The uniform is different but the cycle is the same: territory, power, violence, consequences, repeat. I do not find that cycle interesting to watch.

What I notice about most of these shows is that the drama comes from escalation. Someone makes a bad decision, things get violent, the walls close in, and the characters are trapped inside a world with very few exits. The "grit" is the whole point. But grit, to me, is not the same as tension or intelligence. It is just rawness for its own sake. After a while, it all blurs together, different cities, different characters, same cycle. The show ends, nothing has really changed in your understanding of the world, and you have just spent hours watching people hurt each other inside a system designed to make sure they keep hurting each other.

Breaking Bad is one I respect deeply, and I think it works for a different reason. Yes, it involves the drug trade, which is usually something I avoid, but the core of that show is not really about drugs. It is about transformation; the precise, almost surgical study of how a person dismantles their own identity and rebuilds themselves into something darker. The drug trade is just the setting.

The Isekai, Fanservice, and Harassment Problem

Let me be clear: I am not anti-anime. Some of the most creative, ambitious storytelling I have encountered has come from anime. The medium is capable of doing things that live-action simply cannot, in terms of world-building, visual imagination, and the sheer scale of ideas it can put on screen. But over the years, I have watched my patience with a large portion of the medium quietly disappear, and I have had to be honest with myself about why.

The first dealbreaker for me is the Isekai genre. Specifically the reincarnation-into-another-world formula. A person from our world dies or gets transported, and wakes up in a fantasy world, usually with some kind of special power or knowledge that gives them an edge. There is real potential in that setup, the problem is that most of these shows do not actually care about the premise. They care about the destination: a power fantasy wrapped around a harem.  

Mushoku Tensei: Jobless Reincarnation is a perfect example of exactly this. The show builds an elaborate fantasy world, and then uses all of that as a backdrop for a protagonist who is, at his core, a lecherous adult in a child's body. The "reincarnation" is not a storytelling device. It is a reset button that lets the writers remove all accountability from a character while still giving him everything he wants. Once you see that pattern, you cannot unsee it. 

The whole genre has collapsed, for me, into a single predictable shape: mysterious arrival, instant special status, growing collection of female characters who exist to orbit the protagonist. I stopped giving these shows the benefit of the doubt a long time ago.

The second issue is unnecessary fanservice, and I want to be specific about what I mean, because I think the word gets used loosely. I am talking about scenes that exist purely to be provocative, that have no connection to the story, and that actively break the tone the show has worked to establish. Fire Force is the clearest example I can give. That show has impressive animation, an interesting premise, and real moments of dramatic weight. It also keeps stopping to insert scenes of a female character being groped or leered at, and it's played entirely for laughs. It is jarring every single time. You are in the middle of something that is actually working, and then the show reminds you that it does not entirely respect your attention or its own momentum. The animation quality makes it worse, because it means the people making this clearly had the skill to do something more interesting with those scenes, and chose not to.

The third issue is "comedy" that is really just harassment with a laugh track. The Seven Deadly Sins built this problem directly into its central character. Meliodas repeatedly gropes Elizabeth throughout the series and it's presented as a quirk, a personality trait, something endearing about his character, but it's not. That pattern of behavior, in any other context, would make this character a villain. The fact that the show frames it as a joke does not make it funny, it just makes the show lazy and uncomfortable to watch. And I have run out of patience for it.

What all three of these problems have in common is a lack of respect: for the audience, for the female characters in the story, and for the story itself. Anime can be extraordinary. But when it leans on these patterns as a crutch, it's just noise with good production values.

The Technical War Exception

War films are another genre I keep at arm's length. Most of them follow a recognizable shape: a group of soldiers, an impossible mission, heroism, sacrifice, and a lot of very loud noise. The action is big and the emotions are broad, and by the end you have witnessed a lot of destruction. I find the spectacle empty.

But I have two exceptions, and they are worth explaining because they reveal exactly what I am looking for even in a genre I generally avoid.

1. Dunkirk: This works for me because Christopher Nolan approached it as a technical puzzle before he approached it as a war story. The film is built around three timelines, one hour on the beach, one day on the water, one week in the air, that are running simultaneously and converging on the same event. The experience of watching it is almost architectural. You are not just watching soldiers try to survive, you are watching a director control time and space in an unusually precise way. Most war films want you to feel something, Dunkirk wants you to experience something.

2. 1917: This is the other exception, and it belongs on this list for a similar reason. Sam Mendes and his cinematographer Roger Deakins shot the film to look like a single, unbroken take. Whether you know the technical details or not, you feel the effect immediately, there are no cuts to give you breathing room, you are locked in, moving through the landscape in real time alongside the characters. And the result is something entirely different from anything else in the genre.

What both films share is that they lead with a cinematic idea, a specific, deliberate answer to the question: "How should this story be told?" Most war movies never ask that question. They just assemble the familiar pieces: the squad, the mission, the sacrifice, and point a camera at them. Dunkirk and 1917 are built differently.

What are your "hard pass" genres?

Are there certain types of movies or shows you refuse to watch, even if they are popular or well-reviewed? I am curious whether other people have thought this through as deliberately as I have. Let me know in the comments. I would like to see how many people have a list like mine.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Awards and hype don't matter if the story grinds you down. Here is my "hard pass" list and why I choose to be deliberate about what I watch.

entry.title: RECAP: Elite Season 1
entry.content:
Elite is what happens when you throw three broke kids into a school built entirely on money and secrets. It's messy, it's soapy, and I could not stop watching.

This post contains spoilers for Season 1 of Netflix's Elite.

How it kicks off

Samuel, Nadia, and Christian walk into Las Encinas as outsiders on day one. Their old school, San Esteban, had its roof cave in, and the construction company behind the shoddy job, run by Teo and Ventura, both of whom have kids enrolled at Las Encinas, hands out scholarships as a PR move to make the whole thing look less bad.
