She finds her own way out of it, choosing to go to New York alone rather than live a lie, a decision that comes right after a raw, blistering monologue to her parents about no longer being the daughter they think she is.

By the time graduation approaches, nearly everyone's paying for something. Samuel, Guzman, Valerio, and Rebeka all get expelled over the drug fallout, and the group splinters over who's to blame, with Polo suspected but never confirmed as the one who reported it. Guzman, worn down, admits to Samuel that he's done hating Polo entirely, since hating him clearly hasn't changed anything and Polo seems happier than either of them regardless. Ander, meanwhile, tells his mother that he doesn't have long left and refuses to spend what time remains studying for exams he may not live to take.

At the graduation ceremony itself, everything that's been simmering boils over fast. Yeray forces Teo's hand and installs Carla in charge of the family business as a condition of funding, finally giving her some real power in a life defined by other people controlling her. Polo ends things with Cayetana for good, telling her she never loved him, just the life he could give her. Lu and Nadia win the scholarship together on stage, only for Lu to go off script mid-speech and tear into Polo and his family in front of the entire school, which gets the scholarship pulled entirely by his humiliated mother. Samuel learns the deal he made with police to help Nano was a setup from the start, and that giving up Sandra's location actually got Nano arrested rather than cleared. And that night, over dinner, Polo finally tells his parents the truth: he killed Marina, and he wants it made right by getting Nadia and Lu's scholarship reinstated.

The graduation party that follows brings a strange, quiet peace to a few corners of the group, Guzman and Nadia finding their way back to each other for whatever time they have left, Ander and Omar sharing one last real goodbye before Omar leaves for New York. It's the last calm moment before the body hits the dance floor.

How it all wraps up

Polo shows up to graduation for one reason: he wants the trophy from Cayetana so he can turn himself in. She refuses, and when he demands to know if she's the one who quietly sabotaged his chance to transfer abroad, she admits it, telling him it was because she loves him and couldn't let him go. Before he can process that, Lu storms up drunk and throws a drink in his face, blaming him for wrecking her life. He tries to tell her the scholarship's being reinstated. She's past listening.

The night keeps sliding sideways. Omar refuses to even hand Polo a napkin at the bar. Samuel, drunk and spiraling, spots a knife left behind and moves toward Polo with real intent before Guzman physically pulls him off. Lu, still furious, grabs a champagne bottle from Valerio and jokes to Nadia about smashing it over Polo's head. Samuel even asks Rebeka to have someone rough Polo up. She says no.

Guzman intercepts Polo again near Lu and Nadia, telling him to leave before he gets hurt worse than last time. Polo asks, one more time, if Guzman could ever forgive him once he confesses. Guzman tells him that he never will. In the middle of that exchange, Lu drops her champagne bottle and it shatters, and while everyone's distracted picking up the pieces, the broken neck of it gets kicked out of sight across the floor.

Lu follows Polo into the bathroom now holding that broken bottle neck. She unloads on him, blaming him for everything he's taken from her and from Guzman by killing Marina. Polo lashes back with something cruel, echoing almost exactly what he once said to Marina right before he killed her. Lu snaps. She pins him against the wall, and the bottle in her hand goes into his chest. She's horrified the second it happens, pulling it out and begging him to know she didn't mean it. He tells her he knows. It doesn't stop her from falling apart.

Polo stumbles out bleeding, trying to reach Guzman, but slips and hits a cracked glass barrier that gives way under him. He falls straight through to the dance floor below. Guzman sees it happen and sprints down after him, and Carla, seeing the whole thing, quietly pockets the bottle neck to protect Lu before anyone else notices. By the time Guzman reaches him, there's nothing left to do but hold his hand. He tells Polo he forgives him, the one thing Polo begged for all night and never got, and Polo dies holding onto that.

What follows is the group closing ranks. Carla pulls Samuel aside and tells him the truth: Lu did it, by accident. Nobody argues that Lu deserves to pay for it. Valerio points out that everyone already saw her throw a drink at Polo earlier, so no one's going to believe an accident story anyway. So they get to work covering it up together: passing the bottle neck around so everyone's fingerprints are on it, staging the scene to look like suicide, even letting Cayetana, playing grieving girlfriend, get close enough to press Polo's fingers to the weapon herself. She cuts her own hand doing it and doesn't say a word before tossing the bottle onto the dance floor for the police to find.

When the police start questioning everyone, Guzman comes up with the plan that saves them: everyone claims they saw a different person follow Polo into the bathroom. Samuel names Valerio. Valerio names Cayetana. Cayetana names Ander. Ander names Guzman. Guzman names Omar. Omar, of all people, names his own sister. Nadia names Carla. Carla names Rebeka. Rebeka names Lu. Every statement cancels out the next, and the whole timeline turns to static.

In the middle of it, Ander tells Omar the lie about seeing someone else was just that, a lie, meant to push him away so Omar wouldn't have to watch him die. Omar doesn't forgive it easily. He tells Ander he got exactly what he wanted and walks out. Lu, meanwhile, nearly breaks in her own interview, on the verge of confessing everything, until the Inspector needles her about not really being Polo's friend. That's the thing that finally holds her together. She tells the Inspector, through tears, that whatever else was true, Polo was her friend, that all of them were, messy and broken as that family is.

By morning, some things settle. Guzman and Nadia finally kiss, done pretending they don't want each other. Samuel and Carla share a last kiss on the cheek before she leaves to study abroad. Omar leaves with Malick, Ander left standing alone. Rebeka goes home and tells her mother she's done with the drug business for good.

At the station, the case quietly resolves itself when Polo's own parents hand over the real murder weapon, the trophy he used to kill Marina, and lie to the Inspector, claiming Polo confessed before he died rather than let the investigation reopen and risk the truth about Lu coming out. At his funeral, Cayetana turns down his parents' offer to pay for her education, telling them she's done pretending to be something she's not. Carla hands the family winery over to Valerio to run while she's away.

Time passes. Nadia and Omar are about to board a flight to New York when Omar realizes at the last second he can't actually leave Ander behind, and turns back for the hospital instead, arriving just in time to learn Ander's cancer is in remission. Omar's father, finally coming around, refers to Ander as his son's boyfriend without flinching. Lu, cut off by her own parents for good, is quietly taken in by Nadia's family instead. Guzman leaves Nadia a voicemail promising to wait for her.

Two months later, most of them walk back into Las Encinas for one final year: Samuel, Guzman, Rebeka, Omar, Ander. Cayetana isn't among them as a student anymore. She's the school's new janitor, mopping the same halls she once faked her way through.

What worked

Former enemies who chose each other. In the middle of all that mess, the writers actually got two things right this season: the friendship between Nadia and Lu, and the one between Samuel and Guzman. Think about where Samuel and Guzman started, Guzman actively making Samuel's life miserable, treating him like an outsider who had no business being at Las Encinas. Then Marina died, Nano went to prison for something he didn't do, and something shifted. Two people with every reason to hate each other became each other's most reliable allies, a friendship built on shared stubbornness and surviving something awful together. It's one of the few things holding the season up when everything else is falling apart, because it wasn't built on attraction or strategy. It was built on grief and mutual respect. Nadia and Lu land somewhere similar. Two characters who spent two seasons tearing each other apart over the same scholarship, the same boy, the same need to be the best in the room, finally choosing each other once they see how they'd both been held back by the same toxic people and the same exhausting expectations.

The cover-up. For the first time, instead of protecting themselves at each other's expense, the whole group chose to stand together. These people spent three seasons at each other's throats, betrayal after betrayal, cover-up after cover-up, everyone protecting themselves first. And in that moment they finally chose each other instead. It was the only time their bond felt completely real and unforced, and it was the perfect way to close out this chapter of the show.

A couple of smaller notes: the throuple situation with Cayetana, Polo, and Valerio had its moments, three outcasts finding comfort in each other is a compelling idea, and the show almost pulls it off. And Polo at Las Encinas this season is the saddest the show has ever made a character look, which is remarkable given that he's a murderer. That tension, between what he did and what he became afterward, ends up being one of the most interesting things about the whole season.

What didn't

Two new faces, zero reasons to care. Neither new addition this season was worth the screen time. Malick showed up, dated Nadia as a cover, and then started something with Omar behind her back. He wasn't really a character so much as a plot device with a face, someone the writers dropped in specifically to blow up the one relationship in this show that actually deserved better. That's his whole personality. Yeray was somehow even more pointless. His entire purpose was to buy Carla's affection on her father's behalf. He was a rich guy with a name, and the show didn't even bother pretending otherwise.

What they did to Carla was unforgivable. Carla spent two full seasons being the most calculating, self-possessed person in any room she walked into. She managed an entire murder cover-up in real time in the Season 1 finale, ran circles around everyone including Samuel, and kept Polo from completely falling apart while doing it. She was dangerous and controlled and compelling to watch. Then Season 3 handed her a controlling father, a transaction dressed up as a boyfriend, and a pill bottle, and called it a character arc. Watching her get reduced to a business arrangement by her own father, essentially sold off to maintain a family alliance, was depressing. The Ice Queen, the woman who spent two seasons playing chess with everyone's feelings, reduced to a passenger in her own life. What makes it worse is her arc this season doesn't feel tragic in any meaningful way. It just feels like the writers ran out of ideas for her and stripped away everything that made her interesting. Carla deserved a much better send-off than a plane ticket and a vague sense of freedom.

Drama for the sake of drama. I can't get over what the writers did to Omar and Ander this season. After everything these two survived in Seasons 1 and 2, watching them get dragged through a cheating storyline with no real payoff and no real point was just painful. Clearly the writers had no idea how to write a couple supporting each other through something hard, so they went for the cheapest conflict available instead. Omander were the emotional core of this show for two full seasons, the warmth they brought to a story that's otherwise very cold about human nature. Treating them like a disposable plot point, manufacturing drama just to create tension in an already overcrowded season, felt like a betrayal of everything the first two seasons built. The show eventually walks it back and lets them find their way to each other, but the damage was already done.

Overall thoughts

Looking back, the Season 3 finale really does feel like the natural conclusion to the story Elite started with. Marina's death finally got real closure. Most of the main cast actually grew as people. The last scene at the school played like a goodbye to an era, and the collective cover-up in the finale, the first time these people ever truly chose each other over themselves, paid off three seasons of watching people betray each other in one quiet, coordinated act of loyalty.

I'm currently watching Season 4, and a big part of me thinks the show should've stopped at Season 3. When you have a cast with this much chemistry and a central mystery that kept you hooked for three seasons, it's almost impossible to recreate that energy once you start swapping people out. Elite was always a three-season story. The original mystery begins with a murder Polo committed and ends with his death. Everything in Season 4 so far doesn't look so good.

My Rating: 7.4

What did you think of the season?

Drop your take in the comments. I also want to know if the collective cover-up in the finale made you emotional or if you saw it coming from a mile away.

entry.title: Melissa McCarthy Deserves Way More Credit
entry.content:
She's also one of the few comedic actors alive who can turn around and gut you in a dramatic role without it feeling fake.

Today's Spotlight is about why that mix is so rare, and why nobody's giving her enough credit for it these days.

She Has No Off Switch

McCarthy's whole thing is commitment with zero safety net. She doesn't do the safe, controlled version of a joke where you can tell she's holding back just in case it flops. She goes all the way in, physically and vocally, and dares you not to laugh. Watch her in Bridesmaids doing that unhinged airplane meltdown, or eating a stick of butter like it's a damn snack, and you'll notice she never winks at the camera. She's not performing "look how funny I'm being." She's just fully in the moment, chaos and all, and that total lack of self-consciousness is exactly what makes her impossible to look away from.

There's warmth under all that noise too. Even when she's playing someone crude or a little terrifying, there's a real person in there you end up rooting for. That's a harder trick than people give her credit for. Plenty of comedians can do loud. Not many can do loud and still make you care what happens to them.

She Put In The Work First

McCarthy didn't just fall into this out of nowhere. She started out doing stand-up in New York, grinding through rooms at Stand Up New York and The Improv, and sharpened her improv chops at The Groundlings in LA alongside people like her now husband, Ben Falcone. That background matters. It's why her comedy always feels lived-in instead of scripted at you. She spent years as a working actress before most people even knew her name, playing Sookie on Gilmore Girls for seven seasons and Dena on Samantha Who? before Mike & Molly finally made her a network lead and won her a Primetime Emmy. Then Bridesmaids hit in 2011 and blew the whole thing wide open, landing her a BAFTA nomination and a Screen Actors Guild nomination for a role that could have easily gotten swallowed up by a stacked cast.

What she did after that is the interesting part. Instead of chasing one lane like a lot of actors do once they finally break through, she built a body of work with Falcone through their production company, On the Day Productions, that let her write and produce her own comedic voice in movies like Tammy and The Boss instead of waiting around for someone else to hand her the right script. She stacked that alongside studio comedies like Identity Thief and The Heat, action comedy in Spy, a swing at a legacy franchise with Ghostbusters, a hard left turn into crime drama with The Kitchen, and then a full pivot into prestige territory with Can You Ever Forgive Me? That's not someone playing it safe in one corner of the industry. That's someone actively testing every edge of what she's allowed to do on screen, on her own terms, often enough that it clearly wasn't an accident.

It also helps to remember how much of her early career happened in small, easy to miss roles before Bridesmaids made her a household name. She popped up in stuff like The Nines, The Back-up Plan, and Life as We Know It, quietly stacking reps while most of the industry wasn't paying her any attention at all. When the breakout finally came, it didn't come out of nowhere. It came from someone who'd already put in over a decade of work in the trenches.

Funny Doesn't Mean Shallow

This is where McCarthy actually separates herself from most comedic actors of her generation. Spy is the clearest example of range hiding in plain sight. She plays Susan Cooper as a mousy, overlooked CIA analyst stuck behind a desk, and you watch her physically transform into someone actually dangerous over the course of the movie without ever losing the character's insecurity underneath. It's broad, it's loud, and underneath all that noise it's also a tightly controlled performance with a real arc running through it.

Then there's Can You Ever Forgive Me?, where she plays real-life literary forger Lee Israel, a bitter, isolated, kind of insufferable woman, and somehow makes you understand her without softening a single rough edge. No jokes to hide behind. No physical comedy to lean on. Just a quiet, wounded performance that got her an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress, her second nomination overall and her first in a lead category. Put that next to Tammy, where she's doing broad, messy, borderline slapstick comedy as a woman having the worst week of her life on a road trip with her grandmother, and you start to see the actual range. She's not just a chameleon disappearing into roles. She commits so hard to whatever the material needs, comedy or drama, that the commitment itself is the range.

Even in something like The Boss, where the material's thinner and the jokes don't always connect, she treats the character (a disgraced business tycoon with zero self-awareness, dumped out of prison and forced to rebuild her empire from a suburban living room) like there's real psychology underneath the ridiculousness. Same with Tammy, a movie critics were pretty mixed on, but one that gave McCarthy room to write a woman falling apart in real time. Fired from her job, cheated on, dragging her grandmother along on a disaster of a road trip, and she still finds moments of real sadness buried in the mess. That's the difference between an actor coasting on a persona and one who's actually building a person every single time, even when the script isn't doing her any favors.

Why Isn't She Getting Her Flowers

Here's what pisses me off. McCarthy has two Academy Award nominations, two Primetime Emmy Awards, and a stack of box office hits most actors would kill for, and she still doesn't get talked about with the same respect as her peers when people list off the great comedic actors of this era. Part of that is the industry's tired old habit of treating physical comedy as lesser than dry wit, especially when it's a woman doing it.

Part of it is also just how much bad press followed her career at every turn. From the manufactured "women aren't funny" nonsense that got thrown at Bridesmaids, to the actively ugly, coordinated backlash campaign against the 2016 Ghostbusters reboot before most people had even seen the damn thing. None of that had anything to do with her actual work, and yet it somehow drowned out conversations about how good she is on screen. She's been doing career-best work for over a decade now and still keeps getting filed under "that funny lady from the movies" instead of getting real credit as one of the most versatile performers working today.

The Moment She Stole The Whole Movie

Trying to pick just one scene stealer moment for McCarthy is basically impossible, and that's kind of the whole point of this section. She's built an entire career out of walking into someone else's movie and leaving with it stuffed in her back pocket. But if I had to name the moment that made me sit up and go "oh, she's about to be everywhere," it's the bathroom scene in Bridesmaids, where the whole wedding party gets food poisoning inside a bridal shop. McCarthy's Megan barely gets any dialogue in that whole sequence and still walks away the most memorable person in the room, purely off physical commitment to the chaos of it.

Her underrated work deserves a shoutout here too. In The Kitchen, she plays Kathy Brennan, a mob wife in 1970s Hell's Kitchen who starts out as the most reluctant of the three lead women and ends up the most ruthless once she gets a taste of running things herself. The movie landed with mostly negative reviews and a rough opening weekend, and even the critics who trashed it still singled her performance out. Variety flat out called her performance fierce while ripping the script apart around her. That's the McCarthy pattern with her misses: the movie can fall apart, and she's usually still the one holding it together on screen.

Her SNL Takeover

I can't talk about McCarthy and skip her SNL work, because that's some of the funniest shit she's ever done, full stop. She's hosted the show a handful of times since 2011, and every single time she picked up an Emmy nomination for it, finally winning in 2017. That's not a fluke. That's someone who understands sketch comedy on a completely different level from most film actors who show up to host, read cue cards, and leave.

The Sean Spicer sketches are the obvious highlight, and for good reason. She played then-White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer as a sweaty, unhinged mess barreling through a press conference, chasing reporters around with his podium on wheels, pulling out prop boxes to spell out his points, and at one point spraying a reporter with a literal water gun mid-rant. It's absurd, it's mean in exactly the right way, and it's built entirely on the same fearless physical commitment that makes her movie work so good. She didn't just do an impression. She turned a press briefing into a full blown chase scene and made it look easy.

And that's just one bit. She also strapped into Chris Farley's actual jacket for the SNL 40 anniversary special to pay tribute to Matt Foley, going full body into a character that wasn't even hers to begin with, and it worked because that's just how she operates. Give her a wig, a costume, and thirty seconds of screen time, and she'll find a way to make it the moment everyone's talking about on Monday morning.

TWC Recommends

  • The Entry Point: Bridesmaids (2011). This is the movie that made the whole world pay attention, and it still holds up as one of the sharpest ensemble comedies of the last fifteen years. Easiest, most rewarding place to start if you want to get the whole McCarthy effect in one sitting.
  • The Deep Cut: Can You Ever Forgive Me? (2018). Skip the jokes entirely for this one. It's quiet, prickly, and kind of sad, and it shows you exactly what McCarthy can do once she strips off the comedic armor completely. If you only know her from big loud studio comedies, this one's going to catch you off guard.

Which side of Melissa McCarthy deserves more credit: the comedic chaos or the dramatic restraint?

Drop your pick in the comments, and if there's a McCarthy performance I slept on, tell me so I can go fix that immediately.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Melissa McCarthy's been making us laugh and occasionally wrecking us for years. Time we actually talked about how good she is.

entry.title: The Justice League Animated Series is Underrated
entry.content:
I came into this completely cold. No nostalgia, no childhood memories attached. By the time I finished it, I was annoyed at myself for waiting this long.

Because this show is not great for a cartoon. It is not impressive given what it is. It is just great, full stop, by any standard you want to apply to it.

Justice League and its follow-up Justice League Unlimited are part of the DC Animated Universe, a shared animated continuity that Bruce Timm built across more than a decade starting with Batman: The Animated Series in 1992 and Superman: The Animated Series in 1996. Justice League premiered on Cartoon Network on November 17, 2001, ran for two seasons and 52 episodes, and was followed directly by Justice League Unlimited, which ran from July 2004 to May 2006 for an additional 39 episodes across three seasons. Taken together, these two shows represent the most complete and most ambitious superhero animated universe ever built, and nothing that has come since has fully matched what they pulled off.

Plot In A Nutshell

Seven of the world's most powerful heroes, Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Green Lantern, The Flash, Hawkgirl, and Martian Manhunter, form the Justice League after a global alien invasion forces them to work together for the first time. What starts as an uneasy alliance of very different personalities becomes something more: a team, and eventually a family, working to protect a world that does not always trust them. Justice League Unlimited then expands that team to over thirty heroes and raises every single stake in the process.

My Take

Justice League Season 1 and Season 2 are the SH**! Every single episode. You know how some shows have those stretches where you are just waiting for it to get good again? This show does not have those. It keeps going; arc after arc, threat after threat, and it never lets up. The stakes feel real, the characters feel real, and nothing about it feels cheap or lazy. I was glued to my screen in a way I was not expecting from a show made for Saturday morning Cartoon Network.

What makes it work is the structure. Almost every episode in the original Justice League run is a two-parter, which gives every story room to breathe. You are not getting five-minute action sequences dressed up as plots. You are getting actual storytelling; setup, escalation, character decisions that matter, consequences that carry over. The three-part episodes, the opening "Secret Origins" and the Season 2 finale "Starcrossed", use that extra room to deliver some of the biggest emotional swings in the entire run. "Starcrossed" especially is the kind of finale that recontextualizes everything you thought you knew about one of the main characters and asks you to sit with the wreckage of it. A cartoon did that.

Then Justice League Unlimited comes in and does something I genuinely did not think was possible: it makes the world even bigger without losing what made the original so special. The roster expands to over thirty heroes across the three seasons. Characters from every corner of the DC universe show up: Green Arrow, Black Canary, Huntress, Zatanna, Captain Atom, Booster Gold, the Question, Supergirl. Heroes I had never given a single thought to before this show. And I found myself invested in their individual episodes. Not sitting there waiting for Superman to show up and fix everything. Actually into it, actually caring about characters I had been introduced to twenty minutes earlier. That is a writing achievement. That is what happens when a room full of people genuinely care about what they are making and trust the audience enough to meet them halfway.

JLU Season 2 specifically goes absolutely crazy. The Cadmus arc, which runs through the season as an overarching conspiracy about government accountability and the ethics of unchecked power, is some of the most ambitious storytelling this universe ever attempted. It pays off everything the first two seasons built and then raises the ceiling again. It might be the peak of the whole thing. JLU Season 3 does not quite match it, and the finale does not give everything the sendoff it earned, but honestly everything leading up to it is so strong that the disappointment of the ending is more like a minor bruise than an actual wound.

The Characters

SUPERMAN: My favourite superhero of all time, and this show gets him so completely right that I want to send a personal thank you note to everyone involved. He is not overpowered to the point of being boring. He is not artificially nerfed every episode to create fake tension. He is just Superman: warm, strong, good, and the show lets him be all of that without making it feel corny or naive. Every time he is on screen doing what Superman does I was just sitting there thinking yes. That is him. That is exactly him.

WONDER WOMAN: She is amazing in this. Genuinely, properly amazing. Fierce, principled, and never once pushed to the side or reduced to a love interest or a background presence. She is taken seriously as a warrior, as a leader, and as someone with a fully developed perspective on the world the rest of the team does not share. She came from somewhere completely different and the show uses that difference thoughtfully rather than just as a fish-out-of-water joke. The show makes you feel exactly why the rest of the team respects her the way they do.

HAWKGIRL: This one caught me completely off guard and I need to talk about it. Before this show, I did not care about Hawkgirl. Not even a little. I had given her no thought whatsoever. Wings, mace, background character, moving on. And then Justice League Season 1 happened and she completely won me over in a way I was not remotely prepared for. She is always ready for the smoke. First into every fight, no hesitation, no drama about it, just fully committed to the chaos at all times. And then "Starcrossed" arrives and the show asks her to carry something enormous and she does. Her romance with John Stewart has real heart to it. It takes its time. It earns what it is asking you to feel. I did not expect to have feelings about Hawkgirl. She is one of my favourites now and I will not be taking questions about it.

THE FLASH: The heart of this team. Wally West's Flash is funny without being annoying, he lifts the energy of every scene he is in without undercutting the serious moments, and there is something about the way Michael Rosenbaum plays him that makes you feel like everything is going to be okay even when it really, really is not. You need that in an ensemble show. You need the person who is the glue, whose presence regulates the emotional temperature of the whole thing. The Flash is that person for Justice League the way very few characters manage to be in any team story. His episode in JLU, "The Ties That Bind", and especially the Season 2 finale, give him room to show a different side without losing what makes him who he is. He is brilliant.

MARTIAN MANHUNTER: J'onn J'onzz is a lot. He is deeply, quietly sad in a way the show leans into hard, and after a while that sadness starts to accumulate weight. He is the last of his people. He carries that loss in every single scene. I did not connect with him the way I connected with the others, but the show earns his grief. It is not decoration. It gives the team a different kind of emotional texture: a reminder that behind all the punching and the saving, some of these people are carrying things that never fully go away.

Honorable Mentions

THE QUESTION: This man shows up in a handful of JLU episodes and somehow became one of my favourite characters in the entire show. A faceless conspiracy theorist in a trench coat who is simultaneously completely unhinged and weirdly, magnetically compelling. His JLU episode "Question Authority" is one of the best single episodes in the whole run: sharp, funny, and genuinely unsettling in the way the best episodes of this show get. He deserved so much more screen time and the fact that he did not get it is actually criminal.

GREEN LANTERN (JOHN STEWART): Cool, steady, ex-marine energy. John Stewart is not flashy. He is not trying to be anyone's favourite. He just shows up, does the work, and carries himself with the kind of quiet authority that makes you trust him immediately. His dynamic with Hawkgirl is one of the best things in the original series. His arc in JLU, dealing with the weight of a specific decision he made as a soldier before the show ever started, is where the character truly opens up. A whole generation grew up with John Stewart as their Green Lantern because of this show. That is an important piece of comic book adaptation history. He is the best one.

BATMAN: He is Batman. There is no other. The show does not overuse him or make him the center of everything, which is actually exactly the right call: Batman is most effective as the person who shows up when it matters most rather than the person competing for screen time every episode. Every scene he is in lands because the show is disciplined about it.

Why It Works

This show trusts you. That is the thing. It does not talk down to you, does not wrap everything up neatly, and does not shy away from making its heroes morally complicated. There are episodes where you are not sure the Justice League made the right call. The entire Cadmus arc in JLU is built around that discomfort: a government organization that fears what happens when this much power is concentrated in one place and has no accountability to anyone. The show takes that concern seriously. It lets the heroes grapple with it and does not give them an easy answer. That is not what cartoons were supposed to do in 2004. Nobody told Bruce Timm and his writing team that, apparently.

The writing team across both shows included Dwayne McDuffie, Paul Dini, and Stan Berkowitz, writers who understood that the best superhero stories are never really about the punching. They are about who these people are when the punching stops. What they believe, what they are afraid of, what they owe each other. Justice League understood that and built every arc around it.

And then JLU takes that same foundation and proves it can scale massively without falling apart. Adding thirty-plus heroes should have been chaos. It should have been a mess of cameos and wasted potential. Instead it is one of the smartest expansions of a shared universe ever attempted in animation. The show makes you care about characters you have never heard of, in a single episode, without ever making you feel like you are watching filler.

Final Verdict

Justice League and Justice League Unlimited are the real deal. Not great for a cartoon. Not impressive given the format. Just great, by any measure, against any standard. The kind of show that makes you mad it took you this long to watch it, and then immediately makes you want to start over from the beginning. The JLU finale does not fully stick the landing and that stings a little for something this good. But everything leading up to it is so strong, so consistent, and so full of genuine craft that the ending is barely a footnote. This is a masterpiece of superhero storytelling and it belongs in the Hall of Fame without any debate whatsoever.

Go watch it. Right now. I am serious.

Who was your favourite on the team, and did JLU's massive roster surprise you with anyone you ended up loving?

Tell me in the comments, and please tell me I'm not the only one who completely underestimated Hawkgirl before this show.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: I watched Justice League (2001-2006) with no nostalgia, and it is a masterpiece. Here is why the DCAU is the gold standard for superhero animation.

entry.title: REVIEW: Better Call Saul
entry.content:
Quick Take on Better Call Saul: technically you could watch it without seeing Breaking Bad first. But I wouldn't recommend it.

Better Call Saul is a 2015 crime drama and prequel spin-off that tracks the origin story of Jimmy McGill, the small-time public defender we eventually come to know as the sleazy criminal lawyer Saul Goodman.

Just watch BB, then come straight here.

The Experience

The Highlights:

  • The performances are something else. Bob Odenkirk carries the whole thing on his shoulders and makes it look easy. Watching Jimmy slowly talk himself into every bad decision feels painfully real. And the supporting cast never lets the side down either.
  • The writing rewards your attention. The characters are built so carefully that by the end of the first season you'll already have strong opinions about all of them. It earns every moment it asks you to invest in.
  • Knowing the ending doesn't kill the tension. It actually makes it worse. You spend the whole show watching a man who could've been good choose not to be, over and over again. That's uncomfortable in the best possible way.

Fair Warning:

  • It's a slow burn and it commits to that. Classic Vince Gilligan style. If you went into Breaking Bad expecting a fast pace and got surprised, same thing is happening here. Come prepared.
  • The show loves a long, drawn-out scene. Montages, artistic b-roll, stretches of near silence. Some of it is brilliant. Some of it will test your patience. Usually both at the same time.

Final Verdict

My Rating: 8.4

I think I actually liked this more than Breaking Bad. There, I said it. Watch it if you love deep character work and storytelling that takes its time and means every second of it. Just don't go in expecting a quick ride.

Which slow burn did you enjoy more?

Drop a comment below and let me know if you think Better Call Saul actually managed to outdo Breaking Bad, or if the original is still king.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: I finally binged Better Call Saul, and I think I might prefer it over Breaking Bad. Here is my take on why this prequel is an absolute must-watch.

entry.title: Go Watch Silicon Valley Already
entry.content:
I finished Silicon Valley recently, and I honestly cannot believe it took me this long to watch it.

Six seasons, 53 episodes, and it held up almost the whole way through. Silicon Valley looks like a niche comedy on the surface, but it is doing something way sharper underneath, and it deserves a proper Hall of Fame spot. So here we are.

This post has minor spoilers for HBO's Silicon Valley, heads up.

The plot, in a nutshell

Richard Hendricks is a programmer at a massive tech company called Hooli who builds a revolutionary data compression algorithm in his spare time. His boss tries to buy it off him for 10 million dollars, but Richard turns it down, takes a smaller investment instead, and starts his own company called Pied Piper. What follows is six seasons of everything that can possibly go wrong for a company with a great product and a team of socially awkward people trying to run it.

My Take

Silicon Valley is fun from start to finish. It is stressful in the best way possible, the kind of show where you keep watching not because things are going well, but because you desperately need to see how they claw their way out of whatever mess they just made. The comedy is sharp without trying too hard, and the show is smarter about the tech industry than it looks on the surface.

My only complaint is that Seasons 3 and 4 fall into the same loop a bit too often: Pied Piper nearly dies, something saves it at the last second, they almost pivot into something totally different, that nearly collapses too, and Repeat. Once you spot the pattern it gets predictable. But the cast carries it so well that the details of each new disaster barely matter, because you are watching for the characters. And the finale, where the team destroys their own creation because the AI they built could end up causing serious global damage, hits a lot differently in 2026 than it probably did back when it aired in December 2019.

The Characters

RICHARD HENDRICKS:

Richard is brilliant at exactly one thing and pretty much useless at everything else. He panics constantly, second guesses every decision, and cannot handle confrontation without either freezing up or blowing it out of proportion. The tabs versus spaces breakup basically sums him up completely. He dumps the only girl who has ever shown interest in him over a coding formatting preference that changes literally nothing about how the software works. A genius who will torch his own life over a point of principle that only he cares about. It's frustrating and hilarious at the same time.

ERLICH BACHMAN:

He's the one character I could never fully get on board with. Played by T.J. Miller, his character is loud, self obsessed, and convinced of his own genius at all times. He owns the incubator house where most of the team lives, and inserts himself into every decision with way more confidence than usefulness. There are moments where there's a flash of insight buried under all that noise, but he was just too much for me to handle consistently. I actually enjoyed the show a lot more after he left at the end of Season 4.

BERTRAM GILFOYLE:

The best character on the show, and I am not taking questions on this one. Martin Starr plays him completely deadpan, totally unbothered by whatever disaster is unfolding around him, and somehow funnier than everyone else in the room without even trying. Gilfoyle is the most dangerous person in any low stakes situation, and it never stops being funny.

DONALD "JARED" DUNN

The strangest and most lovable character on the show, no contest. This man was clearly hurt in ways the show never fully explains, but keeps hinting at through these sudden, casual mentions of genuinely disturbing stuff from his past. Jared is also by far the most loyal person on the Pied Piper team, and most of the show's emotional moments land because of him, since he is the one character who actually cares about the people around him and not just the product.

DINESH CHUGTAI:

He is someone who is good enough to know he is not quite as talented as the people around him, which makes him constantly desperate to prove himself in ways that always backfire. On his own he is fine. Against Gilfoyle he is great. Watching the two of them go back and forth in petty one-upmanship is where Dinesh really shines, and Nanjiani's ability to play wounded pride at full volume makes every loss he takes funnier than it has any right to be.

Honorable Mentions:

NELSON "BIG HEAD" BIGHETTI:

Big Head is not very good at his job, has no real direction, and barely seems to know what his job even is at any given moment. By the finale he somehow ends up President of Stanford University. The joke is not just that he is bad at his job, it is that the tech industry sometimes reward people who happen to be in the right place at the right time, no matter what they actually contribute. There is even a real term for this, rest and vest, and Big Head might be the most accurate portrait of it TV has ever made.

GAVIN BELSON:

Hooli's CEO and he is basically a walking portrait of a tech billionaire who has been told he is a genius for so long that he has completely lost touch with reality. He's surrounded by yes-people who enable his worst ideas every step of the way, burning huge amounts of money on vanity projects and making decisions based on his ego before his actual business. He is a joke, but a very specific kind of joke that anyone who has ever worked inside a big company will recognize instantly.

Why it works

The reason Silicon Valley works so well is that Mike Judge (Creator) came at it from the perspective of someone who actually lived inside this culture and found it ridiculous. He worked at a Silicon Valley startup in 1987 and quit after three months, calling it a cult full of people who were "true believers in something" without being able to explain what that something even was. The frustration when watching extremely smart people pour themselves into goals that are either pointless or actively harmful while believing they are changing the world, is what powers every single episode.

The writers also backed all of it up with real research, talking to actual engineers from Facebook, Google, Amazon, and Dropbox to make sure the details held up. The tabs versus spaces debate, for example, came straight out of a dinner the writers had with real programmers. One writer even texted an engineer afterward just to check if the debate was real, and got back a message confirming it was, and that simply bringing it up had already started a screaming match at the bar. They put it in the show almost exactly as it happened. That level of attention to detail is what separates Silicon Valley from other tech comedies that just settle for easy jokes about hoodies and ping pong tables.

Final Verdict

Silicon Valley is sharp, funny, and smarter about the industry it is making fun of than people usually give it credit for. Sure it's not perfect: the middle seasons get a bit repetitive, and sometimes Erlich's a lot to handle. But the cast is one of the best ensembles HBO has ever put together, the finale sticks the landing, and it somehow gets more relevant with every year that passes. Hall of Fame. No question about it.

Who was your favorite character, and do you think the Hall of Fame call is earned?

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Brilliant, stressful, and disturbingly accurate. My deep dive into why Silicon Valley deserves a permanent place in your watchlist hall of fame.

entry.title: SERIES RECOMMENDATIONS: (June 06, 2026)
entry.content:
Somehow this all started with Sam Reid and ended with four shows permanently lodged in my brain.

Two of them feature him, the other two just fit the same vibe: dark, heavy, the kind of stories that sit with you for days.

Good stuff all around. None of these are ranked, just four shows that deserve way more attention than they get.

Interview with the Vampire (2022)

I found this show the way most people find their new obsessions these days, through a TikTok edit. I had never read Anne Rice's novels and had never seen the 1994 Tom Cruise film. I just saw a clip, thought "okay what is this," and pressed play.

The story follows Louis de Pointe du Lac (Jacob Anderson), a vampire who was turned in 1910s New Orleans, now recounting his entire life story to a journalist from a penthouse in Dubai. The framing keeps you constantly questioning how much of what Louis is telling is actually true. At the center of everything is his relationship with Lestat de Lioncourt, played by Sam Reid with an intensity that makes you fully understand why Louis could never just walk away. Romantic, monstrous, funny, and terrifying sometimes all in the same scene. The show also gives us Claudia (Bailey Bass in Season 1, Delainey Hayles in Season 2), a girl turned into a vampire and trapped in a child's body forever, and her arc is where things get genuinely devastating. The visuals, the score, the gothic atmosphere, all of it is exactly as lush and heavy as it should be. This show sent me straight into Sam Reid's entire filmography the moment it ended, and I have zero regrets.

What could have been better: The pacing in a couple of mid-season episodes slows down enough that you feel it, even if the payoff is worth the wait. There are also moments where the show leans so heavily into the emotional spiral between Louis and Lestat that the plot momentum stalls a little. Minor complaints, honestly, for a show that gets so much right.

Quick highlights:

  • Sam Reid as Lestat. He is the whole show. The French accent, the emotional range, the way he makes you root for someone you know you should not be rooting for. Genuinely one of THE best performances in recent prestige TV history.
  • The love story at its core. This is not a vampire show that happens to have a romance. It is a romance that uses vampirism as the framework for examining obsession, codependency, grief, and the particular agony of loving someone who is also capable of destroying you.
  • The visual and tonal commitment. Every frame feels deliberate. The New Orleans period detail, the wardrobe, the color grading. It does not cut corners on atmosphere anywhere, and it shows.

And the timing of this post could not be more perfect, because Season 3 drops tomorrow, June 7th, 2026, and I am barely holding it together. The wait has been genuinely painful and I have been rationing my rewatch energy specifically for this moment.

The Newsreader (2021)

I originally put this on as background noise during a sick day. I already knew Sam Reid could act, so I figured I would let it play while I rested and check in occasionally. That plan lasted about fifteen minutes before I was fully upright and completely locked in. I binged the entire three-season run in two days flat, sick and absolutely unbothered about it.

The Newsreader is an Australian drama series created by Michael Lucas and broadcast on ABC, premiering in August 2021. It went on to become ABC's most-watched drama of that year, ran for three seasons concluding in early 2025, and the fact that it is not talked about more globally is baffling to me.

Set in 1986, the show follows Dale Jennings (Sam Reid), an ambitious young reporter, and Helen Norville (Anna Torv), a brilliant but notoriously difficult news anchor, as they navigate the cutthroat world of a Melbourne television newsroom. The show is set against the backdrop of some of the biggest news events of the late 80s, and it uses that historical texture really well to make the newsroom setting feel alive and grounded.

What could have been better: Season 3 is the weakest of the three, and I say that as someone who loved this show enough to binge it while running a fever. It feels a little slow and repetitive compared to the tightness of the first two seasons, and there are moments where the storytelling feels like it is rushing to wrap things up rather than landing with the same care the earlier seasons had. Still watchable, but the dip is noticeable.

Quick highlights:

  • Anna Torv as Helen Norville. She is the backbone of the entire series. The way she plays a woman navigating a world designed to sideline her, without ever making Helen a simple victim or a simple hero, is something special.
  • The 1980s newsroom atmosphere. The production design and period details are meticulous without feeling like a costume drama. It feels lived in, which is exactly what a story like this needs.
  • Sam Reid before the fangs. Watching him here, all restrained charm and quiet desperation, makes his Lestat performance even more impressive in retrospect. The man has range.

Hellbound (2021)

Few shows have made me physically pound my fists on a table the way Hellbound did, and I mean that as the highest possible compliment. This South Korean supernatural horror series from director Yeon Sang-ho (Train to Busan) dropped on Netflix in November 2021 and it is so worth your time. The acting is excellent, the writing is tight, and it does not let up. Only two seasons are out so far and given that this is Netflix, I honestly have no idea if a third is coming. Fingers crossed.

The premise is simple but unsettling. Supernatural beings start appearing to ordinary people in Seoul, announcing the exact time they will die and be condemned to hell. When that moment arrives, monstrous executors show up and carry out the sentence in public. What follows is a story about how society responds to something no one has the framework to understand. Religious groups, vigilante organizations, legal systems, all of them scrambling to make sense of it. It is horror with a lot on its mind, and it handles both sides of that really well.

What could have been better: The jump in timeline between Season 1 and Season 2 can be a little disorienting at first, and some of the new characters in Season 2 take a few episodes to feel as grounded as the Season 1 cast. Also, three years between Season 1 and Season 2 is unacceptable, Netflix. Three years?! For a show this good. And six episodes per season? SIX? The release schedule alone is its own form of psychological damage, and if Season 3 gets announced and takes another three years to arrive, I will not be okay.

Quick highlights:

  • The social commentary. At its core this show is really about how people respond to fear, how religion, institutions, and group mentality all scramble to control something they do not understand.
  • The premise holds up. The rules of the world are consistent throughout and the show never cheats on them. How each character responds to those rules tells you everything about who they are.
  • Season 2 escalation. It goes to places you genuinely do not see coming. The finale in particular is the kind of ending that makes you want to go back to Season 1 immediately.

Midnight Mass (2021)

Mike Flanagan is one of those creators who takes horror seriously, and Midnight Mass is probably his best argument for why that matters.

Set on a small, isolated fishing island called Crockett Island, the story follows Riley Flynn (Zach Gilford) returning home after a prison stint, just as a mysterious and charismatic priest, Father Paul Hill (Hamish Linklater), shows up with what looks like the power to perform miracles. The community loses its mind over it, and then things go very dark very fast. At its core this is a show about faith, grief, and what people are willing to believe when they are desperate enough.

What could have been better: The vampire elements are there but the show keeps them in the background, which was honestly my biggest frustration. I kept waiting for it to dig deeper into the vampiric mythology and it never quite went there. If you are coming in expecting a traditional vampire story, just know this leans much more toward character study than horror. Still great though.

Quick highlights:

  • Hamish Linklater as Father Paul. The performance is unreal. He makes Father Paul sympathetic, terrifying, pitiable, and utterly believable all at once.
  • The slow burn payoff. Everything the show spends its early episodes building comes crashing down in its final two episodes. The patience is worth it.
  • The themes. It handles faith and community and collective belief in a way that feels honest without being preachy about it.

Which of these four have you already watched, and which one are you adding to your list first?

Drop your thoughts in the comments, especially if you have strong feelings about the Hellbound Season 3 situation, because I know I am not the only one refreshing for that renewal news.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Looking for your next binge? I’m highlighting four deep, dark, and gripping series that deserve way more attention than they currently get.

entry.title: Something Feels Off About Frieren S2
entry.content:
I finally started Frieren: Beyond Journey's End Season 2, and I really wanted to love it.

I did not. Well, not yet anyway.

I am only three episodes in so I am giving it time. But something feels different this season and I cannot fully explain it.

Season 1 caught me off guard in the best way. Yes it was slow, but it was the kind of slow that actually meant something. Every quiet scene carried weight. You felt the grief underneath everything, the loneliness, the way Frieren exists in a world where everyone she meets will eventually be gone. It was melancholic and beautiful and it stuck with you.

Season 2? I am just sitting here waiting for something to happen.

Here is what I have watched so far. The gang leaves Äußerst and heads further into the northern lands. In the first episode they stumble into an underground cave full of crystals that cancel out magic, which briefly puts Frieren and Fern in real danger. Okay, that was tense. I liked that. Then episode 2 has them rolling into some random village to polish a statue. Episode 3? Stark accidentally walks in on the girls bathing and spends the rest of the episode feeling bad about it. They also go looking for hot springs that turn out to be dried up.

I am not joking. That is where we are.

I know what this show is supposed to be. The small moments, the detours, the character bonding in between the big stuff. Season 1 did all of that too. But in Season 1 those little moments still felt like they were adding up to something. Right now Season 2 just feels like the show is wandering around with no real urgency.

And that is what scares me. Is Frieren turning into another Spy x Family?

I actually like Spy x Family. But let us be honest, that show has not had a plot in a long time. It is comfort food now. Cute characters doing cute things with no real stakes. And if Frieren goes down that road, I am going to be genuinely disappointed, because this show was supposed to be different.

The one thing I cannot complain about is the animation. It is gorgeous. Every single episode looks like a painting come to life. The backgrounds, the lighting, the little details in how characters move. Madhouse is doing their job and then some. I just wish the actual story gave me a reason to care as much as the animation does.

Maybe I am being impatient. Maybe it picks up. But right now, three episodes in, something feels off.

Tell me I am wrong in the comments.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Three episodes into Frieren Season 2 and I’m concerned. Is it turning into aimless comfort food, or am I just being impatient? My early thoughts.

entry.title: REVIEW: Supergirl (2026)
entry.content:
It's not the disaster people online made it out to be, and it's not a masterpiece either.

Supergirl hit theaters on June 26, 2026, directed by Craig Gillespie and written by Ana Nogueira, with James Gunn and Peter Safran producing under DC Studios. It's the second film in the new DC Universe, landing about a year after Superman, and it's based on the Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow comic by Tom King and Bilquis Evely. Milly Alcock takes over as Kara Zor-El here, after her brief cameo at the end of last year's Superman, and this is her first real outing as the character.

The story opens with Kara traveling the galaxy with Krypto for her 23rd birthday, planet hopping under red suns so she can feel human for a while instead of carrying Kryptonian strength everywhere she goes. That gets derailed when she crosses paths with Ruthye Marye Knoll, a young alien girl whose father was murdered by a mercenary named Krem of the Yellow Hills, played by Matthias Schoenaerts. Ruthye wants revenge, and Kara gets pulled into the hunt with her.

I won't lie, I was a little skeptical to watch it. The Twitter discourse around this one was brutal from the start, and then it got pushed to digital barely a month after leaving theaters, which never says confidence from a studio. So I braced for something rough but it never came. It was just average, which might be the hardest spot for a movie to land because nobody wants to defend "fine."

The Highlights

  • Milly Alcock as Kara. I'm already a fan of hers from House of the Dragon, so I'll own that bias, but she commits to this role. This version is written with more edge than past takes, someone shaped by watching Krypton die before she ever reached Earth, and Alcock handles that weight well without turning her into a joyless brick. There's still humor and warmth under it, just layered under something heavier.
  • The premise. A revenge road trip across the galaxy with a grieving kid gives the movie a clear emotional core instead of the usual save-the-world plot, and it puts Kara through a more personal kind of test than most origin stories bother with.
  • Krem as the villain. Schoenaerts plays him as a straight up menace the whole way through, no last minute redemption arc, no sympathetic backstory to soften him. He's bad news from start to finish, and that consistency makes him land harder than a lot of recent superhero villains who get watered down halfway in.

Fair Warning

  • The soundtrack. This is the biggest letdown, and it caught me off guard given how strong the music has been in Gunn's other DC and Marvel work. This one just doesn't have that same spark. Nothing in the score stuck with me walking out.
  • Lobo feels underused. Jason Momoa's Lobo was a bigger miss than I expected going in. He's got the biker look down, the teaser they dropped before release looked great, but in the actual film he just kind of exists in scenes without doing much. For a character built on chaos and presence, that's a rough outcome.
  • The action and CGI. Nothing embarrassing, they get the job done, but nothing here is making anyone's list of best superhero fight scenes. Decent is the word, not more than that.

Final Verdict

My Rating: 6.8

It's a shame this one bombed the way it did, because it didn't deserve the pile-on it got. The box office numbers were bad, reviews were mixed to negative, and Alcock personally took a lot of heat online that had nothing to do with her actual performance. A lot of that heat was about things completely separate from the movie itself, which says more about where the internet is right now than it does about Supergirl. Feels like everything gets torn apart these days regardless of what it actually is. If you skipped this because of the discourse, it's worth a watch now that it's on digital. Go in expecting a solid, average superhero movie carried by a strong lead performance and a villain who does his job well, not a disaster and not a triumph. Just a movie.

Did the online backlash change how you went into this one, or did you watch it with an open mind?

Drop your take below, curious if anyone else came away thinking it got treated worse than it deserved.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A review of DC's Supergirl (2026). Was it really as bad as the online backlash claimed?

entry.title: Keanu Reeves Is So Likable
entry.content:
Keanu Reeves is not, by any technical measure, a great actor. And somehow none of that matters.

The man's been doing this since 1986 and he still delivers some lines like he's reading them off a cue card for the first time. And yet he's one of the most lovable people to ever exist on a movie screen. That contradiction is basically the whole point of today's post.

So, Who Is Keanu?

Keanu Charles Reeves was born in Beirut in 1964, bounced around Sydney, New York, and eventually Toronto as a kid, and dropped out of high school to chase acting instead of finishing his education. He broke through as Ted in Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure in 1989, became an action star with Speed in 1994, hit full cultural icon status with The Matrix in 1999, and then spent a chunk of the 2000s and early 2010s doing fine but totally forgettable work in movies nobody talks about anymore. Then John Wick happened in 2014 and rebuilt his whole career from scratch. That's the arc we're getting into today: a guy with genuinely limited range who keeps landing in stuff that works anyway, mostly because audiences just adore him as a person.

Why We're All Obsessed With Him

Here's the thing about Keanu's screen presence: it's not really about technique. He doesn't have the vocal control of an Anthony Hopkins or the chameleon physicality of a Christian Bale. What he's got is sincerity. When Keanu looks sad on screen, you believe it, because the guy seems physically incapable of faking an emotion well enough to hide that he's faking it. That earnestness reads as real even when the performance itself is stiff. Add in the soft voice, the slightly awkward delivery, and those puppy dog eyes, and you get someone who feels approachable in a way most A-list actors don't even try to be. He's not performing charisma. He's just existing, and people fall for it anyway.

His Taste In Projects Is All Over The Place

If you map out Keanu's career choices, they're kind of all over the place. He'll do a massive action franchise, then jump into something tiny and weird like A Scanner Darkly, then voice a toy cowboy stuntman in Toy Story 4, then play a video game character in Cyberpunk 2077, then show up as himself in a Netflix rom-com. There's no master plan here, nothing that looks like an Oscar campaign someone carefully built. It feels like he just says yes to whatever sounds fun or interesting to him, box office logic be damned. He turned down a Speed sequel at the height of his action stardom because he didn't believe in the story. That's not someone managing a career. That's someone following his gut, for better or worse.

Range Vs Just Showing Up And Trying Hard

Time to be real here: Keanu is not a chameleon. He's basically playing some version of the same gentle, slightly melancholic guy whether he's an assassin, an exorcist, or a teenage slacker. What he does bring, though, is full commitment to whatever the role needs physically and emotionally, even when the script doesn't deserve it. He spent months training in jiu-jitsu and gun-fu for John Wick and reportedly does a ton of his own stunt work well into his fifties and sixties. That's not range. That's just refusing to half-ass anything, and somehow that ends up looking like dedication even when the writing around him is thin.

And then there's John Wick: Chapter 4. By that point the franchise had leaned so hard into Keanu's minimalism that his dialogue basically got reduced to single-word answers. "Yeah." Over and over. I get that it's supposed to read as stoic action hero energy, but after the fourth or fifth "yeah," it stops feeling like a character choice and starts feeling like the writers just gave up trying to give the guy actual lines. It's the one spot where his limited range stops being charming and turns into a crutch the franchise leaned on a little too hard.

The Stuff Nobody Gives Him Credit For

People love Keanu the person way more than they respect Keanu the actor, and I think that's backwards in one specific way. Nobody talks about how physically committed his action work actually is. The John Wick fight choreography is some of the best in modern action movies, shot in long unbroken takes specifically because Reeves can actually pull off the moves himself instead of needing a stunt double for every other cut. That takes real years of training, and it gets totally buried under sandwich memes and "internet's boyfriend" headlines. He's underrated as a physical performer in an industry that won't stop talking about Tom Cruise doing his own stunts but barely mentions Keanu doing the same thing with arguably tougher choreography.

The Scene That Made Me A Believer

The moment Keanu went from "guy from the Matrix" to "wait, this guy's actually special" for me was the lobby fight in the original John Wick. It's not the most technically impressive sequence in the franchise once you get to Chapter 4, but it's the one where you first feel the shift happen. A grieving man who just lost his dog grabs a gun and starts taking apart a room full of professional killers with brutal efficiency. No quips, no fanfare, just pure controlled fury. It set the tone for everything the franchise became, and it's the scene where you go "oh, this isn't just another action movie, he actually found his role."

TWC Recommends

  • The Entry Point: John Wick (2014). The most accessible Keanu performance out there, lean and mean at under two hours, and the film that explains exactly why everyone fell back in love with him in the first place.
  • The Deep Cut: A Scanner Darkly (2006). A rotoscoped animated adaptation of a Philip K. Dick novel about drug addiction and surveillance paranoia, and Keanu is unsettling and sad in it in a way his bigger movies never really let him be. It's strange, it's a little uncomfortable, and it's nothing like the guy you think you know from John Wick.

Is Keanu Reeves a great actor we just don't give enough credit, or a guy with limited range who got incredibly lucky with the right roles at the right time?

I think it's the second one, and I don't think that makes him any less worth watching. Where do you land on it?

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Keanu Reeves has limited range and everyone knows it. So why can't we stop watching him? A Spotlight on the actor Hollywood can't quit.

entry.title: REVIEW: Matthias & Maxime
entry.content:
Matthias & Maxime is a 2019 Canadian drama by Xavier Dolan. One kiss for a student film, and everything gets weird.

It's about two childhood best friends in their late twenties, Matthias (Gabriel Freitas) and Maxime (Dolan), whose whole friendship gets weird after they're asked to kiss for a student short film.

That's the whole setup. One kiss they didn't think twice about, and suddenly everything feels off and neither of them knows what to do about it. It's quiet, it's intimate, and it's set in Quebec, shot mostly in French. Very much a Xavier Dolan film in all the best ways.

I found this movie because of a gif on Twitter. Spent way too long scrolling through the comments trying to figure out what it was from, and the second I got the name, it went straight on my watchlist.

The Highlights

  • The leads are incredible together. Freitas and Dolan have this real, easy chemistry that makes you believe every second of their friendship.
  • The cinematography is gorgeous. André Turpin shoots this with so much care. Lingering close-ups, quiet moments that just breathe, no scene hanging around longer than it should. It looks beautiful without trying too hard.
  • Dolan pulls back and it works. If you know his other movies, you know he loves big emotions and bold style. This one's a lot quieter, and it actually fits the story perfectly.
  • It doesn't spell anything out for you. The film trusts you to sit in the awkwardness and figure it out along with the characters. If you like stories that respect your brain, this one's for you.

Fair Warnings

  • It's a slow burn. At 119 minutes, the pace is deliberate. There are parts in the middle that drag, and a few scenes you could cut without losing much. You've gotta be in the right mood for this one.
  • The group scenes can feel pointless. A lot of the movie happens within a wider friend group, and some of those scenes wander before going anywhere interesting. If the group doesn't grab you early, those parts will test your patience.
  • This is not a love story with a neat ending. If you want a clear romance and a satisfying wrap-up, you'll leave disappointed. It's more about figuring yourself out than getting any kind of payoff. Go in knowing that.

Final Verdict

My Rating: 7.5.

If you're into slow, character-driven movies that let things simmer, this one's worth your time. The performances and the emotional honesty carry it even through the slow parts. Just don't go in expecting a typical love story, because that's not what this is.

Have you seen Matthias & Maxime?

Drop your thoughts in the comments. Whether it wrecked you or left you cold, I want to know.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Exploring Matthias & Maxime; a slow-burn look at shifting friendships and internal reckoning. A must-watch if you prefer honesty over neat endings.

entry.title: HALL OF FAME: The Roundup Movies
entry.content:
Let me tell you about the most criminally slept-on action franchise on the planet right now.

The Roundup series is a South Korean action-crime juggernaut built around one man: Detective Ma Seok-do, also known as the Monster Cop, and the absolute carnage that follows him everywhere he goes. His team is perpetually one crisis away from a breakdown, the villains are menacing, and Ma himself just walks through all of it like a force of nature; slapping, throwing, and demolishing anyone dumb enough to get in his way. Online gambling rings, international drug cartels, vicious cross-border syndicates: they all make the same mistake of underestimating him, and they all pay for it spectacularly.

We are four films deep with a fifth already confirmed, and this franchise has absolutely no business being this consistently good. It has that perfect mix of classic buddy-cop energy and hard-hitting modern action choreography that just works every single time. The series has now drawn over 40 million moviegoers across its four films, making it the first Korean film franchise in history to reach that number.

This post contains minor spoilers for the Roundup Korean movies.

The Plot (In a Nutshell)

Detective Ma Seok-Do is a beast of a cop with zero patience for criminals and an uncanny ability to stumble into disasters far above his pay grade. Each film drops him into a new international crisis, a new class of villain, and a new excuse to hit people very, very hard. The cases change. The carnage does not.

The Franchise Breakdown

THE OUTLAWS (2017): This is where it all started, and it is so damn good it almost feels unfair. Directed by Kang Yoon-sung in his feature debut, the film is based on real events from 2004, a brutal gang conflict in Seoul's Garibong-dong neighbourhood dubbed the Heuksapa Incident. Detective Ma is trying to keep a fragile peace between local gangs in Chinatown when a savage new crew from Yanbian, China crosses the border and blows the whole thing up with a bloody turf war. Yoon Kye-sang plays Jang Chen, the villain, and he is unhinged and unpredictable enough that you tense up every single time he appears on screen. This is gritty, raw crime cinema at its absolute best. Kang Yoon-sung won Best New Director at both the Korean Association of Film Critics Awards and the Baeksang Arts Awards for this film, and both wins were deserved. It set a bar so high the rest of the franchise has been chasing it ever since.

THE ROUNDUP (2022): Ma heads to Vietnam to bring back a small-time suspect and, naturally, walks directly into something far, far worse: a ruthless killer targeting South Korean tourists. What is actually wild is that this sequel matches the original almost beat for beat in quality and intensity. The villain is cold, brutal, and completely threatening, the action goes absolutely wild, and The Roundup went on to become the top-grossing Korean film of 2022 with 12.69 million admissions, the first Korean film to pass 10 million viewers since before the pandemic. Choosing between this and The Outlaws for the top spot in the franchise is one of the hardest calls you will ever make as an action film fan. Both of them are that good.

THE ROUNDUP: NO WAY OUT (2023): The weakest entry, and it hurts to say that because the action alone still slaps. Ma joins a new metropolitan unit chasing a dangerous synthetic drug tearing through the Seoul club scene, in a story based on a real 2017 to 2018 methamphetamine smuggling case involving South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan. The problem is the main villain never quite clicks. He feels underbaked compared to what came before. The truly frustrating part is that the secondary villains, a lethal Japanese Yakuza cleanup crew, are so much more electric and menacing that every scene without them is a step down. The film still pulled 10.68 million admissions in Korea, which tells you how devoted the audience is. Worth watching, but it is clearly the odd one out in the lineup.

THE ROUNDUP: PUNISHMENT (2024): The franchise needed a bounce-back after the third entry, and it delivered. The film had its world premiere at the 74th Berlin International Film Festival, and Ma goes after a massive illegal online gambling operation running out of the Philippines with a cryptocurrency money laundering angle. Punishment broke all-time Korean film presale records before it even opened, selling over 834,000 tickets in advance bookings, and went on to reach 10 million admissions faster than any previous entry in the series. The villain, played by Kim Moo-yeol as a ruthless ex-special forces killer, is menacing again in a way the third film badly needed. The action set pieces are some of the best in the whole franchise. The comeback is real, and the franchise is back exactly where it belongs.

The Action: Raw and Masterfully Shot

I cannot move on without talking about how these fights are actually filmed, because they are operating on a completely different level from most of what you will find in Western action cinema right now.

No lazy shaky-cam. No rapid cuts every half-second to hide the fact that nobody can really fight. The camera steps back and lets you see everything: every open-hand slap, every brutal shoulder throw, every hit from Ma Dong-seok landing with full bone-crunching weight. What makes this specific is the physicality. Ma Dong-seok is not performing action like a movie star trying to fake his way through a fight scene. He is built for exactly this, and the choreography is designed around what his body actually does instead of cutting around what it cannot.

The stunt work is impeccable, the framing captures the full chaos of every brawl, and it all feels grounded without ever losing that pure cinematic punch. The action director on the first film, Heo Myeong-haeng, went on to direct the fourth installment, which tells you everything about how much the choreography is understood as the backbone of the whole operation. It is some of the best action filmmaking happening anywhere in the world right now, and it is not even close.

Why It Works

The Roundup series works for the same reason the best action franchises always work: it knows exactly what it is and never apologizes for it. These are not films trying to be prestige cinema in disguise. They are films that want you to feel the hits, root for the good guy, and walk out satisfied. That clarity of purpose, combined with the fact that the films are actually well-made rather than cynically assembled, is what separates this franchise from the pile.

There is also something refreshing about Ma Seok-do as a protagonist in the current landscape. He is not morally conflicted. He is not broken. He is not hiding a secret that will be revealed in the third act. He is a cop who loves his job, is very good at it, and finds it physically efficient to solve problems with his hands. There is something deeply satisfying about a character who sees a problem and just deals with it.

Final Verdict

I am completely locked into this franchise for life. Watch it if you want high-octane, brutally fun action cinema that never lets up and always delivers. Watch the films in order, because the first two are essential. Power through the third. Let the fourth remind you why you started. With a fifth already confirmed, there is no better time to get caught up.

Which film in the franchise hit hardest for you, and are you as hyped for the fifth as I am?

Drop a comment below. I want to know if you also think the Yakuza crew in No Way Out deserved their own film, because that is an argument I am fully prepared to have.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Four films deep and still going strong. I explore why the South Korean "Roundup" franchise is the gold standard for modern, grounded action cinema.

entry.title: MOVIE RECOMMENDATIONS: (May 11, 2026)
entry.content:
Four films. One day. Zero regrets.

This batch covers a lot of ground: a decade-old Korean thriller I somehow missed until now, two fresh 2026 releases that surprised me, and one survival story that goes completely off the rails in the best possible way.
