No ranking here. Just honest takes on everything I watched, in the order I watched it.

The Handmaiden (2016)

The Handmaiden is a 2016 South Korean thriller set in 1930s colonial Korea, built around a young woman hired as a maid to a wealthy Japanese heiress, except her role is part of an elaborate con to steal the heiress's fortune. That is all I will say about the plot, because the less you know going in, the better.

The film is split into three parts, each one replaying events from a different character's perspective, and every time you think you have figured it out, the rug gets pulled again. The visual style is meticulous, almost oppressively beautiful, and it demands your full attention.

What could have been better: Honestly? Very little. If anything, first-time viewers might find the deliberate pacing of the opening act slow before the structure reveals itself. Stick with it. The patience is completely rewarded.

Quick highlights:

  • The three-part structure. Each section changes everything you just watched.
  • The cast. Four extraordinary performances carrying a film that could have collapsed under its own complexity. They never let it.
  • Park Chan-wook's direction. Every shot looks like it was planned a year in advance. The visual precision is on another level entirely.

Hoppers (2026)

Pixar's latest follows a young woman who uploads her consciousness into a robotic beaver to communicate with animals and help defend their forest. Yes, really. And somehow it works completely.

The concept is wonderfully strange, and the forest animals are oddly endearing in the best way. The voice acting is sharp, the art style is gorgeous, and the film balances slapstick comedy for kids with a thoughtful message about empathy and environmental responsibility for everyone else. It never talks down to either audience, which is exactly what Pixar does best when it is firing on all cylinders. Fresh, funny, and surprisingly moving in a few moments you will not see coming.

What could have been better: The premise is so wild that the first act spends a lot of time explaining itself. A slightly leaner setup would have let the actual story breathe sooner.

Quick highlights:

  • The animal ensemble. Completely unhinged in the most entertaining way. Several of them nearly steal the whole film from the lead.
  • Dual-audience balance. The comedy works for kids without condescending to adults, and the emotional core works for adults without losing the kids.
  • Pixar back in form. This is the studio doing what it does best: wrapping a strange, original concept around something that hits you in the chest by the end.

No Other Choice (2025)

No Other Choice follows a man who loses his job and, rather than accept it, begins systematically eliminating every other candidate competing for the position he wants. Dark does not even cover it.

What makes it work is how effectively the film builds empathy for a character doing something completely indefensible. The desperation feels real, the performance is magnetic, and the pacing never gives you a moment to breathe. It is violent and bleak, but also disturbingly watchable.There is a thread of dark comedy running through it that keeps it from becoming purely grim.

What could have been better: The film leans so hard into its protagonist's perspective that some of the supporting characters feel thin by comparison. A little more dimension on the other side would have made the moral question even sharper.

Quick highlights:

  • The empathy problem. The film makes you root for someone doing something terrible, and it never fully lets you off the hook for that.
  • Relentless pacing. It keeps the pressure on from start to finish.
  • Something to say. The desperation driving this story does not feel invented. It feels very current, and that is what gives it its real edge.

Send Help (2026)

Sam Raimi directs this one, and once you know that, the mid-film tonal lurch makes complete sense. Send Help starts as a fairly grounded survival thriller: a plane crash, a remote island, two survivors who happen to be boss and employee. Then somewhere around the halfway mark it just decides to become something far more unhinged. Raimi cannot help himself, and honestly, I respect it.

It is a little predictable and does not land twists the way the other films on this list do, but it is consistently entertaining and never overstays its welcome.

What could have been better: The first half plays it a bit too straight for a Raimi film. If it had leaned into the chaos a little earlier, the tonal shift would have felt like an escalation rather than a detour.

Quick highlights:

  • The Raimi effect. The moment the film stops pretending to be a conventional survival thriller is the moment it becomes fun.
  • McAdams and O'Brien. The dynamic between them keeps the quiet stretches interesting. The power inversion is handled with more nuance than the premise suggests.
  • The Runtime. It knows exactly how long it needs to be and gets out cleanly.

Have you seen any of these?

Drop a comment below and tell me which one you are adding to your watchlist first. And if you have already seen The Handmaiden and never told me to watch it, we need to talk.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A mix of 2026 releases and an essential classic. Here are my latest film recommendations to keep your watchlist fresh this May.

entry.title: REVIEW: Obsession (2026)
entry.content:
Obsession sits in that rare space where a horror movie somehow becomes the actual pop culture event of a season.

Curry Barker wrote and directed it after building an audience on YouTube, and this was his first feature. The movie stars Michael Johnston as Bear, a music store employee too nervous to tell his coworker Nikki how he feels and Inde Navarrette who plays Nikki, a girl whose autonomy is stripped away. It's a supernatural psychological horror movie, and it deserved every bit of the buzz around it this year.

The plot is simple: Bear picks up a novelty toy called the One Wish Willow, initially meant as a gift for Nikki, and instead uses it himself. He wishes for her to love him more than anyone else in the world. The wish works almost immediately. And what starts as every hopeless romantic's fantasy turns into something closer to a nightmare, because Nikki doesn't just fall for him. She loses herself completely.

If you've seen Get Out or Talk to Me, you know the type of horror this leans into. It's less about jump scares and more about the slow, sick feeling of watching someone lose control of their own choices while the person who caused it stands there deciding what to do next.

The Highlights

  • Inde Navarrette as Nikki. She's doing the heaviest lifting in this movie and she absolutely kills it. Watching her body language shift from a normal person to someone stripped of free will is so unsettling. There are some scenes where the "real" Nikki briefly breaks through the spell and begs to be stopped, and they are some of the most upsetting moments I've watched all year.
  • Bear as an uncomfortable mirror. Michael Johnston plays him as the nice guy we've all met at some point. That one that's quiet, a little awkward, and seemingly harmless. You spend the first few minutes rooting for him, and then you watch him choose himself over and over again, even once he knows exactly what's happening to Nikki. I was disgusted by his actions, that scene where the real Nikki begs him to kill her and his response "What's so bad about being with me?" pissed me off in a way that I haven't felt in a long time. He's a coward who made one impulsive wish and the film lets that cowardice curdle into something disturbing.
  • Cinematography and Sound Design. The visuals lean into an eerie, off-kilter feeling without needing a huge budget to sell it, and the score sits right underneath every scene, cranking up the tension exactly when it needs to. Great work there from the cinematographer and sound designer.
  • The pacing doesn't waste your time. Nothing about this movie drags, every scene is pulling you forward, and by the time it gets to the darkest stretch, you're already too invested to look away.

Fair Warning

  • This is a heavy watch. The film deals directly with consent, manipulation, and what it means to take away someone's ability to choose. There are a few scenes that are kind of hard to sit through. Just brace yourself.

Overall Thoughts

Obsession earns its reputation as one of the best horror movies of 2026. It's a gripping, uncomfortable look at what happens when someone decides their feelings for you matter more than your right to choose them. Bear had so many chances to just tell Nikki the truth about how he feels for her. Instead he took a shortcut, and the film makes you watch every consequence of that decision play out.

Also worth noting, for a film made on a budget under a million dollars, it's now sitting north of $500 million worldwide, which makes it one of the most profitable movies ever made, horror or otherwise.

My Rating: 9.1

PS: I keep thinking about how differently this story would have gone if Bear had just told Nikki how he felt in the first place. Though I guess that's the whole point, the shortcut is always tempting but it's never actually free.

Do you think you would have immediately picked up on Nikki's weird behavior, if you were in Bear's position?

Comment below and let me know!

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Bear wishes for Nikki to love him more than anyone else, and gets exactly that. My spoiler-light review of horror's biggest surprise hit of 2026.

entry.title: REVIEW: Dorohedoro Season 1
entry.content:
This is one of those shows that sneaks up on you because you don't expect something this strange to also be this good.

Dorohedoro is a 2020 dark fantasy anime from MAPPA, directed by Yuichiro Hayashi, based on the manga by Q Hayashida. It ran for 12 episodes in Japan between January and March 2020, then landed on Netflix worldwide that May.

Genre-wise it's a mashup: horror, action, comedy, with a heavy dose of body horror and gallows humor that shouldn't work together as well as it does.

The Setup

The story follows Caiman, a man with a lizard head and no memory of his old face or his old life. A sorcerer did this to him, and now he's hunting them, hoping anyone can undo it or at least tell him what happened. His partner in this is Nikaido, a fry cook who fights like she was built for it. The two of them roam a grimy, decaying place called the Hole, a district where sorcerers use regular humans as target practice for their magic experiments.

On the other side of things is the world the sorcerers actually live in, a place with its own politics, gang rivalries, and a crime boss named En who's obsessed with tracking down the lizard-headed man who's been killing his people. His enforcers, Shin and Noi, also get pulled into the hunt, and their dynamic ends up being one of the most unexpectedly sweet parts of the whole show.

What worked:

The characters are the whole show for me. Caiman and Nikaido have a friendship that feels lived in from episode one. There's no forced backstory dump to explain why they trust each other, you just watch them operate as a unit and understand it. Nikaido in particular stood out. She's not written as "the strong female character" in that stiff, checkbox way a lot of shows do it. She's just strong, full stop, and the show never treats it as a novelty.

Then there's Noi. She could have been a throwaway muscle character attached to Shin, but the show gives her actual depth. Her devotion to En, her friendship with Shin, the way she handles herself in a fight, all of it makes her one of the most memorable people in the cast. Shin and Noi's relationship ends up being weirdly tender for a show this violent, and that contrast is part of what makes Dorohedoro click.

The world-building deserves credit too. The Hole and the sorcerer's world are visually and tonally distinct, and the show trusts you to piece together how the magic system and the gang politics work without over-explaining everything. It respects the viewer's intelligence, and I really appreciated that.

Fair Warning:

The CGI takes some getting used to. MAPPA leaned into 3D animation for a lot of the character models and movement, and the style is a real departure from traditional 2D anime. The first couple of episodes, might be a bit jarring for some viewers.

That said, I wouldn't call this a real downside. Once the story pulls you in, the visual style stops being a distraction and starts feeling like part of the show's identity. By the midpoint, I wasn't thinking about it anymore, I was just watching the story.

Rating

8.7 out of 10.

The story, the characters, the tone, all of it worked together in a way I wasn't expecting going in. I loved almost everything about this season, and the parts that took adjusting turned into strengths by the end. If you haven't watched Dorohedoro yet, this is your sign.

PS: Noi and Nikaido are the reason I'll be thinking about this show for a while. More buff women in anime, please and thank you.

Which of the two is your favorite: Noi or Nikaido?

Drop your pick below, no wrong answers here.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A review of Dorohedoro Season 1, MAPPA's dark fantasy anime with body horror, gallows humor, and two of the best-written women in anime, Noi and Nikai

entry.title: Horror, heartbreak, and a flock of very good detectives
entry.content:
Five days, eight movies, and three of them didn't survive past the one-hour mark.

It started with a John Wick rewatch, and somewhere around the credits I decided I wanted horror for the rest of the week. What followed turned into an accidental deep dive on the Evil Dead franchise, which then kept bending into whatever new horror release happened to be sitting in my queue. By the end of it I'd watched a bunch of talking sheep solve a murder and actually got a little emotional about it.

Here's how the whole thing played out, in the order I watched it.

John Wick: Chapter 3 - Parabellum (2019)

This is the rewatch that started it all. Everything gets turned up from the first two films: more assassins, more lore, more absurd fight choreography, more of Keanu Reeves getting thrown through glass than should physically be possible for one person to survive. The movie's not trying to be deep and honestly, it doesn't need to be because sometimes you just want to watch a man break someone's neck with a book. This one gets an 8.3/10. It was a fun watch from start to finish.

The Evil Dead (1981)

This is where I fell asleep on a horror classic, then gave up on the sequels. I went straight into the original, The Evil Dead, the low budget cabin in the woods film that basically wrote the rulebook every possession horror movie since has been copying from. I fell asleep twice trying to get through it but it was okay for most of the runtime, right up until the ending, where the gross practical effects mixed with animation threw me off completely. The acting and the effects both got so over the top so it came in at a 6.0 for me, decent but not a movie I'd rush back to.

I tried to keep the franchise momentum going and it fell apart almost immediately. Evil Dead II went full comedy on me, and that's not what I signed up for, so it got dropped before it had a real chance. Army of Darkness didn't even make it that far.

What did work was the 2013 remake, Evil Dead, watched the same day Army of Darkness got cut loose. It was loud and chaotic, and had all the blood and gore remakes tend to reach for. It's not really my lane of horror, but it held my attention enough to come away with a 7.0. I'm not done with this franchise, Evil Dead Rise from 2023 and the new Evil Dead Burn from 2026 are next on my list. The two I already dropped will stay dropped.

Leviticus (2026)

This one's the queer horror gut punch of the week. It follows two teenage boys in a remote Christian community whose feelings for each other start manifesting as a violent supernatural entity, and the movie doesn't try to hide that it's a metaphor for conversion therapy and religious repression. I really loved this movie. My only complaint was the runtime. It felt too short for how much I'd gotten attached to these two, my poor babies, and I closed it wishing there was an extra twenty minutes to sit in. It still pulled a strong 8.5 out of me, appreciation and mild heartbreak included.

Backrooms (2026)

All atmosphere, no substance is the simplest way to sum this one up. Kane Parsons, the creator behind the viral Backrooms YouTube series, made his feature directorial debut with this one, and the liminal space visuals are properly unsettling on their own terms. My problem is everything wrapped around them. A therapist chasing a missing patient into an alternate dimension had strong potential, but the story kept reaching for a meaning it never quite built up to. Pretentious is the word I'd use to describe this film, and a 6.3 feels about right to me. I know some people loved this one and will tell me I just don't get it. That's fine, let's just agree to disagree.

Hokum (2026)

This is the one that just didn't work. Hokum wrapped up the week, and it's where things finally fell apart for good. Damian McCarthy, the director behind Oddity, brings the same slow burn atmospheric style to a story about a novelist confronting a witch legend while scattering his parents' ashes at a remote Irish inn. Its got cheap scares, and a whole lot of meh. I know it's supposed to be sitting with grief underneath all the ghost story trappings, but I couldn't bring myself to care. I dropped it around the one hour mark.

The Sheep Detectives (2026)

This is a (sheep) whodunit mystery. After Backrooms and Hokum I just needed something to pass the time, so I put on The Sheep Detectives without expecting much, and it ended up being the best surprise of the whole week. Hugh Jackman plays a shepherd who reads murder mysteries to his flock every night, fully convinced they can't understand a word of it, right up until he turns up dead and the sheep decide they're the ones who have to solve it. Based on the novel Three Bags Full and directed by Kyle Balda in his first live action feature, it's a brilliant little movie with a solid twist and it gets a rating of 8.3 from me.

That's the full ride: a John Wick comfort watch, an Evil Dead franchise that couldn't decide if it wanted to scare me or lose me, two horror movies I actively regret finishing, and a flock of sheep that somehow ended up being the best thing I watched all week. If nothing else, this week proved that horror won't always deliver, but the movie you expect the least from sometimes will.

What have you seen recently?

Drop a comment if you disagree with some of my ratings.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Ratings and honest takes on the movies I watched this week, from the Evil Dead franchise to a murder-solving flock of sheep.

entry.title: The Anime vs Cartoon Debate: What's Actually the Difference?
entry.content:
People argue about anime vs cartoon constantly, and most of the argument comes down to a technicality nobody explains properly

So this whole discourse has been living rent free in my head. Is anime only Japanese? Or is it just any animated show?

Here's what set me off: the second you call a Japanese show a "cartoon" in front of a certain type of fan, you'd think you just insulted their whole bloodline. But the word anime literally comes from the word animation. So who's actually right here? Let's actually break this down, because the answer is way messier than either side of this argument wants to admit.

What Anime Actually Means In Japan

Let me start with the boring but important part: the actual word. "Anime" is a shortened version of the English word "animation," pronounced the Japanese way. In Japan, that's exactly how the word gets used, as a catch all term for any animated work, no matter where it's from or what it looks like. SpongeBob is anime in Japan. The Simpsons is anime in Japan. There's an actual Japanese DVD cover out there that describes Betty Boop, the old American cartoon character from the 1930s, as an "antique anime." Not a joke, not a meme, an actual product label.

So on a pure technical level, it's correct. Peppa Pig is anime. Phineas and Ferb is anime. If it's animated, and you're using the word the way Japan uses it, it qualifies. That part of the argument isn't a stretch, it's just linguistically accurate.

This actually happens with a bunch of words that jump between languages. It's less "anime is a secret conspiracy word" and more "this is just what happens when a general term gets exported." The word travels, picks up a narrower job in its new language, and the original broad meaning stays behind in the country it came from. Anime is doing exactly what plenty of loanwords do, it just happens to be the one currently causing group chat arguments.

Anime vs Cartoon: Why English Speakers Draw a Line

Outside Japan, in English, the word did something words do all the time: it narrowed. English dictionaries define anime specifically as "a style of Japanese animation", not animation in general. So while the word was born as a generic term, the moment it crossed over into English it picked up a much more specific job: describing animation that is either made in Japan, or made in that recognizable Japanese house style.

There's even a theory that the French had something to do with this. Anime became massively popular in France in the late 1970s and 1980s, and some believe the French phrase "dessin animé" which roughly means "animated drawing", helped cement anime as a distinctly foreign, Japanese label once it filtered into English through European fandom circles. Nobody agrees on the exact etymology, but the pattern is clear either way: what started as "animation" in general somehow became shorthand for "animation from Japan specifically" once it left Japan.

So when someone insists Peppa Pig is anime, they're technically using the Japanese definition. When someone insists it isn't, they're using the English one. They're both right, they're just speaking two different versions of the same word.

So Why Do Fans Get So Defensive?

This is the part that actually explains the attitude you've probably noticed. It's not really about the dictionary. It's about what "cartoon" has come to mean in casual English. For a lot of people, "cartoon" quietly translates to "kids stuff, not serious, doesn't have real stakes." Anime fans who grew up getting mocked for watching subtitled shows with swords and blood and actual character death in it are not exactly thrilled to have their favorite thing lumped in with a label that carries "this is for children" baggage.

There's also the visual style argument people love to bring up. Anime traditionally used something called limited animation: fewer drawings per second than the full, fluid animation style Disney and old school Toei built their reputation on. Studios like Mushi Production, leaned into this out of necessity because they simply didn't have Disney money. Fewer frames, static shots held on dramatic close ups, dialogue heavy scenes instead of constant movement. That "limitation" ended up becoming a defining stylistic signature instead of a flaw, and it's part of what people point to when they insist anime looks and feels different from Western animation, even though "different visual technique" and "different medium entirely" are not the same claim.

The bottom line is, the gatekeeping isn't really about linguistics. It's a defense mechanism built out of years of anime fans getting told their favorite thing wasn't a real form of storytelling. That doesn't mean the gatekeeping makes total sense, but it explains where it's coming from.

Think about the actual content difference too. A lot of what gets grouped under "cartoon" in casual conversation, at least in the West, tends to lean toward sketch comedy, slapstick, or shows built around a joke of the week format. Anime, on the other hand, will casually hand you a multi season war epic, a slow burn tragedy, or a psychological thriller with a body count, all animated. When someone's entire mental picture of "cartoon" is built on Saturday morning comedy, and you hand them a show where a teenager watches his whole village get slaughtered in episode one, you can see why fans get twitchy about the label. The frustration isn't really irrational, it's just aimed at the wrong target. The word isn't the problem. The narrow Western idea of what a cartoon is allowed to be, that's the actual problem.

The Blurry Middle Nobody Wants To Deal With

And then you've got the shows that break the whole argument. Avatar: The Last Airbender is the classic example. American studio, American writers, American voice cast, but it's soaked in anime influence: the pacing, the fight choreography, the way emotional beats get held on a character's face. Fans have argued about whether to call it "anime influenced" or just anime for years, and there's still no clean answer. The Legend of Korra gets the same treatment. So does The Boondocks.

There was even a real attempt at this outside Japan entirely. A studio based in Abu Dhabi made a show called Torkaizer in 2013, marketed as "the Middle East's first anime," following a young Emirati hero fighting off an alien invasion, animated in a clearly Japanese inspired style and even partly set in Japan. It kicked off the exact same argument all over again: if it's not made in Japan, can it actually be called anime, or is it just anime flavored?

Nobody's fully settled this. Some fans treat it like the pizza argument: pizza came from Italy, and you can make an amazing pizza anywhere in the world, but purists will still tell you it's not "real" Neapolitan pizza unless it followed the actual regional process. Anime works the same way for a lot of fans. Country of origin becomes part of the definition, not just the style.

Where I Actually Stand On This

Here's my honest take: you're not wrong to clown the discourse, because it is objectively funny that a word literally meaning "animation" gets treated like sacred vocabulary the second it leaves Japan. But I also get why the distinction matters to people who use it. Words shift meaning when they travel. "Anime" left Japan as a generic term and came back into English as a specific one, the same way "sushi" doesn't just mean "rice" even though that's technically what the word refers to in Japanese. Language does this constantly, it's not some big anime fan conspiracy.

So no, calling Peppa Pig anime isn't wrong exactly, it's just using a different dictionary than the one most English speakers agreed to use. And calling anime a cartoon isn't wrong either, it's just poking at a word some fans have spent years trying to distance themselves from for reasons that have way more to do with stigma than semantics. Both sides have a point. Both sides are also being a tad bit dramatic about it, and that's the funniest part of the whole thing. Nobody's actually arguing about language here, they're arguing about respect, and the word "anime" just happens to be the battlefield they picked.

The real answer nobody wants to hear: it's all just animation. Some of it happens to come with subtitles, a specific visual pedigree, and a fanbase ready to throw hands over what you call it.

And look, I say all this as someone who watches plenty of it myself. I'm not trying to dunk on anime fans from the outside, I'm one of the people in the crowd laughing at how seriously this argument gets taken. It's a good bit precisely because there's a real answer buried in there somewhere, it's just wrapped in enough internet passion that nobody can have the conversation calmly.

So where do you stand, is anime just Japanese cartoons with better marketing, or is there an actual meaningful difference?

Drop your take in the comments, and if you've got a favorite "wait, is this technically anime" example, I want to hear it.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.

entry.title: REVIEW: Common Side Effects
entry.content:
Have you seen Common Side Effects? A mycologist discovers a mushroom that cures anything and naturally, everything goes wrong.

Common Side Effects is a 2025 adult animated dark comedy-thriller that follows Marshall Cuso, a mycologist who discovers the Blue Angel Mushroom, a rare fungus that appears to cure any illness or injury imaginable.

When word gets out, he and his old high school friend Frances find themselves caught in a dangerous cat-and-mouse conspiracy involving a ruthless pharmaceutical giant and a government dead set on burying the discovery. Think a paranoid thriller wrapped inside a darkly funny commentary on corporate greed and the broken healthcare machine.

The Experience

The Highlights:

  • Sharp, Witty Writing. The dialogue is clever without trying too hard. It tackles corporate corruption and systemic healthcare issues without dumbing things down or beating you over the head with the message. Refreshing.
  • Well-Developed Characters. Marshall and Frances feel like real people with actual histories and motivations. The supporting cast, including a delightfully detached pharmaceutical CEO voiced by Mike Judge himself, adds texture and keeps things unpredictable.
  • Distinctive Animation Style. It's a fascinating hybrid of anime sensibility, Funko Pop aesthetics, and classic 2D adult animation. Takes a couple of episodes to fully click, but once it does, you start to appreciate how intentional it all is. The color contrast between the corporate world and everything connected to the mushroom does a lot of quiet storytelling on its own.
  • Tight Pacing. Very little filler. Each episode ends leaving you ready to jump straight into the next one. Bingeable in the best possible way.
  • The Timing is No Accident. A show about big pharma suppressing a miracle cure landing in early 2025 feels sharp and urgent without ever getting preachy about it.

Fair Warning:

  • The Animation Has Its Rough Patches. There are a few moments where the frame rate drops and the motion feels choppy. If you're not used to limited animation styles, it can be a jarring distraction early on. Not a dealbreaker, but worth knowing going in.
  • The Slow Burn Requires Patience. The show builds deliberately. If you're expecting instant payoffs, you might check out before the story fully opens up. Stick with it.
  • Season 2 Is Still Not Here. Not a flaw of the show itself, but finishing that first season and having nowhere to go is genuinely frustrating. The wait feels unfair.

Final Verdict

My Rating: 8.5.

Common Side Effects is sharp, weird, and surprisingly moving. If you're into conspiracy thrillers, dark comedy, or animation that actually has something to say, don't sleep on this one. Watch it now so you're caught up when Season 2 finally drops.

Did You Sleep on This One Too, or Were You Already a Fan From the Start?

Drop your thoughts in the comments and let me know what you're hoping to see when Season 2 finally arrives.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Common Side Effects is a weird, bingeable take on corporate greed. Here’s why this adult animated series is worth your time before Season 2 drops.

entry.title: REVIEW: FROM Season 4
entry.content:
Binging it is the best way to experience it because watching this show once a week would have driven me up the wall.

Season 4 of From premiered in April 2026, and thank heavens, it was actually better than season 3. These town people have been through so much at this point, and I made the decision early on to wait for the whole season to finish before watching it. Best decision I made all year.

This post contains spoilers for season 4.

The Plot

The season opens with a new arrival throwing the town into chaos, while Jade and Tabitha are still reeling from what they learned at the Bottle Tree, and Boyd has to sit with what Smiley's return actually means for everyone. It does not take long before a gruesome discovery sends the whole town into a panic, and Jade and Tabitha keep carrying the weight of their revelation through the early episodes. Boyd tries to talk Acosta back from the edge while Julie starts digging into a set of abilities she is only beginning to understand, and Tabitha takes a desperate gamble that puts her right in the middle of the danger.

As the season moves forward, an unsettling discovery puts Boyd's inner circle on edge, Julie keeps trying to figure out how to actually use what she can do, and Sara continues to be tormented by the voices in her head that will not leave her alone. Boyd and Jade go on a search for answers that starts messing with their heads in ways neither of them expects, while a routine food run to the settlement turns into something much darker than anyone planned for.

The middle of the season is where the tension between Boyd and Jade really comes to a head, especially over whether they can actually trust what is inside Jade's head, and word from the settlement starts filtering back to the town that makes everyone uneasy. Tabitha and Jade's complicated history finally gets pulled into the open, another resident starts unraveling under the pressure, and Boyd decides he wants to test out a theory that could put the whole town at risk.

By the back half, a dangerous plan starts taking real shape, and the show forces the question of how much Boyd is actually willing to gamble for a real shot at getting everyone home. Fatima and Henry end up at two very different, very disturbing crossroads, and Victor steps up to help Tabitha and Ethan get ready for whatever is coming. The residents are left standing at a crossroads unlike anything they have faced before as Boyd sets his plan into motion, and the finale pushes Boyd's quest to lead everyone home into a terrifying place that changes the town for good.

What worked:

The villains were actually threatening this season, and that matters more than people give it credit for. A show like this lives or dies on whether the danger feels real, and season 4 finally made me nervous for these characters again in a way season 3 had not managed to do consistently.

The plot itself was strong from start to finish. Things actually moved, decisions had weight, and I did not feel like I was watching filler episodes waiting for the real story to show up. And the communication issue I have been going on about since season 2 was noticeably better this season. The residents actually started sharing what they knew with each other more often, and it made the group feel like they were finally working with each other instead of constantly working around each other.

What didn't:

I hate a character now. The Boy in White can piss off, honestly. He never gives straight answers, he just shows up whenever the residents are trying to make an actual plan and goes "don't do this" or "don't do that" without a single word of explanation. Tell us why! He cannot keep appearing every time people are trying to figure something out and shutting it down with zero context. It is maddening to watch characters who have earned a little trust from me get undermined by a figure who refuses to just communicate, of all things, in a season that was otherwise doing so much better with that exact issue.

Rating

7.8 out of 10.

Season 4 pulled the show back up after a shakier season 3, with real threats, a plot that kept moving, and residents who finally started talking to each other. The Boy in White knocked some points off for me personally, purely because his whole deal is the opposite of everything the show finally started getting right. Word is season 5 will be the last one, and if that holds, they need to wrap this up well. There is a lot riding on how they land this.

Does the Boy in White frustrate anyone else as much as he frustrates me, or am I alone in wanting him to just explain himself once?

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: From season 4 review: real threats, real growth in communication among the residents, and one infuriating character I can't stand. My honest take.

entry.title: RECAP: Elite Season 5
entry.content:
This season was such a slog to get through.

Somewhere underneath all the chaos there's an actual plot this time, one that finally circles back to something that's been buried since Season 4: Armando's body. So before we get into what worked and what absolutely did not, let's walk through how we get from a fundraiser party to a man in handcuffs by a swimming pool.

This post contains spoilers for Season 5 of Netflix's Elite.

How it kicks off

The season opens mid-apology. Phillipe's trying to make things right with Cayetana after everything from last season, when the lights suddenly cut out and a video starts playing. It's Elodie, the girl he confessed to abusing in a voice message back in Season 4, and this time she's not keeping it quiet. She tells everyone watching that Phillipe raped her.

Then the show jumps straight to the police station, where Samuel sits across from the Inspector and confesses to murder. Real this time, or so it seems, with a body already shown floating face-down in a swimming pool before the show even explains whose it is.

From there it rewinds to the start of the school year, just after Elodie's video goes public. Las Encinas responds by locking phones away and enforcing strict distance between students, though none of it does much to contain the fallout. Phillipe becomes public enemy number one overnight. Someone slips a pair of scissors into his bag with a note telling him to castrate himself. He's technically been cleared of charges before, and Benjamín goes as far as addressing the school directly, calling the treatment against him unacceptable. Phillipe, desperate, asks Cayetana to publicly vouch for him, hoping her word might cool things down. The one person on his side without being asked is a new student, Isadora.

Patrick's dealing with his own mess at home, a blowup with his father sends him straight to Omar for comfort, the two of them sleeping together that same afternoon while Ander, off on the other side of the world, stays silent and unreachable. Patrick also starts circling a new guy, Ivan, who insists he's not gay while stripping down in front of him in the locker room, which is about as convincing as it sounds. Ivan's home life isn't easy either, his father Cruz constantly out partying instead of around. One afternoon at Ivan's place, things get physical between the two boys, and when Patrick ends up frustrated and slips off to the bathroom alone, it's Cruz who catches him there and, instead of looking away, gives him an encouraging thumbs up. It's exactly as uncomfortable as it sounds, and it's only episode one.

Back at school, Mencia tells the Inspector she was assaulted, on top of everything already unraveling around Ari. It's too much for Benjamín, who blames himself for not watching Armando closely enough, Samuel assures him that Armando isn't coming back. Cayetana, nudged along by Isadora, goes on camera and publicly stands by Phillipe, telling everyone she doesn't want him thrown out of school.

The episode closes back where it started, in that interview room, where Samuel admits that he killed someone.

The twists and the escalation

Back in the interview room, Rebe tells the Inspector that Samuel didn't actually kill anyone, though whether that holds up is anyone's guess at this point. Meanwhile Benjamín's grip on the school tightens fast: strict rules, phones locked away, and it comes out that he's tracking students' locations through the school app. When they push back, he threatens to tank their grades if they keep resisting. Patrick leads the pushback, throwing a party partly just to get a moment with Ivan, while Cayetana and Phillipe stay out of it entirely. Cayetana's also pushing Phillipe to see the school counselor, Greta, who bans him from drinking and calls him a predator.

Benjamín walks in on Ari and Samuel having sex and drag both into his office separately, Samuel's scholarship suddenly on the line again. Meanwhile Omar takes in a homeless teenager named Bilal, offering him a dishwashing job out of pity, only for Bilal to try stealing the tip jar the same day. Omar throws him out, unmoved by his claims that dangerous people are after him.

At Patrick's party, things spiral fast. Rebe and Ivan kiss on the dance floor, caught on video and sent straight to Mencia. Patrick, already crushed watching that unfold, gets Ari to try drugs, and when he confronts Ivan about hiding who he really is, Ivan responds by kissing Samuel in front of him, pure spite dressed up as flirting.

Benjamín escalates the war on his students by handing out drug tests tied to grades, positive results meaning expulsion. The students revolt, tossing the tests out entirely, so Benjamín turns them against each other with an anonymous vote to expel one of their own. It comes down to Samuel and Omar, and Omar votes for Samuel out loud, getting him kicked out for three days and shattering whatever trust was left between them. Samuel throws him out of the house that night.

Bilal keeps circling back, and during a lakeside fundraiser Samuel catches him pick pocketing a guest and kicks him out again, right as Omar, following Samuel outside, spots a body floating in the lake and dives in convinced it's Bilal. It isn't. It's Armando, who was killed and dumped at the end of last season, finally surfacing. Bilal shows up to help pull the body out. Rebe, Omar, and Bilal end up disposing of it together on the beach, Omar furious nobody told him the truth sooner. Eventually Samuel calls the police himself, and the flashforward the season opened comes with a shocking twist: the body in the pool everyone's been building toward. It's Samuel.

While that unfolds, Phillipe drifts further from Cayetana and toward Isadora, eventually breaking things off with Cayetana entirely and kissing Isadora in full view of everyone. Patrick, meanwhile, catches Ari and Ivan having sex out on the water and falls apart over it, and it's Cruz, of all people, who comforts him. The two end up kissing. Rebe and Mencia's relationship keeps fracturing too, worsened when Mencia sees Rebe with another girl, Jess, at a drive-in. In the chaos of the fundraiser, Mencia finds a second SIM card hidden in her own phone, planted there by Armando, and traces the number on it straight back to her father.

Ivan and Patrick, bonding over shared father issues, finally sleep together. Cruz tried to pull Patrick into his room, gets stood up, as Patrick chose Ivan instead. Benjamín, meanwhile, gets pressed by the Inspector over the very investigation Mencia's SIM card ties into, and has Mencia hide a second phone for him, unaware the Inspector's watching it all on camera. Isadora's drinking spirals hard enough that Cayetana ends up taking her home, and later, finding her stash laid out and Isadora finally sober enough to talk, gets a rare honest glimpse into how lonely Isadora's life actually is underneath the chaos.

Cruz confronts Patrick in front of Benjamín with a line that lands like a threat (to me) dressed as heartbreak: I waited for you. Before it can go further, police arrive to search Benjamín's office. In the scramble, Mencia's caught stashing his second phone, and just before she can say anything to the investigator, Samuel bursts in and confesses to Armando's murder himself. It comes out that Benjamín had already offered him a deal beforehand: take the fall, and Benjamín would make sure his life afterward was taken care of completely.

Samuel plays along at first, coached by Benjamín to stay calm while bail gets arranged. The group scrambles to raise the twenty-five thousand euros needed to get him out, and it's revealed the SIM card was never Benjamín's to begin with, Armando had hidden it in Mencia's phone specifically because it was the last place anyone would think to check. Mencia's already made her own copy of everything incriminating, not fully trusting her father either. Ivan, moved by how much Ari clearly cares about Samuel, decides to help raise the bail money, especially once Cruz, learning Ivan slept with Patrick, refuses to contribute out of spite.

The group throws a charity auction to cover the rest, "Buy Your Valentine," which pairs Ivan with Ari and Patrick with Cruz, the two couples splitting off privately. Ivan and Ari end up kissing. Patrick and Cruz end up in a bathtub together, and later, a pool, which Ivan catches sight of and sends Ari away. Samuel finally walks free, thanking Benjamín warmly for coming through, until Ari tells him that it wasn't Benjamín's money that got him out. It was Ivan's. The episode flashforwards and shows Patrick standing over samuel, covered in blood.

By episode seven, the investigator's pushing Samuel harder, laying out evidence that Benjamín and Armando had been trafficking blackmail material on powerful people. He offers Samuel a way out: help build the case against Benjamín in exchange for his own freedom. Whether he takes it stays hanging. Ivan, furious over what happened with Patrick, confronts both his father and Patrick directly, calling Patrick manipulative and demanding he stay out of his life entirely, a claim that lands a little rich given Ivan's own behavior. A flash cuts back to that bloody night: Samuel crawling away while an injured Patrick calls out for help.

Back at school, Rebe learns about the SIM card and convinces both Cayetana and Mencia to help track it down as the evidence that could finally clear Samuel and take Benjamín down for good. Cayetana breaks into the school at night to search Benjamín's office while Rebe searches his home, and it's ultimately Mencia who hands it over, telling Rebe she loves her and refuses to let an innocent man go to prison over her father's secrets. Benjamín gets tipped off that Cayetana was caught snooping around his office the same night.

Phillipe, meanwhile, tells Isadora that no amount of glitter and money fills the emptiness underneath, refusing to date her while she's still spiraling. She responds by flying out to a party in Ibiza via helicopter. Worried, Phillipe follows her out there. During a dinner at Benjamín's house, Patrick shoves him in a moment of rage over everything with Ivan and Cruz, and later admits to Cruz just how conflicted falling for him has left him. They kiss again. In the middle of it all, a drunk Ivan leaves a voicemail confessing his real feelings for Patrick, and by mistake, sends it straight to Ari's phone instead.

In Ibiza, Isadora collapses at the party, unconscious. Phillipe, barely conscious himself, is slumped against a wall nearby when three men at the party notice she's out cold and decide to take advantage of the situation, locking the door behind them.

How it all wraps up

Ari shows up late one night to see Rebe and Samuel, and pulls Samuel aside privately. With the SIM card now in his hands, enough to bury her father for good, she tells him it's his call what to do with it, kisses him on the cheek, and leaves him to sit with the decision alone. Rebe reminds him afterward that Benjamín's never really valued him, just tolerated him, right up until he was ready to shake him off.

At school, Ivan and Phillipe both claim to remember only pieces of what happened in Ibiza, though Isadora's visibly traumatized, and Phillipe, given his own history, is terrified he might have been part of whatever happened to her. Ivan tells Patrick he's moving to Qatar with his father, and Patrick retreats into the showers alone. Isadora ends up there too, and when she starts bleeding, it becomes clear something far worse happened that night.

Cayetana finds her there and talks to her through the shower wall, no longer even employed at the school after getting caught snooping through Benjamín's office. Isadora breaks down the second she's alone.

The truth comes out through a video. One of the boys from that night filmed the whole thing and shows it off to Phillipe and Ivan. In it, Ivan tries to stop the three of them and collapses before he can. Phillipe crawls toward Isadora and passes out too. The boys assault her while both of them are down, and when Phillipe manages to lash out afterward, one of them mocks him over his own assault allegations, which is enough to make Phillipe hit him.

That night, Phillipe finally tells Isadora the truth, that he actually cares about her, and the two kiss as thunder rolls overhead. Around the same time, Cruz (remember he's Ivan's father), sits Patrick and Ivan down together and admits he can't keep doing this to either of them. He decides against Qatar entirely, telling Ivan to go be happy and chase what he actually wants with Patrick.

Samuel heads to the police station with the SIM card, but Benjamín calls first, begging to talk in person given everything between them. Samuel agrees. That night, Benjamín tries to buy him off completely: an Oxford business scholarship, tuition, housing, three thousand euros a month, in exchange for the SIM card and his silence about Armando. Samuel turns it down and tries to leave. Benjamín grabs for the bag, and in the struggle Samuel goes down hard, cracking his head against the edge of the pool and slipping into the water, blood spreading out around him while Benjamín just watches, frozen.

Patrick finds them and pulls Samuel out and calls everyone to tell them what's happened. Benjamín tries to stop them from calling the police.

Samuel survives. Barely conscious, he still manages to tell everyone the truth. The SIM card ends up lost in the pool water, and once Rebe realizes what happened, she goes after Benjamín herself, knocking him down before Mencia steps in to pull her off.

The police finally arrive and arrest Benjamín, leading him away in handcuffs while Patrick watches, Ivan standing beside him. Patrick and Ari break down sobbing, while Omar and Rebe quietly walk away from the wreckage of it all.

Where we left everyone:

  • Samuel: Pushed into the pool by Benjamin, hits his head, and nearly drowns, but survives, conscious enough to name Benjamin as the one responsible. After five seasons of this show using him as a punching bag, at least this time he lives to say so.

  • Benjamin: Arrested. Handcuffed in front of his three children by a swimming pool.

  • Patrick: Pulls Samuel out of the pool and watches his father get taken away.

  • Ivan: Stays in Spain instead of going to Qatar because Cruz tells him to follow his heart. After all the back and forth this season, I'd stopped caring.

  • Cruz: Steps aside. After spending the entire season pursuing his son's classmate. Sure.

  • Rebe and Mencia: Pulled apart and pushed back together so many times this season that the emotional whiplash became its own subplot.

  • Ari: Her love story with Samuel was one of the flattest things this season produced, which is a shame because these are two characters who should work together on paper and simply don't on screen.

  • Omar: Walks away from the finale with Rebe. His whole Bilal subplot goes essentially nowhere. Omar's been coasting on the goodwill of his earlier seasons for two years now and the writers genuinely owe him a real storyline.

  • Cayetana: Fired from the school partway through the season and still hanging around anyway. I don't know what else she's here for and based on the evidence, neither do the writers.

  • Isadora: Survives an assault the season never gives proper weight to. Season 6 has a chance to actually do something with her. Whether it will is a different question.

What worked and what didn't

I can see what the writers were going for with Isadora: a wealthy, untethered girl who uses parties and chaos as a substitute for a life her absent parents never bothered to give her. The problem is the show skips the part where you actually build investment in her before piling on the trauma, and having her show up defending Phillipe within her first few episodes, acting like she'd been there the whole time, just felt gross.

The Benjamin and Samuel dynamic was a little interesting, and credit where it's due, there's something almost poignant about Samuel who's never had a reliable father figure gravitate towards Benjamin over and over, even knowing it would end badly. The reveal that he's the body in the pool at the end of episode four was the one moment this season actually shocked me.

The Patrick, Ivan, and Cruz subplot. I can't believe this storyline made it through a room full of adults, got pitched, approved, shot, edited, and released onto Netflix. I was rooting for Patrick and Ivan. Then Cruz happened, and it's the same predatory, completely inappropriate dynamic between a grown man and a teenager the show's leaned on before. The resolution, where he graciously steps aside and urges his own son to chase down the boy he'd been pursuing all season, gets played as redemptive, even touching. It pissed me off. I hated it.

Rebe and Mencía ended Season 4 in a good place, so naturally Season 5 spends its entire runtime dismantling that, pulled apart and pushed back together so many times across eight episodes that by the finale I was just exhausted.

I wrote in my Season 4 post that the writers have never figured out what to do with Cayetana. Updated assessment: it's now Season 5 and they still haven't. I hope I don't see her in Season 6.

Overall thoughts

This season was a mess, and not in the fun, chaotic way earlier seasons managed to pull off. Isadora spending part of the season defending Phillipe against assault allegations, only for the show to turn around and put her through an assault of her own, felt less like irony and more like the writers not thinking through what they were doing. Ivan flip-flopping between Ari and Patrick for eight straight episodes, Ari, doing the same thing on her end, bouncing between feelings for Samuel and Ivan with no real throughline connecting any of it.

And then there's Cruz. A grown man pursuing his own son's teenage classmate all season, and the show wraps it up by having him step aside like it's a gracious, mature decision instead of the bare minimum. That's a man stopping something he never should have started, and the show treats it like growth. Sick work by the writers, honestly.

Season 5 isn't the disaster Season 4 was, but it's forgettable. This season made me tired.

The pieces are there for Season 6 to do something interesting. Benjamin is in handcuffs. The Blanco Commerford era is officially over. In theory that clears the stage for a proper reset. Whether the show has the discipline to actually use that space is the only question I have going into the next season. And yes, before you ask: I'll be watching. Against all available evidence and better judgment. Because apparently this is just who I am now.

My Rating: 6.0

What are your thoughts on this season?

Drop it in the comments. I need to know I wasn't alone in this. Also if you somehow enjoyed the Cruz storyline unironically, I really want to understand your reasoning.

← Prev: Season 4 Next: Season 6 →

entry.blogger:metaDescription: Elite used to make me feel things; now it just makes me tired. Here is my breakdown of why Season 5 was such a slog to get through.

entry.title: Best Movies I've Watched This Year (So Far)
entry.content:
I built a database to track every movie and show I've watched since 2025. I know how that sounds.

But it means when someone asks me what's actually been good this year, I don't have to scroll through my brain trying to remember. I just check the database.

This isn't really a recommendation post. I'm not telling you what to watch or building a themed list around a mood. This is just me pulling up my own ratings and counting down the ten movies that scored highest for me so far this year.

No spoilers, just my honest read on how much I enjoyed each one. Some of these are new, some are old, none of them are ranked by anything other than how much they got their hooks into me.

10. Dhurandhar (2025) - My rating: 7.7

I saw a tweet about this one and figured I'd give it a shot. Dhurandhar is a Bollywood spy thriller from Aditya Dhar, starring Ranveer Singh as an undercover Indian intelligence agent who infiltrates Karachi's criminal underworld. It's a big, loud, ambitious movie and it does not feel like a typical Bollywood outing.

The ending caught me off guard because it just sort of stops. Turns out that's because the story splits into two parts, and the sequel already dropped earlier this year (I haven't gotten to it yet). Fair warning: this thing runs long, over three and a half hours long. But it's the kind of long where you settle into it rather than fight it. Take your time, don't rush it, and you'll be fine.

09. End of Watch (2012) - My rating: 7.9

My brother put me onto this one. He just said "watch it" and didn't elaborate, so I did. End of Watch follows two LAPD partners, played by Jake Gyllenhaal and Michael Pena, patrolling one of the roughest divisions in South Central LA. It's not a movie I'm rushing back to rewatch, but it did exactly what it set out to do.

The found footage style takes a minute to adjust to, but once it clicks, the friendship between these two carries the whole thing. Gyllenhaal and Pena have the kind of chemistry that makes their banter feel completely unscripted, and that's what sticks with you more than the action does.

08. The Gift (2015) - My rating: 8.3

I'd heard about this one for years and never got around to it. Watched it this year and holy shit. The Gift is unnerving from the first scene to the last. Jason Bateman and Rebecca Hall play a married couple who run into an old acquaintance from Bateman's character's past, played by Joel Edgerton (who also wrote and directed this, which I didn't know going in).

What starts as an awkward reunion slowly turns into something much darker, and the film never rushes it. The tension builds so gradually you don't notice how uncomfortable you've gotten until the ending hits, and that ending will sit with you in a way you don't see coming.

07. Marty Supreme (2025) - My rating: 8.6

This one gave me Uncut Gems vibes immediately, and it turns out that's not a coincidence: it's directed by Josh Safdie, solo this time without his brother Benny. Not that it's operating on the exact same level, but the anxiety it creates is the same kind. Timothee Chalamet plays Marty Mauser, a hustler in 1950s New York obsessed with becoming a table tennis champion nobody respects.

It's noisy. There is so much happening on screen at once that my own anxiety spiked watching it. It took me two days to finish because I needed breaks between sittings. That's not a complaint, that's just what this movie does to you.

06. No Other Choice (2025) - My rating: 8.8

This one starts out as soft workplace comedy. A man loses his job. His family starts struggling to keep up with bills. And then everything switches up so fast you start questioning what you're even watching anymore. No Other Choice is directed by Park Chan-wook, and once you know that, the shift makes a lot more sense.

Lee Byung-hun plays a paper industry veteran who gets laid off after 25 years and decides the only way to secure a new job is to eliminate the competition, literally. It's so fucking good. The runtime is a little long, but every minute of it earns its place once the back half kicks in.

05. Transformers One (2024) - My rating: 8.9

This is the best Transformers movie ever made, and once you watch it, you'll realize I'm not exaggerating. It's an animated prequel that tells the origin story of Optimus Prime and Megatron, back when they were coworkers named Orion Pax and D-16 working in the mines of Cybertron.

It got absolutely brutal marketing, the kind that made it look like a kids' movie and tanked it at the box office despite great reviews. The story is layered, the friendship at the center of it is the actual emotional core, and the betrayal hits harder than anything in the live action films. I loved it. I just hope we eventually get the sequel this story deserves.

04. John Wick (2014) - My rating: 9.0

This was a rewatch, and according to my database it's sitting near the top of my ratings for the entire year so far. That should tell you something. John Wick is so stylish, so confident in what it is. The action choreography still holds up over a decade later, and Keanu Reeves brings a level of physical commitment that elevates the whole thing.

No disrespect to him, but I say this with love: I didn't expect him to actually act in this one, and he does. What started as a simple revenge movie about a man and his dog ended up kicking off one of the most beloved action franchises of the last decade, and watching the first one again reminds you exactly why.

03. Hoppers (2026) - My rating: 9.0

I only watched this because of a TikTok edit, which feels like a very 2026 way to discover a Pixar movie. Hoppers follows Mabel, a college student who transfers her consciousness into a robotic beaver to communicate with animals and protect their habitat from a mayor's development plans.

I had an absolute blast from start to finish. The story gets genuinely chaotic about halfway through and just never lets up after that. The voice cast, especially Piper Curda and Bobby Moynihan, fully commits to the insanity of the premise, and the movie is better for it.

02. Predator: Killer of Killers (2025) - My rating: 9.4

I'd never seen the original Predator movies. The first one I actually watched was Prey, and I liked it well enough. So when I heard there was a new animated Predator anthology coming out, I went in with low expectations. I came out with my mind blown.

Killer of Killers tells three separate stories across three different eras, a Viking raid, a feudal Japan duel between brothers, and a WWII dogfight, all building toward something bigger. The art style is gorgeous. Slick, brutal, and confident in a way that animated action rarely is. I need more of this.

01. The Handmaiden (2016) - My rating: 9.4

I'm a little late getting to this one, but I'm glad I finally did. The Handmaiden is told from multiple perspectives, and without spoiling anything, it's a queer love story that actually gets to have a good ending. That alone makes it worth the watch.

The way the story keeps recontextualizing itself as it unfolds is what makes it unforgettable. I love this movie so much. It's the kind of film that rewards a rewatch almost immediately because you start noticing what was hiding in plain sight the whole time.

Have you watched any of these? And more importantly, what's been the best thing you've watched so far this year?

Drop it in the comments. I'm always looking for the next thing to add to the database.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.

entry.title: Is Breaking Bad Really The Best Show Ever Made?
entry.content:
Breaking Bad is one of those shows the internet will not stop talking about. Everyone acts like it's basically a religion.

But once you actually sit down and watch it, there's this weird gap between what people promised you and what you're actually getting, at least at first. Let me explain what I mean.

This post contains spoilers for AMC's Breaking Bad

Let's look at the numbers

Breaking Bad sits at a 9.5 out of 10 on IMDb, which is one of the highest scores any TV show has ever gotten. Rotten Tomatoes has it at 96%, and regular viewers rated it even higher at 97%. The Irish Times even said it holds a Guinness World Record for being the most critically loved show of its time. That's a lot of praise.

And then there's Season 5 Episode 14 (Ozymandias), for 13 years this was the only episode of TV ever to get a flat-out perfect 10/10 on IMDb. Rolling Stone put it at the top of their "greatest TV episodes ever" list back in 2024. That perfect score finally slipped to a 9.9 in early 2026, but only because a fandom war with a newer show led to a bunch of coordinated low ratings. Even that whole drama tells you something about how intense this fanbase is.

So yeah, on paper, this show is basically untouchable. The real question is whether it actually feels that way when you're watching it.

So what's the show actually about

Breaking Bad ran on AMC from January 2008 to September 2013, five seasons total. Walter White is a high school chemistry teacher in Albuquerque who finds out he has terminal lung cancer, and decides to start cooking meth so his family isn't left broke after he's gone. He brings in his old student Jesse Pinkman to help, and what starts as a desperate move to protect his family slowly turns into something way darker, because it turns out Walt is really, really good at being bad.

Vince Gilligan created it, and his pitch was famously simple: turn Mr. Chips into Scarface. That one line sounds simple, but the show takes its time with it in a way most shows just don't. Gilligan wasn't trying to make a typical crime drama. He was trying to show a full moral collapse, step by step, without skipping anything. That's the best and most frustrating thing about the show, depending on where you are in it.

Walter White's slow fall is really the whole point

The reason people can't stop talking about this show is Walt. Cranston plays him in a way that makes it hard to pin the guy down. At the start you actually feel for him. He's underpaid, disrespected, working two jobs just to get by, and clearly smarter than the life he's stuck in. Then he gets a cancer diagnosis and finds out his family will be financially wrecked because of it. You get why he makes that first bad call. You might even be on his side for it.

But the real question the show is asking isn't "why did he start doing this?" It is "when did he stop being the victim?" There's that line in Season 4, "I am the one who knocks" where he basically flips the script on Skyler and uses fear to control her instead of protecting her. And then the finale gives you the real answer when he finally admits, "I did it for me. I liked it. I was good at it. And I was really... I was alive." That's the show quietly confirming what it's been building toward the whole time. He wasn't doing any of this for his family. He was doing it because it made him feel powerful, after years of feeling small. The cancer was just the excuse he needed to finally become who he always thought he should've been. Watching a guy justify every terrible thing he does, one step at a time, is weirdly gripping television. And the show's answer, given slowly over five seasons, is yeah. He was always like this underneath it all.

Jesse Pinkman is why you keep watching

The thing about Walt is that he's fascinating, but he's not really likeable. And the show knows that, which is exactly why Jesse exists. Jesse is basically the heart of the whole thing. He's the one who still has a conscience after Walt's has completely checked out. He actually feels the weight of what they're doing, while Walt just buries it under excuses and ego.

Their whole dynamic works because they're two totally different reactions to the same mess. Walt shuts down and rationalizes everything. Jesse feels every bit of it and falls apart. And as Walt becomes less and less someone you can root for, Jesse becomes the guy you actually want to see make it out okay. Some of the hardest moments in the whole show come from watching Jesse slowly figure out exactly who Walt really is.

The Gus Fring effect

Ask any Breaking Bad fan when the show really clicked for them, and most people will say the same thing: when Gus Fring showed up. Played by Giancarlo Esposito, Gus runs a chicken restaurant chain called Los Pollos Hermanos as a front for his meth operation, all while staying so squeaky clean publicly that he's friendly with the local DEA. He's not loud or threatening in the usual villain way. He's polite, professional, smiles at his customers, his employees love him, and all that good stuff.

Then in the Season 4 premiere, without saying a word, he slits a guy's throat with a box cutter right in front of Walt and Jesse, just to prove a point. Then he calmly takes off his hazmat suit, cleans up, and asks if anyone needs medical help. That scene is scarier than any typical loud villain moment because of how cold it was. The message is clear: I am more disciplined than you, I am more patient than you, and I can ruin you whenever I decide to. Esposito has said he made a point of not playing Gus as a stereotype, leaning into the fact that real people have light and dark in them instead of playing a cartoon bad guy. That choice is exactly why it works so well. His arrival in Season 3 is the moment the show goes from "really good" to "that show everyone won't shut up about."

Let's be honest about the slow start though

None of the high praises changes the fact that the first two seasons ask a lot of you. Even critics agree Season 1 is the weakest part of the show. It has an 86% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, which sounds great until you compare it to the near perfect scores the later seasons get. Early on it feels more like a suburban family drama than a crime thriller. Walt and Jesse fumbling through their first cook in a janky RV. There are long stretches of tension between Walt and Skyler at home. The pace is slow and can feel like a slog if you're used to faster shows. Season 1 also got cut short by the writers' strike, so it only has seven episodes and never really builds to a proper climax.

The thing is, the early seasons aren't actually bad. If you rewatch them once you know the whole story, they're kind of chilling. Every small selfish choice Walt makes, every smooth lie, hits completely differently once you know who he becomes. But you don't know any of that on your first watch, especially when the internet is telling you this is the best show ever made before you've even hit play. That hype creates a weird kind of pressure. You're sitting there in Season 1 watching Walt deal with a school bully and argue with his son about a car, wondering if everyone online lied to you. The show does eventually become everything people promised. But that gap between the hype and the early episodes is real, and it trips a lot of people up.

The ending actually works

The finale does something most shows never manage. It gives you what you want without cheating to get there. Walt doesn't get some clean escape or a redemption arc that wipes away what he did. He gets to wrap up his loose ends on his own terms, protecting his family, settling scores with the people who wronged him, setting Jesse free, and then he dies in the meth lab, surrounded by the equipment he ended up loving more than his own family. It just fits because it's what the story had built toward.

By the time the finale hits, Ozymandias had already done most of the heavy lifting anyway, with the deaths, the confessions, everything Walt built coming apart. The finale just had to land the plane, and it does. Most shows this hyped up fumble the ending and make you regret the time you put in. Breaking Bad doesn't do that, so when you tell a friend to watch it, you don't have to give the "yeah but the ending kind of sucks" disclaimer.

So, is it actually the greatest show ever made?

Breaking Bad is genuinely well made, with a clear vision, great performances, and a great ending. Watching one man completely fall apart morally, with no shortcuts taken, is one of the best things TV has ever pulled off. It even gave us Gus Fring, one of the best villains.

But greatest show ever made? That's where things get complicated. Going in with the reputation the internet has built up around this show almost makes the rough early episodes harder to get through, because you're comparing them to a legend they haven't earned yet on screen. 

I think, the greatest show ever probably shouldn't require you to push through a patience test before it becomes the greatest show ever. That said, still watch it. Just go in with normal expectations instead of the impossible ones everyone online hands you. Give it until Season 3. Let Gus show up. You'll get it by then. Just don't be surprised if you spend the first couple seasons wondering what the fuss is about. That's completely normal.

Did the hype mess with your first watch too?

Drop a comment and let me know, did you push through the slow start or bail before it got good? And do you think "greatest show ever" is earned here, or is it just internet hyperbole at this point?

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Does the hype match the reality? An exploration of Breaking Bad and why you should push past the slow start to see it for yourself.

entry.title: Quick Take: Squid Game
entry.content:
Squid Game is still worth it, even with everything that came after Season 1.

Look, I could open this post by telling you Squid Game is a masterpiece. I could also say Season 1 was lightning in a bottle and everything after was Netflix squeezing money from a finished story. Both of those takes exist somewhere on the internet, neither of them is quite right.

Here's the version I actually believe: Squid Game is a great show that made some bad strategic decisions, and a lot of my frustration around Seasons 2 and 3 has less to do with the quality of the writing and more to do with how Netflix chose to release it. We'll get to that. But first, let me tell you who made this thing.

Hwang Dong-hyuk first wrote the idea for Squid Game in 2008. He was pulling from his own financial struggles and from the kind of class inequality that was baked into South Korean society in ways that were hard to talk about directly. He took the script around to studios for years but nobody wanted it. He eventually shelved it and moved on to other projects. Then Netflix came looking for international content in 2019, picked it up, and the rest of it is one of the most surreal success stories in the history of television. Season 1 dropped September 17, 2021 and it hit number one in 94 countries. It pulled 265 million views in its first 91 days. By the time Season 2 launched in December 2024, Season 1 had 330 million viewers and 2.8 billion hours watched. The stress of making it cost Hwang six teeth. Six actual teeth.

This post contains minor spoilers for Netflix's Squid Game

What makes Season 1 untouchable

The games in Season 1 are Red Light Green Light, honeycomb carving, tug-of-war, marbles, glass stepping stones, and the title game. These are things Korean kids played in the street. They're drenched in nostalgia. And the show takes that nostalgia and weaponizes it completely, dropping adults at their economic rock bottom into a structure designed for childhood play, then watching them tear each other apart for a prize worth 45.6 billion won that most of them won't live to collect.

It works because the desperation is real before anyone steps into an arena. The main character, Seong Gi-hun, has gambled away everything. He borrows from loan sharks, misses his daughter's birthday, can't stop even when he knows he should. He's technically not a good person, and the show is smart enough to fill the other 455 spots with people who each have their own version of that same story. A North Korean defector trying to get her family out. A man with terminal cancer who figures this is the only gamble left worth taking. A Pakistani migrant worker owed wages he'll never see through normal channels. Season 1 builds an ensemble that feels like a cross-section of everyone the economy has already failed, and the stakes hit differently because the show slows down enough to make you care about specific people before it starts killing them.

The visual design is doing a lot of work too. The dormitory looks like an enormous pastel-colored playground. The guards are in identical pink coveralls and animal masks. The administrators are all sharp angles and black suits. There's something genuinely wrong about how beautiful it all looks, and that wrongness is entirely the point. It's one of the most visually coherent shows I've seen.

Where it starts to slip

Hwang was always clear that he conceived this as a standalone story. But Netflix had a show that generated an estimated 900 million dollars in value for the platform, paid him his flat contractual fee for it, and then came back with an offer to continue it. He's been pretty open about the fact that his compensation from Season 1 didn't match what the show was actually worth, so coming back for Seasons 2 and 3 was partly about correcting that. Can't blame him for it.

In Season 2, Gi-hun is back in South Korea, determined to find the recruiter and get back into the games to take them down from the inside. He does. He tries to organize a rebellion among the players and it fails badly. The season had things going for it: some of the new players were interesting, the dynamic between Gi-hun and the Front Man. Seven episodes, a fresh cast of players, and then a cliffhanger ending that left everyone waiting six months for Season 3.

Season 3 arrived June 27, 2025, and picked up exactly where Season 2 stopped. Which confirmed what a lot of viewers suspected: Seasons 2 and 3 are functionally one 13-episode season that Netflix split into two release events. The pacing only makes sense when you understand that. Watching them as separate seasons with months between them, is a momentum killer.

The VIP characters, the obscenely wealthy spectators who fund the whole operation and watch it for entertainment, remain one of the show's most persistent weaknesses across all three seasons. Rich people treating human suffering as a spectator sport, it's exactly the kind of critique the show should be making. But the characters are so thinly written and so unconvincingly performed that they end up undercutting the commentary.

The Front Man, played by Lee Byung-hun, is where Season 3 most clearly wastes its best card. Lee Byung-hun is a compelling actor. The character is one of the show's most layered: a man who once played the games, won, and then chose to serve the machine rather than burn it down. He's the dark mirror to Gi-hun. The confrontation between them is supposed to be the thematic payoff for everything that comes after Season 1 and Season 3 barely uses him. He disappears for most of it and comes back for a finale that doesn't give that confrontation anywhere near the weight it needed.

What holds up anyway

Here's the thing though: the show never got lazy about what it looks like. Production values stayed extraordinary across all three seasons: Season 1 cost around 21 million dollars, Season 2 jumped to 84 million, and Season 3 had 69 million for just six episodes. The game environments stay inventive, the color work stays sharp.

Lee Jung-jae holds every season together. He won the Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series for Season 1, the first Korean actor to win in that category, and his performance across the full run earns it. Gi-hun is stubborn and grief-soaked and doesn't become heroic cleanly, and Lee never lets the character get reduced to a symbol. Even when the writing gets soft around him or the plot asks him to do something that stretches logic, the performance stays true.
