The class argument never disappears either, even when the execution wobbles. Every season keeps returning to the same core idea: the game isn't the problem. The game is just a more honest version of the world these people already live in. The arena kills you fast but the world outside kills you slow. That idea, which Season 1 states plainly is why this show resonated globally. Debt and desperation aren't uniquely Korean experiences.

The actual problem with Seasons 2 and 3

A lot of what people read as creative failure in the later seasons is actually structural failure caused by how Netflix released them.

Season 1 dropped all nine episodes at once and the world binged it together. That communal experience is part of why it felt like such a moment. Season 2 dropped seven episodes on December 26, 2024, ended on a cliffhanger, and made viewers wait until June 2025 for the rest. Six months, for the back half of what is functionally one story.

That's a subscriber retention strategy and it worked commercially: Season 2 hit 68 million views in four days, breaking the premiere record that had been held by Wednesday. Season 3 hit 106 million views in ten days, the fastest any Netflix series in any language has ever reached that number. The numbers are great, Netflix wins.

But the storytelling takes a real hit. Momentum matters in serialized narrative. When you split one story in half and force a six-month gap, you're asking the audience to carry emotional investment that the narrative wasn't built to support across that kind of distance. Viewers forget who characters are, subplots that were building slowly in Season 2 feel cold when Season 3 picks them up. The continuity breaks in ways that make the writing look weaker than it actually is.

So should you watch it?

Yes. Start from Season 1 and watch through Episode 6, the marbles episode, which is one of the best single episodes of television in recent memory. If the show hasn't grabbed you completely by then, it probably won't. If it has, you're finishing it.

The later seasons are imperfect: the release strategy was cynical, the VIPs never worked. But Season 1 alone is some of the best TV of the decade, and Seasons 2 and 3 watched back to back, without the enforced wait, are a better experience than most people who watched them as they aired will give them credit for.

Did the ending satisfy you, or do you think the show used up everything it had in Season 1?

Let me know in the comments. I'm especially curious from anyone who binge-watched the whole thing straight through whether the later seasons felt different that way.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Stunning visuals meet high-stakes tension. Here is my quick take on Squid Game and why it remains a must-watch despite its uneven later seasons.

entry.title: Let's Talk About Bill Skarsgård.
entry.content:
There are actors who are good at their job, and then there's Bill Skarsgård, who seems to operate on a completely different frequency.

Son of Swedish acting legend Stellan Skarsgård and younger brother to Alexander (True Blood) and Gustaf (Vikings), Bill has been around the industry his whole life but he's not coasting on a famous last name. From his breakout in the Swedish film Simple Simon (2010) to his current status as one of Hollywood's most compelling leading men, Skarsgård has built a career defined by bold choices, full physical transformation, and a rare ability to be charming and terrifying, sometimes in the exact same scene. That combination is almost impossible to pull off. He makes it look easy.

The Magnetism

Bill Skarsgård has this very specific quality: warmth and menace living in the same face at the same time. His eyes, his voice, his whole physical presence is calibrated somewhere between "someone you'd trust immediately" and "someone you probably shouldn't." It creates this low-level tension whenever he appears on screen, even in quieter scenes, because your brain just can't fully relax around him. And that's not a trick of makeup or direction. That's just him.

What makes it work is how expressive he is without announcing it. There's a lot happening behind his eyes in almost every scene. The drooling, wandering-eyed chaos of Pennywise. The cool, aristocratic stillness of the Marquis in John Wick: Chapter 4. The hollow, ancient dread radiating off Count Orlok in Nosferatu. Each one feels like a completely different person, and yet the same fierce commitment runs through all of it. That's magnetism.

The Project Selection

Look at the shape of his career and you'll notice something: Bill Skarsgård doesn't move in a straight line. He zigged into horror with Hemlock Grove (2013), Netflix's early vampire series, then zagged into spy territory with Atomic Blonde (2017), then exploded into the mainstream as Pennywise in IT (2017). From there, instead of cashing in on back-to-back horror projects, he went sideways into dark drama with The Devil All the Time (2020), a home-invasion thriller with Barbarian (2022), a villain role in John Wick: Chapter 4 (2023), a completely unhinged deaf-mute revenge film called Boy Kills World (2024), and then prestige horror under Robert Eggers as Count Orlok in Nosferatu (2024).

That's not someone chasing a formula. That's someone deeply invested in staying unpredictable. He keeps finding new rooms in his range and kicking the doors open. You never quite know what version of him is coming next, and that's a big part of why he's so worth following.

The Range vs. The Commitment

Some actors jump genres and you can still see the seams. You never fully buy in because you're always vaguely aware of the performance happening. Skarsgård doesn't have that problem. When he disappears into a role, he's gone. Pennywise is not Bill Skarsgård in clown makeup. Count Orlok is not Pennywise in a cape. The Marquis is not Count Orlok in a suit. Each one is a full reset, built from scratch, with different physicality, different voice, different internal logic.

And the method behind it is fascinating. The Pennywise lip curl? Something he'd been doing since childhood that finally found the right character. The wandering eye? A real condition he controls deliberately, weaponized perfectly for a creature that doesn't quite understand how a human face is supposed to work. He mines himself for the role rather than layering a costume on top. That's why the performances feel lived-in from the very first frame.

The Underrate Factor

Mention Bill Skarsgård to a casual moviegoer and they'll say Pennywise. They might not even know his name, but they know the clown. And while that speaks to how iconic that performance is, it also means everything else he's done flies under the radar for most people. The fact that he played a cold, elegant villain in one of the biggest action franchises on the planet, then turned around and headlined a Robert Eggers film that earned Academy Award nominations, in roughly the same stretch of his career, is remarkable. Most actors would build an entire era around either of those. He just kept going.

The gap between his talent and his mainstream recognition is baffling. He's been working since he was ten years old, and the output has never been lazy or safe. That makes him the kind of name that film people quietly pass to each other as a recommendation. It feels like only a matter of time before the wider world catches up.

The Scene Stealer

The storm drain scene in IT (2017). No competition. Georgie crouches down at the edge of the gutter, and there's Pennywise crammed impossibly into the drain, offering back the paper boat with that wide, wrong smile. What Skarsgård does in those few minutes is so precise it still holds up to frame-by-frame analysis years later.

He's playing something ancient and ravenous that's also working very hard to perform friendliness for its prey. The drooling, apparently unscripted, and the wandering eye he deliberately deployed combine to create an organism barely holding a mask in place. You can feel the thing straining underneath. It's the moment you realize this isn't just a scary movie clown. This is something that shouldn't exist. All of that, without ever raising his voice.

TWC Recommends

  • The Entry Point: Start with IT (2017) if you somehow haven't seen it. But if you have and want a completely different side of him, go straight to John Wick: Chapter 4 (2023). He's all polished menace and dry arrogance, and he carries it without the safety net of heavy prosthetics or horror atmosphere. A great showcase for how well he holds his own in a big action franchise.
  • The Deep Cut: Clark (2022) on Netflix. It's a Swedish limited series where Skarsgård plays real-life criminal Clark Olofsson, the man whose story inspired the term Stockholm Syndrome. The show is chaotic, darkly funny, and wildly stylish, and it gives him room to be charming, monstrous, and oddly pathetic all in the same episode. It's the kind of performance that refuses to fit any single category, which makes it the most him of anything he's ever done. Required viewing.

What's your favorite Bill Skarsgård performance, and do you think he gets enough credit for his range outside of Pennywise?

Drop your take in the comments, and if there's another actor you think deserves the Spotlight treatment, let me know.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Beyond Pennywise, Bill Skarsgård is a master of total transformation. I break down his best roles and why he deserves more mainstream recognition.

entry.title: REVIEW: FROM Season 3
entry.content:
After two seasons that had me fully hooked, this one was the weakest of the three so far.

It is not a bad season by any means, but compared to what came before it, it felt like it was running in place for a good chunk of its runtime. The town is colder this season, the residents are more desperate, and somehow, after everything they have survived, they still cannot manage to talk to each other properly.

This post contains spoilers for season 3.

The Plot

Boyd opens the season feeling the town slip away from him as the weather turns colder and the people around him grow more desperate by the day. Jim and Kenny head into the forest looking for Tabitha, who is off on her own frantic search, and that separation sets the tone for a season where everyone seems to be chasing something on their own instead of together. The town says goodbye to one of their own early on, Fatima's health starts to decline in a way that worries everyone around her, and Tabitha ends up finding help from an ally nobody expected.

From there, the season moves through Kenny leading a group into the forest hunting for food while Donna and Ellis try to talk Boyd out of a plan that could get people killed. Tabitha makes a discovery that genuinely messes with her sense of reality, and Fatima starts questioning whether her unborn baby is even safe in a town like this. When new arrivals show up at nightfall, Boyd is forced into a decision he clearly does not want to make, and Victor spends this stretch digging into memories from his past, hoping they hold some kind of answer.

The middle of the season slows down to deal with the emotional weight of everything happening. Victor has to face something painful from his history, Julie is left trying to cope with her own trauma, and Boyd starts losing the trust of the people he is supposed to be protecting as his judgment gets questioned more openly. Fatima and Ellis are forced into a major decision about her pregnancy, tension builds inside the Matthews house, and Randall, of all people, opens up to Marielle about what actually scares him.

By the final stretch, concern over Fatima's pregnancy reaches a breaking point, Jade follows a trail of clues into the forest, and Julie and Randall try to grab a moment of normal life in the middle of all the chaos. A tragedy forces accusations into the open, Victor manages to recover memories that had been buried for a long time, and Julie and Ethan start digging into the mysterious ruins out in the woods. The final two episodes turn the tension all the way up, someone from the town goes missing, Boyd gets pushed to his absolute limit as time runs out for someone he loves, and Tabitha's journey ends the season on a genuinely shocking turn.

What worked:

Victor's storyline continues to be the strongest thread the show has, and this season gave him some of his best material yet. Watching him dig through buried memories from his childhood in the town, and finally face a painful piece of his past directly, hit just as hard as I expected it to. He remains the character this show does the most right by, and I will keep saying that every season if it stays true.

The season also deserves credit for at least attempting to address the communication problem I have been complaining about since season 2. When Tabitha comes back, there is a moment where it genuinely looks like the show is going to let its characters actually talk to each other and share what they know. That is progress, even if it does not last, and I will get into why it does not last in a second.

What didn't:

They tried the whole communication thing when Tabitha came back, and then nothing came of it. These town people are honestly insufferable at this point. I do not fully blame them, they are traumatized and scared and stuck in a place that keeps killing people around them, but come on. They do not even do anything useful with the information they have, and they still cannot manage to listen to each other when it matters. At some point this stops being a character flaw and starts being a writing crutch the show leans on to manufacture tension that should not need manufacturing anymore.

Ellis is a waste of a character this season, and I will die on this hill. He is only attached to Fatima and barely exists outside of that connection. It is honestly a little pathetic watching him have almost nothing going on beyond his relationship to her, especially when the show has other characters doing so much more with far less screen time. Kenny is more of a son to Boyd than Ellis will ever be, and the show does not even seem to be hiding that anymore.

The season also ends with another massive cliffhanger, which by this point I expect, but my issue still stands. Communicate! My goodness. This season drags a lot in the middle stretch, the questions keep piling up without matching answers, and word going around is that a chunk of the delay and pacing issues might trace back to the 2023 writers strike affecting the writers room before filming started. I cannot confirm that fully, but if it is true, it would explain a lot about why this season feels less tight than the two before it.

Rating

7.2 out of 10.

Season 3 is still watchable, still has Victor doing the heavy lifting emotionally, and still ends on a cliffhanger that makes me need the next season immediately. But the pacing issues and the refusal of these characters to just talk to one another are dragging the show down in a way it was not doing in season 1 or 2. I am hoping season 4 course corrects, because the bones of this show are still strong even when the execution slips.

PS: Kenny is more of a son to Boyd than Ellis will ever be, and I said what I said.

Am I wrong for thinking Ellis has wasted his entire arc so far, or does anyone actually rate his storyline this season?

Tell me if I am being too harsh on him.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: From season 3 review: Victor gets his best material yet, but the town's refusal to communicate and a saggy middle drag this season down.

entry.title: My Unpopular Actor Opinions
entry.content:
Every fanbase has that group of celebrities everyone loves and you just cannot get the appeal of. This is mine.

The Men

Taron Egerton: He goes first since he is the easiest to actually explain. There is nothing wrong with him exactly, he is just missing that extra gear, the thing that makes me sit forward. Black Bird is probably the best thing he has done, that Apple TV+ miniseries opposite Paul Walter Hauser, and even there Hauser was the highlight for me. Kingsman is still his biggest commercial win, and he is fine as Eggsy, but he was never the reason people showed up. Carry-On is the more recent example. That Netflix Christmas Eve thriller against Jason Bateman ended up being one of the platform's biggest debuts in recent memory, which is great for him, but if you ask me, he was the wrong pick for the lead. The role needed someone who could sell quiet desperation, and Egerton plays everything a little too boyish for that tension to build properly.

Matt Damon: A completely different situation. With pretty much everyone else on this list I have at least sat through their filmography. Not him. If we are counting the Bourne movies that is cheating, since that was my mom's TV choice when I was a kid and I definitely was not paying attention. Never went back after that. No specific incident, no bad performance I can point to, I just never bothered, and two decades later it is basically permanent.

Michael B. Jordan: He comes off as a genuinely nice guy every time I see him interviewed, which makes it harder to explain why I do not care more. People always bring up Black Panther as his big mainstream moment, but honestly that film gets more credit than it deserves, and his performance in it does not change that for me. Outside those, he is fine in a few things I have seen. Just fine. Nothing pulls me toward whatever he does next. I haven't even seen Creed.

Channing Tatum: He does not really need explaining. I do not care, I never have, and I do not expect that to change.

Christian Bale: The hardest one to justify, because objectively he is one of the best actors working right now. The transformations, the accents, the way he vanishes into a role instead of just playing it, all real, all deserved. I am just not a fan.

Terrence Howard: This one's a bit more personal. It is his voice, something about it makes me tune out the second he is on screen. There is one silver lining though: he played James Rhodey Rhodes in the first Iron Man and was originally supposed to come back for the sequel. That did not happen, reportedly over a pay dispute with the studio, and Don Cheadle took over instead. Both of them have said it is water under the bridge now. I am just relieved it worked out that way, because Iron Man 2 with the original casting would have been rough for me to sit through.

The Women

Gal Gadot: She tests my patience the most out of everyone here, because the acting itself just is not good. She seems warm and likable enough in interviews, which almost makes it worse, since people extend her a grace the performances themselves do not earn. The first Wonder Woman got away with a lot because the character was a fish out of water by design, so playing stiff and unsure actually worked in her favor. The sequel removed that safety net completely, and suddenly the limitations were impossible to ignore. I think a lot of people who fell for the first movie quietly noticed during the second, and honestly, that correction was way overdue.

Ruby Rose: She has built a whole career around one expression, and it shows up whether the scene calls for it or not. She broke out on Orange Is the New Black, moved into a run of action roles like Resident Evil, xXx, and John Wick: Chapter 2, and eventually landed the lead on Batwoman. She just tries too hard if you ask me.

Gwyneth Paltrow: This is kind of hard to put a finger on. It's not one bad role I can point to, it's more just her general presence that feels off. Her voice, her eyes, the way she carries herself on camera, something about her always seems slightly removed from everyone else in the scene, like she is not quite from around here. I cannot prove it yet. Still working on that theory.

Joey King: Probably the least fair entry on here, because I do not think this is really about her acting at all. It's her face. Something about it just does not work for me on screen, even though she seems perfectly likable whenever I catch her in interviews. So this one might say more about me being petty than anything about her actual performances. Fair enough, I will take that one on the chin.

So who is on yours?

The actor or actress you cannot fully explain not liking, nothing to do with talent, just something that never clicked. Drop the name in the comments.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A rundown of the actors and actresses who throw me off the second they're on screen.

entry.title: Whatever Happened to Good Dwayne Johnson?
entry.content:
Dwayne Johnson has been a fixture in Hollywood for over two decades now, and somewhere along the way he turned into a completely different actor than the one I actually liked. This Spotlight is basically a breakup letter.

Johnson made his way into movies off the back of a massive wrestling career as The Rock, first showing up on screen in The Mummy Returns in 2001 before headlining The Scorpion King a year later. For a solid stretch after that, he was actually fun to watch. Then something shifted, and here we are.

The Dwayne Johnson I Liked

Early Johnson had real presence. Not the "look how big my arms are" kind, the kind where he could carry a scene on charisma alone. Watch him in The Game Plan, playing a football star who suddenly has to raise the daughter he didn't know existed, and you can see an actor who knows how to be funny and a little vulnerable without losing his screen presence. Same with Tooth Fairy, a silly premise that only works because he commits to it instead of coasting on muscle. That's the version of Dwayne Johnson I signed up for.

The Project Selection

Early on, his choices were actually varied, Get Smart, Tooth Fairy, The Game Plan, Journey 2: The Mysterious Island, Pain & Gain. That last one deserves a shoutout. Michael Bay's Pain & Gain gave him an unhinged, layered performance as a bodybuilder caught up in a kidnapping scheme gone wrong, and it's one of the only times post-wrestling Johnson actually got to play a person instead of a brand.

Then Fast Five happened in 2011, and Luke Hobbs became the role that redefined him. It worked, at first. But somewhere after that, his choices calcified into one formula: unstoppable, indestructible, superhuman. Rampage, San Andreas, and Skyscraper are technically three different movies with three different premises, but they all star the same guy surviving the same kind of catastrophe with the same blank invincibility. Hobbs & Shaw took the bit and ran it into the ground, and it was just tiring to watch.

Then came the real low points. Red One turned into a mess both on screen and off, with reports of a production that ballooned to around $250 million partly because of Johnson's own scheduling issues on set. Black Adam, his big DC swing, lost Warner Bros. an estimated $50 to $100 million against a roughly $195 million budget, and any franchise plans got shelved almost immediately after. Two different genres, two expensive misfires, same problem: leaning on him as the entire selling point wasn't enough anymore.

Range vs. Commitment

This is the part that actually pisses me off, because the range is clearly there when he decides to use it. Pain & Gain proved it years ago. More recently, The Smashing Machine, where he plays real life MMA fighter Mark Kerr under Benny Safdie's direction, is a genuinely strong, stripped down performance. No persona or invincibility gimmick, just a guy dealing with addiction and insecurity. It got a fifteen minute standing ovation at Venice and Golden Globe buzz, even if the box office didn't follow and the Oscar nomination never showed up.

But that's the exception. Most of the time, Johnson picks the version of the role that asks the least of him emotionally and the most of him physically, and he commits to that one note every single time. Full effort, zero range. He shows up, he's massive, and he survives things no human should survive, then he moves on to the next one.

The Drama Follows Him

Behind the scenes, Johnson's had his fair share of noise. The Fast & Furious years brought a very public, very long feud with Vin Diesel, one that reportedly started on the set of The Fate of the Furious and dragged on for years before the two patched things up around Fast X. Tyrese Gibson got pulled into his own back and forth with Johnson too, specifically after Hobbs & Shaw underperformed compared to the mainline franchise. Add in that persistent, half-mocking rumor that he's never actually lost a fight on screen, and the sense that he tried to make himself the new center of the Fast & Furious universe at Diesel's expense, and you get a pattern of a guy who wants to be the biggest name in every single room.

Then there's Red One, where reports about him being chronically late to set, sometimes by hours, came with a detail nobody asked for which he later confirmed to GQ that yes, he peed in bottles on set to save time. He brushed the whole thing off as overblown, and his costar Chris Evans backed him up publicly, but it's exactly the kind of story that sticks to a career already losing goodwill.

And then there's the steroid conversation that just will not die. Johnson has admitted to trying steroids briefly at eighteen or nineteen and has denied using anything since, most recently after showing up noticeably leaner at Venice for The Smashing Machine and catching a fresh wave of speculation online. He calls it "100% not true" every time it comes back up. Believe him or don't, but the fact this conversation keeps resurfacing after two decades says something.

The Moment It Went Too Far

If one scene sums up where his choices ended up, it's that Hobbs & Shaw helicopter bit. Johnson physically holding back a helicopter mid-flight with one arm isn't a cool moment so much as a warning sign, the exact point where "unstoppable" stopped being a character trait and just became the whole personality. It's not an isolated incident either because it has become the blueprint for basically everything he's done since.

Most recently, that same instinct to lean on spectacle over substance showed up again with the live action Moana remake, where his return as Maui came with a wig so widely mocked online that even Weird Al Yankovic joked about the resemblance to his own hair. Johnson laughed it off publicly, but it's one more project riding on his name instead of earning attention on its own.

TWC Recommends

  • The Entry Point: The Game Plan (2007). This is peak actually likeable Dwayne Johnson, funny, a little sentimental, and built around him actually acting instead of surviving explosions. Start here if you want to remember why people liked him in the first place.
  • The Deep Cut: The Smashing Machine (2025) strips the whole persona away completely and this was the proof he could still do it when he wanted to. It's quiet, vulnerable, and easily the best thing he's done in years, even if barely anyone watched it in theaters.

Do you think Dwayne Johnson still has range in him, or has he leaned so far into the invincible action guy thing that there's no coming back?

Drop your take in the comments, I want to know if I'm the only one who misses old Dwayne.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A Spotlight on Dwayne Johnson's career, from underrated early roles to the same superhuman action guy formula on repeat. Where did the range go?

entry.title: The Planet of the Apes Trilogy is Underrated
entry.content:
The Planet of the Apes reboot trilogy does not get nearly enough credit, and I am tired of pretending otherwise.

These are not just good blockbusters, they are great. And if you have actually sat through all three, you already know I am not being dramatic.

Rise came out in 2011 on a $93 million budget and pulled $481.8 million worldwide. Nobody saw that coming. This was a franchise that had already been rebooted once in 2001 under Tim Burton and landed with a thud critically despite turning a profit. The idea of going back to the well again felt desperate rather than promising. It was more than fine. It was the start of one of the most quietly consistent trilogies in modern blockbuster filmmaking. Dawn followed in 2014 and grossed over $710 million worldwide on a budget that ballooned past $170 million. War closed it out in 2017, earning $490 million globally off a roughly $150 million budget. Three films. $1.5 billion combined. Critical scores of 81%, 91%, and 94% on Rotten Tomatoes respectively. A franchise that got better with every single entry. Hall of Fame. No debate.

The Plot (In a Nutshell)

A genetically enhanced chimpanzee named Caesar grows up caught between the human world that raised him and the ape world he belongs to, eventually leading a rebellion that changes the course of both species forever. It starts small, a San Francisco scientist testing an Alzheimer's drug on chimps in the hope of saving his own father, and by the third film it has become a full reckoning between two species fighting over what's left of the planet. Each film picks up where the last one left off, building one continuous story across three chapters without ever losing the emotional thread. No filler. No reset buttons. Just one tight, escalating arc from beginning to end.

My Take

What gets me about this trilogy is how quietly it does everything right. No single film announces itself as a masterpiece. Each one just comes in, does its job with real craft and real feeling, and leaves you sitting there a little stunned by how much you cared. Rise is an origin story that builds every emotional beat without leaning on spectacle. Dawn is a morally complex war film dressed up as a blockbuster sequel that most blockbuster sequels would not have the nerve to attempt. War is a biblical epic that closes the whole thing out with the exact amount of weight it deserves.

Part of why Dawn and War feel so cohesive is that Matt Reeves took over for both, after Rupert Wyatt directed the first one. Reeves reportedly came in on a script that had been written before he signed on, one that pushed the apes further into the future and gave Caesar a smaller role, and asked to rebuild it from the ground up around Caesar's perspective instead. That decision is the reason this trilogy reads as one continuous character study instead of three separate movies wearing the same skin. Three films, two directors, zero drop-off in quality.

The thing that makes all three work is the same thing: character first, spectacle second. Every action sequence in this trilogy exists because of something a character is going through. The Golden Gate Bridge sequence in Rise works because you spent the whole film watching Caesar become the kind of leader capable of it. The dam standoff in Dawn works because you understand every person on both sides of it. The finale of War hits the way it does because you have been with Caesar across three films and you know exactly what it cost him to get there. None of it is decoration. All of it is story.

The Characters

CAESAR: The center of gravity for all three films and one of the great protagonists in modern blockbuster cinema. Andy Serkis builds him from a curious, wide-eyed chimp in Rise into a grieving, conflicted leader in War, and every step of that journey feels completely deserved. The moment in War where Caesar starts recognizing Koba's anger in himself is the best thing the trilogy does, a character terrified of becoming the thing he spent three films fighting against. Serkis does all of this through motion capture, without a single frame of his actual face on screen. That's a remarkable feat of acting, and the Academy still owes him an apology for never giving performance capture the recognition it deserves, even with multiple Saturn Award wins backing him up.

MAURICE: Played by Karin Konoval, the gentle giant of the group and the conscience of the whole operation. The big orangutan who barely raises his voice but somehow always says the most important thing. There's a moment in War where he insists on taking in a mute human girl named Nova that nobody else wants to deal with, and it tells you everything about who Maurice is without a single speech. He just does it. Quiet, observant, and steady in a way that makes him the emotional anchor of every scene he's in. Every great ensemble needs a Maurice.

ROCKET: Played by Terry Notary, who built his entire mo-cap career studying ape and primate movement, and you can feel that training in every scene. When we first meet him in Rise, he's the bully of the primate shelter. Aggressive, dominant, not someone you root for. By the time War rolls around he's one of the first to break rank and follow Caesar on a mission that could get them all killed, purely because he won't let his friend go alone. That arc, from antagonist to devoted companion, is one of the most quietly satisfying character journeys in the whole trilogy. No big speeches. No dramatic turning point moment. Just a character who changed slowly and believably over three films. That kind of restraint is hard to execute and easy to take for granted.

LUCA: Luca doesn't get nearly as much screen time as the others, but his presence carries a quiet dignity the film never has to explain. The loyal gorilla who rides with Caesar on the most dangerous part of the whole journey, and in the moments where the film needs a visual of what loyalty actually looks like, Luca is it.

Honorable Mentions

KOBA: One of the best movie villains of the 2010s and I will die on that hill. Toby Kebbell plays him as a bonobo who was tortured and experimented on by humans for most of his life, and his hatred is not cartoonish or randomly generated. It is fully earned by what he went through. The humans really did do a number on him, and watching him channel all of that pain into something destructive and calculating is disturbing in the best way. He doesn't see the peace Caesar is building as survival. He sees it as submission. The scariest part is that you don't agree with him, but you completely get it. Every scene he shares with Caesar in Dawn is quietly building toward his betrayal, and Kebbell plays the tension so well that you find yourself watching Koba even when he's not the focus of the scene.

COLONEL McCULLOUGH: Exactly the kind of villain War needed for its finale. His full name, J. Wesley McCullough, barely matters next to what Woody Harrelson does with him. He's not driven by cruelty or wounded pride but by cold, terrified logic, a belief that wiping out the apes is the only way to save what's left of humanity from the Simian Flu. What makes him hit harder than a standard movie villain is the personal cost he inflicts before we even properly meet him: he kills Caesar's wife Cornelia and their eldest son Blue Eyes in a raid early in the film, which is exactly why Caesar's quest for revenge feels less like a plot device and more like grief with nowhere else to go. Harrelson plays McCullough's conviction so carefully that there are moments where the argument almost lands before you catch yourself. He's not Koba. He's something different and in some ways more unsettling, a man who has convinced himself that his worst impulses are actually a form of love.

BAD APE: Steve Zahn's Bad Ape is the comic relief War desperately needed and used at exactly the right moments. A hermit ape who escaped a Portland zoo enclosure and survived the Simian Flu years in total isolation, he has no idea how to be around other apes anymore, and that disconnect is where most of the comedy comes from. He brings warmth and real laughs to a film that is otherwise carrying enormous emotional weight.

CHARLES RODMAN: John Lithgow's performance as Will's father, whose Alzheimer's is the original reason the ALZ-112 drug got developed in the first place, gives Rise its most vulnerable and most human moments. The disease taking him piece by piece while Caesar watches is the quiet emotional underpinning of everything that follows. A small role that does enormous work.

Why It Works

This trilogy works because it never once forgets that spectacle without character is just noise. Every action sequence exists because of something a character is going through. The visual effects, handled by WETA Digital across all three films, are some of the best ever committed to screen and hold up completely on rewatch today. But the effects were always in service of the performances underneath them. When Caesar is grieving, you see it in his face in the specific, quiet way a person looks when they're trying to hold it together and failing. When Koba performs friendliness while rage sits just underneath, you catch it in his eyes before anything else in the frame tips you off. The technology gave the actors a way to be fully present, and the result is that you never stop to think about how the apes were made. You just watch them like they're there.

The one honest criticism is that War underperformed commercially relative to its scale, earning $490 million on a budget reported anywhere from $150 to $190 million, which turns into a thin profit once marketing costs get factored in. The trilogy never got the mainstream cultural recognition it deserved during its original run, which is baffling given the quality. Rise got 81% on Rotten Tomatoes. Dawn got 91%. War got 94%. A franchise that improved with every entry, treated its audience as intelligent adults, and stuck its landing. It just did it quietly, and quiet excellence gets overlooked more often than it should. The fact that the franchise was confident enough in this trilogy's foundation to keep building on it, with Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes picking up the story generations later in 2024, says everything about how much groundwork these three films actually laid. That's partly what this post is for.

Final Verdict

The Planet of the Apes reboot trilogy is one of the best things blockbuster filmmaking produced in the 2010s, and it's not particularly close. Three films. One continuous story. Zero filler. Character-first storytelling dressed up in stunning visuals, with a lead performance that should have changed the conversation around motion capture entirely. If you haven't seen it, fix that immediately. If you have, you already know I'm right. Hall of Fame. No debate whatsoever.

These movies have no right being this good, so what is your excuse for sleeping on them?

Drop your film ranking in the comments and tell me which character surprised you the most. And if you are not emotionally wrecked by the end of War, I genuinely want to know how you managed that.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Quiet excellence that improved with every entry. A deep dive into why the Planet of the Apes reboot is the best trilogy you might have missed.

entry.title: Worst Movies I've Watched This Year (So Far)
entry.content:
I already wrote about the best movies I've watched this year, so it only feels right to flip it and talk about the bad ones too.

These are the movies that either just didn't work for me, or were so bad they somehow became good again. My apologies in advance if you loved anything on this list.

I'm counting down from number 10, the least painful of the bunch, all the way to number 1, the one that hurt the most.

10. Goat (2026) - My rating: 6.2

This is an animated sports comedy from Sony Pictures Animation, the same studio behind the Spider-Verse movies. It follows Will, a small goat who gets a shot to play roarball, a basketball-style sport dominated by bigger, fiercer animals. The animation is genuinely good. I like the artstyle, it's got that same stylized energy you'd expect from the Spider-Verse team.

But the story is so predictable I could see every beat coming from a mile away. It's just an hour and 39 minutes of average. Not bad, just forgettable.

09. Anaconda (2025) - My rating: 6.0

I actually tried avoiding this one for a while before I finally caved and watched it. Anaconda is a meta comedy where Jack Black and Paul Rudd play lifelong friends who decide to remake their favorite cult movie from childhood, the original 1997 Anaconda, deep in the Amazon. Of course, a real giant anaconda shows up and turns their shoot into a survival situation.

It's just so fucking stupid, and a little cringe if I'm honest. I don't know how much they paid Paul Rudd and Jack Black to be in this, but it feels like a lot for how dumb the whole thing is.

08. Whistle (2026) - My rating: 5.7

This is a horror mystery about a group of high school misfits who find an ancient Aztec death whistle. Blow it, and the sound summons your future death to come hunt you down. It was just so bland and boring. Imagine a boring horror movie.

The acting is subpar, the scares are weak, nothing about this one really worked. It's honestly so disappointing, especially with a premise that had real potential.

07. War Machine (2026) - My rating: 5.4

This one switched genres on me halfway through and I was not ready for it. It starts as a grounded military drama about a soldier going through Army Ranger training, and then suddenly we're in alien shooting machine territory. What the hell?

The acting is decent, Alan Ritchson is a believable lead, but my goodness is the plot dumb. It plays like a cheaper Predator with a Transformers paint job, and it never quite earns the tonal whiplash it puts you through.

06. Mercy (2026) - My rating: 5.0

This one stars Chris Pratt and Rebecca Ferguson. The premise is actually interesting on paper: a detective accused of murdering his wife has 90 minutes to prove his innocence to an AI judge. But in execution, it's just Chris Pratt's face for the entire runtime since his character is strapped to a chair the whole movie.

If you want a movie that uses this kind of screen-and-camera setup well, just go watch Missing or Searching instead. Those actually use the format to build tension. This one just traps you in a room with Pratt's face.

05. Jurassic World Dominion (2022) - My rating: 4.7

Story-wise, this is shite. They brought back the original Jurassic Park characters, Sam Neill, Laura Dern, Jeff Goldblum, and I just did not care. The 4.7 rating exists purely because of the dinosaurs.

Take those away and this movie gets a 1 from me, easy. It's a perfect example of a franchise running on fumes and hoping nostalgia covers for a lack of actual story.

04. Shelter (2026) - My rating: 4.5

A typical Jason Statham film, through and through. He plays a former MI6 assassin hiding out on a remote Scottish island who ends up protecting a young girl after rescuing her during a storm. It's predictable from start to finish, and the action scenes are pretty meh by Statham standards.

But I will always support Jason. The man knows his lane and he stays in it, even when the movie itself isn't doing him any favors.

03. The VelociPastor (2018) - My rating: 4.0

Oh boy. This is a micro-budget film made for around $35,000, about a priest who turns into a velociraptor and fights ninjas. It is so bad it's actually good. The acting is shite, the effects are even worse, the action scenes are terrible in the most charming way possible.

I had an absolute blast watching this one. It fully knows what it is and commits to the bit completely, and that's exactly why it works.

02. The Last Airbender (2010) - My rating: 3.0

Awful. Just awful. This is the 2010 M. Night Shyamalan movie based on the genuinely excellent animated show Avatar: The Last Airbender. Character names got pronounced wrong, the elemental bending looked stiff and lame on screen, and he changed so many things that made the original show so good and somehow ruined nearly all of it.

Fans have memed this movie so hard over the years that some genuinely joke it doesn't exist. I understand why.

01. Kung Fu Panda 4 (2024) - My rating: 2.0

This movie was not needed. Everything about it sucked. The moral lesson felt recycled, the Furious Five barely show up despite being a core part of the franchise's identity, the plot is thin, and the villain is weak as hell.

They just shat all over a franchise that used to actually mean something, and I am still livid about it months later.

Did any of your least favorites make this list? Or am I about to start a fight in the comments?

Let me know what you'd add to my worst-of pile. I clearly have room for more disappointment in my life.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A personal countdown of the 10 worst movies I've watched this year so far, ranked using my own movie tracking database. No spoilers, just brutal hones

entry.title: REVIEW: The King of Pigs.
entry.content:
I finished The King of Pigs at some unreasonable hour of the night and just sat there for a while after it ended.

Not because I was processing some big twist. Because I needed a minute before I could go back to being a normal person.

The King of Pigs is a 2022 Korean thriller, twelve episodes, that aired on TVING. It's adapted by screenwriter Tak Jae-young and directed by Kim Dae-jin for Studio Dragon, based on Yeon Sang-ho's 2011 animated film of the same name. Yeon later went on to direct Train to Busan, and the DNA of that same unsparing instinct runs through this drama too.

This post contains minor spoilers for TVING's The King of Pigs.

The Plot

The story is built around a specific hierarchy that existed in Korean schools: pigs and dogs. Students from poor families were labeled pigs. Students from wealthy families were dogs, and the dogs didn't just look down on the pigs, they brutalized them, with the tacit permission of teachers and administrators who either didn't notice or didn't care.

Twenty years later, Hwang Kyung-min (Kim Dong-wook), one of the former pigs, has rebuilt a life that looks stable from the outside. Then something snaps, and he starts hunting down the people who tormented him. Investigating the murders is Detective Jung Jong-suk (Kim Sung-kyu), who was also a pig back then, also shaped permanently by what happened. The killer isn't hiding from him either, he's sending Jong-suk messages, naming himself, wanting to be seen by the one person who might actually understand.

Holding the whole thing together is Kim Cheol, the King of Pigs the title refers to, seen mostly through flashbacks. He was the lowest of the low in school and became something unexpected in that environment: a protector, a kid with nothing to lose who decided to fight back. He's the character the show loves most and treats most cruelly, and his arc is the emotional spine of the whole series.

What worked:

Kim Dong-wook plays Kyung-min without letting him become a simple villain. You watch him polished and controlled in the present, then watch the flashbacks showing what was done to him as a child, and the show keeps asking you to hold both of those realities at once. It doesn't ask you to sympathize with the murders, it asks you to understand them, and that's a much harder thing to pull off convincingly.

Kim Sung-kyu's Jong-suk carries the same damage but channeled into becoming someone who hunts killers for a living. He's the closest thing the show has to a good guy, and it never lets him be purely good either. He knows things about the past he hasn't said, made choices back then that aren't clean, and Kim holds all of that history in how the character sits in every scene.

What separates this from most bullying dramas is that it refuses to treat the trauma as backstory. The flashbacks don't explain the murder investigation, they run parallel to it, given equal weight, refusing to recede. By the midpoint, everything happening in the present is still happening twenty years ago. The murders aren't a plot, they're a continuation.

The ending doesn't hand you a clean way to feel about any of it either. Kyung-min is committing murders, and some of the people he's hunting destroyed lives without ever facing consequences. Jong-suk is doing his job while carrying his own unanswered compromises from that school. The show holds all of it at once and refuses to resolve the tension by declaring one of them right. What it's really asking is whether justice that arrives twenty years late, through illegal violence, still counts as justice, and it leaves that question sitting there instead of answering it for you.

What didn't:

The bullying sequences are genuinely rough to get through, and the show does not ease up once. I get why it's shot the way it is, softening it would undercut the whole point, but there were stretches where I had to pause and step away, and I don't think every viewer is going to want to push through that.

The dogs, the actual people Kyung-min is hunting, never feel like more than targets. They show up, they get their scene, and then they're gone, with almost none of the interiority the three leads get. That imbalance started to bother me the more episodes I got through, because a couple of the kills ended up feeling like the plot checking a box instead of a confrontation that had been built up to.

Rating

9.0 out of 10.

The imbalance in how much depth the leads get versus everyone else keeps this from a perfect score, but everything the show is actually trying to do, it does with total conviction. Twelve episodes, pacing that never lets up, and an ending that refuses to let you feel settled about any of it. That's rare, and it's why this one's stuck with me longer than most.

Has this one found you yet, or am I about to ruin your next few evenings?

Drop a comment below. I need someone else to process the Kim Cheol of it all with.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: The King of Pigs is a psychological revenge thriller that is criminally overlooked. I break down why this unhinged series is a must-watch.

entry.title: RECAP: Elite Season 4
entry.content:
Half the original cast was gone, the internet was already in meltdown mode, and I went in bracing myself. Turns out I wasn't bracing hard enough.

As you know several of the original cast had left the show. People who had been there from the very beginning, characters who were the backbone of what made Elite worth watching in the first place. That kind of shakeup is never not worrying. I had already seen the noise online: Reddit threads, Twitter arguments, TikTok videos of people completely losing it over this season. But internet reactions are always dialed up to eleven. You can never fully trust the doomsday energy of a fandom mid-crisis. So I told myself: surely it can't be that bad. This is Elite. The show knows what it's doing.

Right?

Right??

This post contains spoilers for Season 4 of Netflix's Elite.

How it kicks off

Season 4 opens with a flash forward to New Year's Eve, fireworks going off in the background while Guzman sits frozen in a chair, and somewhere nearby a girl is pulled from a lake, unconscious, maybe dead. A police officer wants answers he doesn't have yet. Then it rewinds to the start of the school year, and you find out how everyone gets there.

Las Encinas gets a new principal right out of the gate: Benjamín Blanco, a wealthy CEO who fires Azucena on her very first day back, then stands in front of the whole school promising a "new chapter" built on discipline, excellence, and merit. Translation: Samuel and Omar are told they now have to sit an advanced placement exam just to prove they still deserve their scholarships, a hurdle nobody else on scholarship faced before.

Benjamín brings three kids with him, and each one immediately tangles into the group. Ari catches both Guzman's and Samuel's attention immediately, sharp and unreadable in a way that makes her hard to pin down from the jump. Patrick is openly gay and starts flirting with Ander almost the second they meet, though the two nearly come to blows in class when Patrick defends his father over the exam situation. Mencía zeroes in on Rebeka, flirting hard enough that Rebeka, despite still refusing to speak to Samuel after last year's betrayal, actually takes the bait.

The exam sparks a real protest, students sitting in front of the school entrance to block Benjamín and his kids from walking in. Mencía, trying to impress Rebeka, joins the sit-in herself, furious to her father and siblings. She also hands the group useful intel: Benjamín's one weakness is Ari, the only person he actually listens to. That sends Guzman off to work Ari directly, hoping to get her to talk her father into scrapping the exam.

Rebeka and Mencía's flirtation turns into an actual date, drinks at a club, real chemistry, until Rebeka gets cold feet mid-hookup and bails without explanation. Mencía doesn't make it home until morning, which earns her a furious lecture from her father and siblings about being reckless.

Guzman takes Ari out too, opening up about losing Marina and Polo, and Ari, who's lost her own mother, meets him with real understanding rather than pity. It works. She agrees to talk to her father. But it costs Mencía something: cut off financially by Benjamín after she blows off a family dinner in a mood, she retaliates by telling Ari the truth, that Guzman only took her out to manipulate the exam situation.

Mencía spirals from there, wandering into a bar alone after Rebeka stands her up, where an older man named Armando buys her drinks and, it turns out, a lot more. Meanwhile Patrick offers Omar the exam answers in exchange for Ander joining him at a gay club that night. Omar hesitates, knowing Ari should be the real target, but Ander, tempted, goes anyway. Samuel makes his own desperate move too, cornering Benjamín at the restaurant where he bartends to beg him to drop the exam requirement for Omar, and gets fired on the spot for it. Benjamín almost softens, until Ari talks him out of it.

At the club, things between Ander and Patrick heat up fast, clothes coming off, right up until Patrick tries to go further and Ander shuts it down, insisting he'd never betray Omar. He storms out. Across town, Armando reveals he's a wealthy businessman and offers Mencía a room in a luxury hotel, free, no strings attached, or so it seems. She sleeps with him that night, and wakes up to find cash left at her bedside.

Exam day arrives, and Patrick slips Omar the answers anyway. Omar hesitates but uses them, scoring a 97, while Samuel passes on his own merit, both scholarships secured. Ari isn't fooled by any of it. She pulls Samuel and Guzman aside and makes it clear she sees exactly what they tried to do.

Then it cuts back to New Year's Eve, and the girl in the lake finally has a name. It's Ari. Paramedics work frantically to revive her while everyone watches, frozen, until a voice crackles through on a radio: she's still alive.

The twists and the escalation

Prince Phillipe's arrival gets treated like a state visit, security cameras and metal detectors installed just for him, all courtesy of a father back home who shipped him off to get away from unspecified rumors. Cayetana's instantly starstruck, rattling off his credentials to anyone who'll listen, though Ari wastes no time outing her as the school janitor in front of him, humiliating her before Phillipe can even respond. He tells her privately he doesn't care about her social class. It's the first hint of charm that turns out to be doing a lot of covering.

Mencía's still seeing Armando behind everyone's back, insisting each time is the last, though it never is. Sandra (Rebeka's mom) spots the two of them together and warns Mencía directly that Armando's known for going after young girls this way. Mencía brushes it off completely.

The Guzman, Samuel, and Ari triangle starts forming not too long after. Guzman admits he's attracted to Ari but tells her he's with Nadia, and the tension between him and Samuel over her doesn't take long to surface. Rebeka gets dragged into her own mess when a new screening policy forces her to disclose her mother's criminal record to the entire class. Mencía tries comforting her with a kiss in the locker room, and they get caught by Benjamín, who now looks at Rebeka like a delinquent. Mencía, stung by the rejection that follows, goes right back to texting Armando.

The old guard starts pushing back against the new regime, organizing a rebellious towel party at Samuel's house that turns into a release valve for everything simmering underneath. Ander, Omar, and Patrick end up in a three-way hookup. Rebeka and Mencía finally get together for real. Guzman tries video-calling Nadia mid-party, only for her to catch him dancing with Ari on camera.  He steps outside to call Nadia, and the two of them agree to pause the relationship while they figure out if long distance is even sustainable. And Ari, rarely one to drink, gets drunk enough to lower her guard completely and ends up sleeping with Samuel.

Phillipe and Cayetana's hookup that same night gets complicated: the room turns out to be wired with hidden cameras, something Cayetana discovers later, along with a stash of footage showing Phillipe with other women. He explains it away as protection against false assault claims he's dealt with before. It's a strange, unsettling justification that nobody pushes back on hard enough at the time, and the show flashes forward just after to Ari lying in a hospital bed, unconscious and worsening.

Guzman and Nadia officially call it off not long after. Ari starts noticing things too, suspecting Phillipe was with Mencía the night she went missing, and warning Cayetana to be careful of him, though a search online turns up nothing to confirm it.

Mencía's arrangement with Armando spirals further. One of his associates gets aggressive with her, tying her down and refusing to let her leave, and it's Rebeka, using a hotel key she'd found earlier and assumed meant Mencía was cheating, who tracks her down and pulls her out. Benjamín, meanwhile, finds a stash of cash Mencía's been hiding and jumps straight to blaming Rebeka's family instead of asking the real question.

Ander and Omar's relationship doesn't survive the tension either. Ander breaks things off, and Omar takes it hard, packing up and moving his things out before Ander even has the chance to properly process it. Guzman keeps circling Ari and Samuel too, and a flashforward drops a strange detail into the mix: Samuel gets arrested trying to visit Ari in the hospital, a thread the season doesn't explain yet.

By episode six, Ari's trying to wall off her private life from Samuel entirely, telling her father never to invite him around again, even as the two of them keep colliding anyway. Patrick, chasing concert tickets to a show he wants to attend, starts pushing boundaries harder, at one point groping Ander in the middle of class, which Samuel witnesses and clearly disapproves of. Phillipe, cornered by Cayetana in the janitor's room, asks her outright whether people actually like him or just want what he can give them, a question that lands heavier in hindsight. His father warns him separately not to let old rumors resurface.

At a family dinner, Guzman, there as Ari's date, compares Mencía to his late sister Marina and quietly needles Benjamín over how he treats his own daughter. Later that night, a drunk Ari initiates sex with Guzman at the club itself and gets caught by Samuel mid-act. Guzman apologizes and leaves. It's messy, and it's clear Ari's stringing both of them along without fully deciding on either.

Patrick, meanwhile, figures out enough about Phillipe's past to use it as leverage, threatening to expose him unless he gets concert tickets for himself and Ander. At the show itself, Patrick catches Ander kissing someone else and spirals, accidentally busting Ari's lip in the process. After the dust settles, Ari kisses Samuel again anyway. A flashforward not long after shows Patrick noticing a fresh bruise on Guzman and asking, pointedly, who he'd beaten up.

By episode seven, the show layers in one more thread: Phillipe's mother arrives to manage his image and is horrified to learn he's involved with the school janitor. Armando resurfaces too, now positioning himself as a financial donor to the school itself, using the access to blackmail Mencía into staying quiet about their arrangement, threatening to expose her to her own family if she says a word.

The Christmas social event Phillipe invites Cayetana to, becomes the season's ugliest turning point. Cayetana meets her dream fashion designer there, only for him to make it clear he'll only look at her work if she goes back to his hotel room with him. She turns him down, and Ari, watching the exchange, gains a real respect for her because of it, going as far as commissioning a dress from her. Mencía, caught in an almost identical situation the same night, doesn't have the same ending. She gives in to Armando again despite Rebeka begging her not to.

Later that night, alone with Cayetana in a limo, Phillipe pushes past her repeated no, and she has to physically escape the car to get away from him. It confirms every rumor that trailed him from home. He's left shaken, seeming to realize, almost too late, exactly what he's done.

The scene closes with Ari finally coming clean to both Samuel and Guzman at once, admitting through tears, that she loves them both and doesn't want to choose. Guzman is furious while Samuel is left stunned.

How it all wraps up

Guzman doesn't take the news well. He calls Samuel an awful friend on the spot, and when Samuel tries to smooth things over right there, Guzman shuts him down and walks off. Not long after, he and Ander sit down for what looks like an early goodbye, Ander having decided to leave Las Encinas mid-year entirely.

Rebeka makes her own hard call, telling Ari the truth about Mencía and Armando, knowing full well it likely ends whatever future she and Mencía might've had together. She does it anyway. Meanwhile Phillipe corners Cayetana in the janitor's room, trying to apologize, but undercuts it almost immediately by claiming she'd given him "mixed signals" the night before. She walks off disgusted. When Ari confronts Mencía about what Rebeka revealed, Mencía breaks down and threatens to cut Ari off entirely if she takes it to their father.

Learning Ander's actually leaving, Omar asks for one more shot at their relationship, and after a moment of hesitation, Ander agrees. They kiss, with Patrick watching from a distance, furious.

Phillipe's mother pulls Cayetana into Benjamín's office next, trying to buy her silence, dangling the idea that Phillipe chose her over anyone else and that a life with him would end her family's money troubles for good. She even excuses her son's behavior as simple biology, men just being men. Cayetana sits through it visibly uncomfortable.

At the New Year's party, with everything the season's been building toward closing in, the Royal Highness pushes Cayetana one more time to approve of Phillipe publicly. Cayetana refuses outright, telling her that her son's aggression isn't biology, it's how he was raised. Phillipe and his mother are left stunned. Phillipe turns the accusation back on his own mother, blaming her for raising him to be exactly this kind of person. She tells him if he wants to be treated like an adult, he needs to own the consequences of his own choices.

Back together with Omar, a lighter Ander pushes Guzman to finally talk to Ari, but before he gets the chance, Samuel beats him to it, asking Ari to leave him alone and go back to Guzman. Guzman sees the exchange from across the room and reads it wrongly, which only deepens his anger. Inside, Patrick watches Ander and Omar dance together until he can't anymore, giving up and hooking up with a stranger instead.

Omar finds out Ander's real reason for leaving is just to see the world, and instead of holding him back, tells him to go, promising he'll wait. Around the same time, Phillipe records a voice message to a girl named Elodie, someone he'd hurt before, finally admitting to it and telling her to do whatever she wants with the confession.

Then everything collides at once. Rebeka catches Armando getting physically aggressive with Mencía down by the lake and attacks him herself to get her out of there. A drunk, distant Ari watches it happen and realizes Rebeka's been telling the truth the whole time. She confronts Armando alone, threatening to expose him to her father, and starts calling him before Armando cuts her off by hitting her. He keeps hitting her as she tries to crawl toward her phone. At the exact same moment, Guzman and Samuel finally boil over into a real fight inside the club, Guzman beating Samuel badly before catching sight of a message on his phone from Ari, asking him to meet her by the lake. It all happens right as the clock strikes midnight.

Guzman stumbles outside and finds Ari barely conscious on the dock. She begs him to go after Armando. Trying to stand, she reaches for her phone and falls into the lake instead. Guzman finds Armando in a storage room, and the fight that follows ends with Guzman grabbing a flare gun and shooting him dead. He goes back for Ari, not realizing she's already in the water, and searches the wrong places for her.

He finally runs back into the club begging Samuel and Rebeka if they've seen her, breaking down and telling them everything that just happened. The three of them agree to call the police, but only with part of the truth. Ari's rushed to the hospital in critical condition and, after everything the season's been flashing forward to, survives.

Once she's conscious again, Guzman sits with her, tells her he already knows she loves Samuel, not him, and lies about what really happened to Armando, saying he ran off. He says goodbye as she begs him to stay.

Not long after, Guzman and Ander leave Las Encinas together to travel, saying tearful goodbyes to Omar, Cayetana, Rebeka, and Samuel before driving off. Mencía, wracked with guilt over ever bringing Armando into their lives, asks Ari to stand with her while she finally tells her father everything. Benjamín's reaction is pure rage, tearing his own house apart once he hears it. And in the last quiet reveal of the season, it comes out that Guzman, Rebeka, and Samuel are the ones who dumped Armando's body into the lake, one more secret this group is going to have to carry together.

Where we left everyone:

  • Samuel: Helps dump Armando's body in the lake and tries to move forward. Back to being the guy the plot punishes for existing.

  • Guzman: Killed Armando to save Ari, covered it up, and leaves Spain to go travelling with Ander. Carrying a secret that will follow him wherever he goes.

  • Ander: Learns Omar wants him to go see the world instead of staying behind out of guilt, and leaves for real this time, Omar promising to wait for him. It's framed as bittersweet. It mostly just feels sad.

  • Omar: Does the selfless thing, tells Ander to go live his life, and stays behind holding onto a promise with Patrick still hovering around.

  • Rebeka and Mencia: End the season together, which is the one sweet note this season manages. Rebe is now sitting on the secret of Armando's death without Mencia knowing.

  • Ari: Survives Armando's attack, ends up in hospital, and Guzman lies to her face about what actually happened.

  • Patrick: Got played by both Ander and Omar, ends the season alone. Hard to feel much about it either way.

  • Cayetana: Still here.

  • Phillipe: The SA allegations go mostly unresolved. Ends the season with his reputation intact enough. The show just kind of moves on.

Where Season 4 lost me

They destroyed the best friendship on this show for a girl. This one hurts the most, so let's start here. Samuel and Guzman started as actual enemies, then slowly, through shared grief and the total hellscape of what went down with Marina and Polo, these two built something real. A proper friendship. By the end of Season 3, their bond was one of the few things on this show I loved without reservation. Then Ari shows up and the writers throw it all in the bin. Both of them have feelings for her, and suddenly two guys who survived a murder cover-up together are giving each other death stares in the hallway like they've never met. It's so generic, so far removed from who these characters actually are at this point that it feels like the writers started fresh without reading their own previous scripts. Guzman especially gets done dirty. This is a guy who showed real, visible growth across three full seasons, and now he's just being petty and territorial over someone he met a few weeks ago. All that work, undone in about two episodes for a love triangle that doesn't even pay off in any interesting way. And here's the thing: Ari isn't even interesting enough to justify any of it. She's fine. She's pretty and she moves the plot around. But she's not the kind of character you burn a friendship over.

The new family is predictable, cliché, and kind of boring. Bringing in new characters is fine, it makes sense when your original cast starts leaving. But there's a right way to do it, and Season 4 does it the wrong way, giving us characters so clearly telegraphed from their very first scenes. The show seems to think expensive clothes and dramatic family secrets count as personality. Compare any of them to Lu from the earlier seasons. Lu was annoying, scheming, snobbish, awful a lot of the time. But she was also funny and surprisingly insecure, and her whole dynamic was strange and uncomfortable enough that you couldn't look away. She surprised you. The Blanco Commerford kids never surprise you once.

Omar and Ander deserved so much better. Omar and Ander were never just another Elite couple. From the very first season they were the couple for me, the one that felt real, the one where no matter how bad things got, they kept finding their way back to each other. Season 4 sets it on fire for shock value, and the show frames the mess that follows as bold storytelling. It's lazy, chaotic writing that blows up a beloved relationship with nothing meaningful on the other side of it. The "leaving it open ended" framing at the finale is nonsense. Omar deserved better. Ander deserved better. And honestly, so did I.

Mencia, Armando, and Rebeka is a mess the show made on purpose. Mencia's storyline is uncomfortable, and not always in the ways the show intends. A grown adult man blackmailing a teenager he's been sleeping with, and the show treats it like top-tier drama rather than something that should make you deeply uncomfortable about how it's being framed. The Mencia and Rebeka relationship is one of the better things this season does, and it's a shame the show buries it under so much chaos that it barely gets room to breathe. The Armando situation remains the most irresponsible piece of storytelling this season produces: sometimes the show frames him correctly as a predator, then the camera lingers on their scenes with charged music and a dark romantic glow, making it look like a complicated love story instead of what it actually is.

Cayetana got a prince this season and I still didn't care. I almost forgot she was still in this show, and that says everything. The whole point of Cayetana has always been the exhausting performance of pretending to be something you're not, so a prince who might not be what he seems could work for her story in theory. In practice it's flat, rushed, and dropped almost as quickly as it's introduced. Seems like the writers have never figured out what to do with her after Season 3. Why is she still here? I'm genuinely asking, because the show clearly doesn't know either.

The nudity issue: these are supposed to be teenagers. Elite has never been a shy show. Sex and nudity have always been part of its DNA, and that's fine, nobody sat down to watch this expecting something wholesome. But Season 4 takes it to a point where it starts to feel like the show is using bodies as a substitute for actual storytelling. There's a moment where you stop watching a scene and start wondering if the writers ran out of ideas and just decided skin would fill the time. Nudity and sex scenes work on television when they actually tell you something and Elite used to do this reasonably well. The intimacy between Omar and Ander in earlier seasons meant something because you were invested in them as people. This season it just feels gratuitous, scene after scene of heat and bodies that connects to nothing emotionally meaningful. It starts to blur. I became numb to it, and when you're numb to the intimacy on a show that relies on intimacy to drive its drama, that's a real problem. The Patrick chaos, the whole spiral he drags Omar and Ander through, is shot with this glossy, almost celebratory energy that feels completely disconnected from the emotional damage being done to characters you've spent three seasons actually caring about. The camera is having a great time. I'm not.

The ending was a lot of setup for a very soft bang. Eight episodes of buildup, all these threads supposedly converging, and the twist doesn't land the way it should, and the reason is the Ari reveal in episode one. The moment the show confirms she's alive, the urgency drains out and never comes back. You spend the remaining episodes just waiting for the show to confirm what you already figured out. And Guzman killing Armando should feel enormous. Instead it just kind of happens, because Armando was never a real character, just the villain the plot needed. His death brings relief, not devastation. After everything Guzman survived across four seasons, he deserved so much better than a trauma and a one-way ticket out of the country.

Overall thoughts

Not much worked this season, if I'm being real. The show's still visually stunning, and the actors are still good at what they do, but the writing was so messy that it's hard to find much to praise beyond the Mencia and Rebeka relationship, which is sweet, well-acted, and does a decent job of showing how complicated it can be to navigate love and trauma together. That's about it. The rest of the season feels like a series of missteps and missed opportunities.

Will I quit watching this show? No. Why? I don't fully know, and that's the most honest thing I can say about Elite Season 4. It frustrated me constantly. It wasted characters I've loved since Season 1. It brought in new ones I couldn't bring myself to care about. It took one of the show's most important relationships and put it through a shredder for drama that didn't even pay off properly. It handled really dark subject matter carelessly. And it wrapped up its central mystery with all the energy of someone quietly closing a browser tab they forgot they had open.

And yet here I am, still watching, still annoyed enough to write all of this, still holding onto the memory of what this show was at its best: the chaos of Season 1, the gut punch of Marina's death, the slow unraveling of Polo's guilt, the way Omar and Ander made you actually believe in something. Elite at its best was great television, messy and addictive and surprisingly emotional underneath all the drama and the glamour. Season 4 is a big step away from that. Whether it can step back is the only question I have left going into Season 5.

My Rating: 5.3

Are there people who have actually finished the show?

Lemme know in the comments. Am I crazy for still watching?

← Prev: Season 3 Next: Season 5 →

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: From hollow new characters to a shredded friendship, I explore why Elite Season 4 was such a frustrating departure from the show's peak.

entry.title: RECAP: Elite Season 3
entry.content:
Season 3 is basically a season-long autopsy of a tragedy that was set in motion the moment Marina died back in Season 1.

This post contains spoilers for Season 3 of Netflix's Elite.

The real question isn't just who did it, it's how everyone got pushed far enough to let it happen in the first place.

Once again we're in flash-forward territory, and it's heavy, claustrophobic, and kind of all over the place. The writers clearly knew where this era of the show needed to end, but getting there meant juggling so many storylines at once that the whole thing kept buckling under its own weight. New characters, new love triangles, new traumas stacked on top of old ones that were never properly dealt with to begin with.

How it kicks off

The season opens at a graduation party gone wrong, a body crashing down through the club's upper level onto the dance floor below while Carla stands nearby, stunned, next to shattered glass. Then it rewinds five months, and the real story starts.

Polo's out on bail, but the case isn't closed. A judge orders a formal confrontation between him and Carla to compare their accounts, and Carla tells him that she's done covering for him, though she'll give him a chance to confess first. Her father, on the other side, has other plans. He blackmails her into staying silent, warning that the truth coming out risks exposing his own dealings and taking her mother's business down with it.

A new face shows up at Nadia's family store: Malick, another Muslim student at Las Encinas, and there's a little chemistry between them. Elsewhere, a postcard from Nano finally arrives, sent from Asilah in Morocco. He's healthy and settling into a new life, though even from a distance he doesn't sound convinced Polo will ever actually face justice for what he did.

Ander finds a growth that worries him enough that Omar pushes him to see a doctor, a thread that's going to matter a lot more soon. Valerio drags his own mess back into frame too, showing up at school strung out on cocaine and living out of his car after getting disowned. Lu, guilty and protective despite everything, invites him to stay the night while their father's away, only for their father to come home early and catch them together. Lu takes responsibility, insisting nothing forced ever happened between them and that she chose it. He doesn't care and tells her that if she wants to live like an adult, she'll be cut off financially and thrown out the moment she turns eighteen.

Samuel makes one more attempt to reach Carla, telling her he loves her no matter what she decides about testifying. She slaps him for it, accusing him of only loving her on the condition that she does what he wants. He tries to push back, insisting the opposite's true.

At the college fair, the pressure keeps stacking. Polo's unraveling, calling Ander over and over only to be ignored, terrified of a future where he's always waiting to get caught. Cayetana still won't get rid of the murder weapon, insisting it's safer sitting in her closet than anywhere else right now. Nadia gets hit with fallout from Lu's leaked video when a university recruiter tells her, impressive résumé or not, the rumors following her around are enough to cost her a scholarship. Ander gets his test results back and breaks down in front of Rebeka. And when Guzman spots Polo casually flipping through an Oxford brochure, the same school that was Marina's dream, something in him snaps and he attacks Polo on the spot, hard enough that the principal threatens expulsion for anyone who steps out of line again.

At the actual confrontation, Polo looks like he's finally about to break and admit everything, until Carla cuts in first and claims the whole accusation was a lie.
