Guzman turns on Samuel for it, convinced Carla just proved she was never trustworthy to begin with. Samuel doesn't back down. If anything, it hardens his resolve to get Polo caught no matter what it costs. He even tells his own mother to leave for Morocco and be with Nano, choosing to stay behind alone.

Then the timeline snaps back to the future, to the body on the dance floor, and a detail nobody saw coming: someone stabbed him before he ever hit the ground. Carla tells the Inspector she ran straight down after the fall, but what actually happened is she followed a blood trail to the bathroom first and pocketed a broken, bloody bottle before anyone could find it. When the Inspector searches her bag, though, it's gone. Carla insists, shaken, that she could never have hurt him, she loved him. Because the body on the floor isn't a stranger. It's Polo.

The twists and the escalation

Nadia's got real motivation to land the scholarship this time, especially once it comes out that the funding's coming from Polo's mothers, basically a bribe dressed up as opportunity for anyone connected to the case. Lu's chasing the same scholarship for real reasons now too, cut off financially by her father. Nadia tries to pressure her out of the running by threatening to expose her and Valerio, but Lu calls the bluff, and it's Nadia who backs off once she learns just how broke Lu actually is.

Guzman starts playing a longer game with Polo, acting friendlier, letting him believe he's finally been forgiven. He lures Polo to his house, drugs him, ties him up, and plays Marina's old dance footage on a loop while demanding to know where the trophy is. Polo finally cracks and admits he killed her, insists it was an accident, but won't give up the trophy's location. Guzman nearly strangles him before Samuel steps in to pull him off, and what's left is a Guzman who's become scared of what he's capable of.

Samuel's situation gets messier by the episode. His mom leaves to join Nano in Morocco, leaving him alone with rent he can't cover, and Valerio, freshly disowned and living out of his car, moves in once he cleans himself up enough to function. Somewhere in all of it, Samuel also strikes a deal with the police: help take down Rebeka's mother's drug operation in exchange for progress clearing Nano's name. He agrees, not realizing how badly that choice's about to complicate things with Rebeka, who he's also started something real with.

Ander's world changes fast. What starts as a worrying growth turns into a leukemia diagnosis, and he spends weeks trying to hide it before finally telling his mother and Omar. He tries to push Omar away out of guilt, insisting Omar deserves better than watching him get sick, but Omar refuses to leave his side. As the treatment drags on and starts failing to respond the way it should, Ander spirals into isolating himself, eventually lying to Omar about being with someone else just to force him out the door and spare him the ending he thinks is coming.

Someone starts impersonating Polo online, tweeting confessions about Marina's murder and taunting details of her final moments, which throws suspicion onto both Samuel and Guzman. Neither one confirms or denies it. It later comes out that at least one of those tweets, the cruelest one, mocking Polo's suicide attempt, actually came from Cayetana, which nobody in the group finds out for a long time.

Rebeka and Valerio's drug business becomes its own slow-motion disaster. Samuel keeps feeding information to the police behind the scenes, all while Rebeka has no idea he's the reason her mother ends up arrested. Guilt eats at him the whole time, especially once Rebeka and Valerio start dealing again out of financial desperation. It all comes crashing down at a blackout party, where UV paint exposes Samuel's hands as the one who stole evidence meant to identify who tipped off the police, and in the same reveal, Omar and Malick's secret affair, and Nadia saw them. Rebeka ends things with Samuel on the spot. Nadia slaps Malick and walks out.

Carla's spiral runs almost parallel to all of it. Pushed by her father to stay attached to Yeray for the family's financial survival, she starts using heavily to cope, culminating in her nearly drowning in a pool mid-party after taking too much, saved only because Polo happens to notice in time. It's Rebeka, ironically, who sold her the drugs that put her there, and the guilt of that moment's enough to push Rebeka to finally quit dealing, at least for a while.

Polo, Cayetana, and Valerio end up in a relationship together, something that briefly seems to work until Polo's parents catch them and make their disgust with Valerio impossible to ignore, quietly torching Valerio's chances at studying abroad with Polo's help.

Nadia's storyline tangles further when her father essentially forces her into an engagement with Malick to keep the peace, not knowing about the affair. She finds her own way out of it, choosing to go to New York alone rather than live a lie, a decision that comes right after a raw, blistering monologue to her parents about no longer being the daughter they think she is.

By the time graduation approaches, nearly everyone's paying for something. Samuel, Guzman, Valerio, and Rebeka all get expelled over the drug fallout, and the group splinters over who's to blame, with Polo suspected but never confirmed as the one who reported it. Guzman, worn down, admits to Samuel that he's done hating Polo entirely, since hating him clearly hasn't changed anything and Polo seems happier than either of them regardless. Ander, meanwhile, tells his mother that he doesn't have long left and refuses to spend what time remains studying for exams he may not live to take.

At the graduation ceremony itself, everything that's been simmering boils over fast. Yeray forces Teo's hand and installs Carla in charge of the family business as a condition of funding, finally giving her some real power in a life defined by other people controlling her. Polo ends things with Cayetana for good, telling her she never loved him, just the life he could give her. Lu and Nadia win the scholarship together on stage, only for Lu to go off script mid-speech and tear into Polo and his family in front of the entire school, which gets the scholarship pulled entirely by his humiliated mother. Samuel learns the deal he made with police to help Nano was a setup from the start, and that giving up Sandra's location actually got Nano arrested rather than cleared. And that night, over dinner, Polo finally tells his parents the truth: he killed Marina, and he wants it made right by getting Nadia and Lu's scholarship reinstated.

The graduation party that follows brings a strange peace to a few corners of the group, Guzman and Nadia finding their way back to each other for whatever time they have left, Ander and Omar sharing one last real goodbye before Omar leaves for New York with Nadia and Malick. It's the last calm moment before the body hits the dance floor.

How it all wraps up

Polo shows up to graduation for one reason: he wants the trophy from Cayetana so he can turn himself in. She refuses, and when he demands to know if she's the one who sabotaged his chance to transfer abroad, she admits it, telling him it was because she loves him and couldn't let him go. Before he can process that, Lu storms up drunk and throws a drink in his face, blaming him for wrecking her life. He tries to tell her the scholarship's being reinstated but she's past listening.

The night keeps sliding sideways. Omar refuses to even hand Polo a napkin at the bar. Samuel, drunk and spiraling, spots a knife left behind and moves toward Polo with real intent before Guzman physically pulls him off. Lu, still furious, grabs a champagne bottle from Valerio and jokes to Nadia about smashing it over Polo's head. Samuel even asks Rebeka to have someone rough Polo up. She says no.

Guzman intercepts Polo again near Lu and Nadia, telling him to leave before he gets hurt worse than last time. Polo asks, one more time, if Guzman could ever forgive him once he confesses. Guzman tells him that he never will. In the middle of that exchange, Lu drops her champagne bottle and it shatters, and while everyone's distracted picking up the pieces, the broken neck of it gets kicked out of sight across the floor.

Lu follows Polo into the bathroom now holding that broken bottle neck. She unloads on him, blaming him for everything he's taken from her and from Guzman by killing Marina. Polo lashes back with something cruel, echoing almost exactly what he once said to Marina right before he killed her. Lu snaps. She pins him against the wall, and the bottle in her hand goes into his chest. She's horrified the second it happens, pulling it out and begging him to know she didn't mean it. He tells her he knows, but it doesn't stop her from falling apart.

Polo stumbles out bleeding, trying to reach Guzman, but slips and hits a cracked glass barrier that gives way under him. He falls straight through to the dance floor below. Guzman sees it happen and sprints down after him, and Carla, seeing the whole thing, quietly pockets the bottle neck to protect Lu before anyone else notices. By the time Guzman reaches him, there's nothing left to do but hold his hand. He tells Polo he forgives him, the one thing Polo begged for all night and never got, and Polo dies holding onto that.

What follows is the group closing ranks. Carla pulls Samuel aside and tells him the truth: Lu did it, by accident. Valerio points out that everyone already saw her throw a drink at Polo earlier, so no one's going to believe an accident story anyway. So they get to work covering it up together: passing the bottle neck around so everyone's fingerprints are on it, staging the scene to look like suicide, even letting Cayetana, playing grieving girlfriend, get close enough to press Polo's fingers to the weapon herself. She cuts her own hand doing it and doesn't say a word before tossing the bottle onto the dance floor for the police to find.

When the police start questioning everyone, Guzman comes up with the plan that saves them: everyone claims they saw a different person follow Polo into the bathroom. Samuel names Valerio. Valerio names Cayetana. Cayetana names Ander. Ander names Guzman. Guzman names Omar. Omar, of all people, names his own sister. Nadia names Carla. Carla names Rebeka. Rebeka names Lu. Every statement cancels out the next, and the whole timeline turns to static.

In the middle of it, Ander tells Omar the lie about seeing someone else was just that, a lie, meant to push him away so Omar wouldn't have to watch him die. Omar doesn't forgive it easily. He tells Ander he got exactly what he wanted and walks out. Lu, meanwhile, nearly breaks in her own interview, on the verge of confessing everything, until the Inspector needles her about not really being Polo's friend. That's the thing that finally holds her together. She tells the Inspector, through tears, that whatever else was true, Polo was her friend, that all of them were, messy and broken as that family is.

By morning, some things settle. Guzman and Nadia finally kiss, done pretending they don't want each other. Samuel and Carla share a last kiss on the cheek before she leaves to study abroad. Omar leaves with Malick, Ander left standing alone. Rebeka goes home and tells her mother she's done with the drug business for good.

At the station, the case resolves itself when Polo's own parents hand over the real murder weapon, the trophy he used to kill Marina, and lie to the Inspector, claiming Polo confessed before he died rather than let the investigation reopen and risk the truth about Lu coming out. At his funeral, Cayetana turns down his parents' offer to pay for her education, telling them she's done pretending to be something she's not. Carla hands the family winery over to Valerio to run while she's away.

Time passes. Nadia and Omar are about to board a flight to New York when Omar realizes at the last second he can't actually leave Ander behind, and turns back for the hospital instead, arriving just in time to learn Ander's cancer's in remission. Omar's father, finally coming around, refers to Ander as his son's boyfriend without flinching. Lu, cut off by her own parents for good, is taken in by Nadia's family instead. Guzman leaves Nadia a voicemail promising to wait for her.

Two months later, most of them walk back into Las Encinas for one final year: Samuel, Guzman, Rebeka, Omar, Ander. Cayetana isn't among them as a student anymore. She's the school's new janitor, mopping the same halls she once faked her way through.

What worked

Former enemies who chose each other. In the middle of all that mess, the writers actually got two things right this season: the friendship between Nadia and Lu, and the one between Samuel and Guzman. Think about where Samuel and Guzman started, Guzman actively making Samuel's life miserable, treating him like an outsider who had no business being at Las Encinas. Then Marina died, Nano went to prison for something he didn't do, and something shifted. Two people with every reason to hate each other became each other's most reliable allies, a friendship built on shared stubbornness and surviving something awful together. It's one of the few things holding the season up when everything else is falling apart, because it wasn't built on attraction or strategy but on grief and mutual respect. Nadia and Lu land somewhere similar. Two characters who spent two seasons tearing each other apart over the same scholarship, the same boy, the same need to be the best in the room, finally choosing each other once they see how they'd both been held back by the same toxic people and the same exhausting expectations.

The cover-up. For the first time, instead of protecting themselves at each other's expense, the whole group chose to stand together. These people spent three seasons at each other's throats, betrayal after betrayal, cover-up after cover-up, everyone protecting themselves first. And in that moment they finally chose each other instead. It was the only time their bond felt completely real and unforced, and it was the perfect way to close out this chapter of the show.

A couple of smaller notes: the throuple situation with Cayetana, Polo, and Valerio had its moments, three outcasts finding comfort in each other's a compelling idea, and the show almost pulls it off. And Polo at Las Encinas this season is the saddest the show has ever made a character look, which is remarkable given that he's a murderer. That tension, between what he did and what he became afterward, ends up being one of the most interesting things about the whole season.

What didn't

Two new faces, zero reasons to care. Neither new addition this season was worth the screen time. Malick showed up, dated Nadia as a cover, and then started something with Omar behind her back. He wasn't really a character so much as a plot device with a face, someone the writers dropped in specifically to blow up the one relationship in this show that actually deserved better. That's his whole personality. Yeray was somehow even more pointless. His entire purpose was to buy Carla's affection on her father's behalf. He was a rich guy with a name, and the show didn't even bother pretending otherwise.

What they did to Carla was unforgivable. Carla spent two full seasons being the most calculating, self-possessed person in any room she walked into. She managed an entire murder cover-up in real time in the Season 1 finale, ran circles around everyone including Samuel, and kept Polo from completely falling apart while doing it. She was dangerous and controlled and compelling to watch. Then Season 3 handed her a controlling father, a transaction dressed up as a boyfriend, and a pill bottle, and called it a character arc. Watching her get reduced to a business arrangement by her own father, essentially sold off to maintain a family alliance, was depressing. What makes it worse is her arc this season doesn't feel tragic in any meaningful way. It just feels like the writers ran out of ideas for her and stripped away everything that made her interesting. Carla deserved a much better send-off than a plane ticket and a vague sense of freedom.

Drama for the sake of drama. I can't get over what the writers did to Omar and Ander this season. After everything these two survived in Seasons 1 and 2, watching them get dragged through a cheating storyline with no real payoff and no real point was just painful. Clearly the writers had no idea how to write a couple supporting each other through something hard, so they went for the cheapest conflict available instead. Treating them like a disposable plot point, manufacturing drama just to create tension in an already overcrowded season, felt like a betrayal of everything the first two seasons built. The show eventually walks it back and lets them find their way to each other, but the damage was already done.

Overall thoughts

Looking back, the Season 3 finale really did feel like the natural conclusion to the story Elite started with. Marina's death finally got real closure. Most of the main cast actually grew as people. The last scene at the school played like a goodbye to an era, and the collective cover-up in the finale, the first time these people ever truly chose each other over themselves, paid off three seasons of watching people betray each other in one coordinated act of loyalty.

I'm currently watching Season 4, and a big part of me thinks the show should've stopped at Season 3. When you have a cast with this much chemistry and a central mystery that kept you hooked for three seasons, it's almost impossible to recreate that energy once you start swapping people out. Elite was always a three-season story. The original mystery begins with a murder Polo committed and ends with his death. Everything in Season 4 so far doesn't look so good.

My Rating: 7.4

What did you think of the season?

Drop your take in the comments. I also want to know if the collective cover-up in the finale made you emotional or if you saw it coming from a mile away.

← Prev: Season 2 Next: Season 4 →

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: From Polo's tragic downfall to the final collective cover-up, I break down why Elite Season 3 stands as a satisfying conclusion to the story.

entry.title: REVIEW: Carry On (2024)
entry.content:
The setup is basically Die Hard reworked for a TSA badge instead of a cop's. On paper, it should deliver wall-to-wall tension.

Carry-On is a Netflix thriller directed by Jaume Collet-Serra, the guy behind The Shallows and a string of Liam Neeson vs. a ticking clock movies like Non-Stop and The Commuter. Ethan Kopek (Taron Egerton) is a junior TSA officer at LAX on Christmas Eve when a stranger, credited only as the Traveler (Jason Bateman), drops an earpiece on his station and starts giving orders: let one specific carry-on through the scanner, or Ethan's girlfriend Nora pays for it.

What follows is Ethan racing to outsmart the Traveler in real time, all while stuck behind a security desk in front of a packed terminal. The bag isn't just contraband either, it's a nerve agent rigged to kill everyone on a specific flight if Ethan doesn't play along.

The film leans into that one-guy-against-impossible-odds formula Collet-Serra has built a career on. The problem is the film keeps tripping over itself to get there.

The Highlights:

  • Jason Bateman. This might be biased because I am a huge fan but he brings a coiled, controlled menace to a role that could have easily been one-dimensional.
  • The Premise. An airport on Christmas Eve, a hidden threat, and a man trapped between two impossible choices. The first act sets it up well enough to keep you leaning in.
  • It Moves Fast. The pacing is relentless and the film never lingers long enough for you to get bored. If you want something loud to fill an evening, it does that job.

Fair Warning:

  • The Script Leans Too Hard on Convenience. Too many moments only work because the plot needs them to. Characters keep making choices no real person would ever make, and after the third or fourth time, it starts to eat away at the tension the film is working so hard to build.
  • Taron Egerton Felt Miscast. This is not about his ability as an actor, it is about the fit. The character needed someone who reads as more grounded and weathered, and he never quite convinced me he belonged in that uniform.
  • The Stakes Never Fully Hit. For a movie this loud and fast, it is surprising how little emotional weight it actually has. You end up watching things happen instead of feeling them.

Final Verdict

My Rating: 5.0

This movie is basically the definition of a perfectly average thriller. All the ingredients are there, but the execution fumbles just enough that it never turns into anything memorable. It did rack up huge numbers for Netflix in its opening week, so clearly the premise alone was enough to pull people in. Watch it if you need some background noise with a bit of adrenaline in it. Otherwise, just rewatch Die Hard instead.

Am I being too harsh?

If you've already seen Carry-On, I want to hear your take. Drop a comment below, especially if you think Taron Egerton was actually the right call.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Is Carry-On worth your time, or is it just background noise? I break down the hits and misses of this Netflix thriller.

entry.title: REVIEW: Dorohedoro Season 2
entry.content:
Six years we waited for this season, and I'm going to tell you straight up: drop everything and go watch it because every bit of the wait was worth it.

The second season of Dorohedoro picks up right where the first season left off, no hand-holding, no recap episode. MAPPA and director Yuichiro Hayashi came back to this world and just kept moving like no time had passed at all. This season had eleven episodes, streamed from April 1 to May 27, 2026, and I made the right call waiting for the whole thing to drop before starting. One episode a week would have broken me.

More of Everything

Everything that made the first season good got amplified here. The action is nastier, the drama actually has weight behind it, the twists come at you from angles you don't see coming, and the gore, if you thought Season 1 was graphic, this one does not hold back.

The season leans hard into the Cross-Eyes, a chaotic gang that's been circling Caiman and Nikaido's story since the first finale hinted at bigger things. Their internal mess, their obsession with their missing boss, and how all of that collides with En's sorcerer family gives the season a scope that Season 1 didn't have room for. There are a lot of moving pieces here, Shin and Noi have their own arc, Risu is out here chasing his own answers, and somehow none of it feels like too much. The show trusts you to keep up, and it's worth keeping up.

The Story, No Complaints

I have zero issues with the story this time. Every thread this season pulls on connects back to something bigger about Caiman's past and why he ended up with a lizard head in the first place. The flashbacks hit harder here because you actually care about the people in them by now. It's tightly written from the first episode to the last, nothing felt like filler or rushed

The CGI, No Issues Either

This season doesn't have that adjustment period with the 3D animation like in season 1. Whatever MAPPA fixed or refined between seasons, it shows. The movement is smoother, the action sequences land with actual weight behind them, and at no point did the visual style pull me out of a scene.

Binge It

I'm glad I waited until the whole season finished airing before starting. I watched all eleven episodes back to back, and it was awesome from start to finish, no dips, no filler stretch in the middle where you start checking the time. Shows that can hold that kind of momentum for a full season are rare, and Dorohedoro Season 2 pulled it off.

This Is Peak Fiction

This season has earned every bit of the hype it's gotten: it balances the humor with dread, the violence never feels gratuitous even when it's extreme, every character beat pays off something planted earlier. Everything just works.

And here's the best part: we're not waiting another six years for the next one. Season 3 was announced right after the finale, and from what I've heard, it's already in the works. No more agonizing multi-year gaps this time around.

Rating

9.2 out of 10.

This season is what happens when a show knows exactly what it wants to be and executes it without hesitation. I have nothing to complain about here. If Season 1 was the setup, Season 2 is the show fully realized.

PS: This season will have you googling theories and things you missed on your first watch. Don't be surprised if you end up rewatching an episode or three before moving on.

Which storyline got you the most this season: the Cross-Eyes, Shin and Noi, or Caiman's past?

Let me know below, I want to hear the theories.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A review of Dorohedoro Season 2, MAPPA's long-awaited follow-up that turns the action, drama, and gore up a notch.

entry.title: The Legend of Vox Machina Is Peak
entry.content:
The Legend of Vox Machina is one of the best things animation has given us this decade, and I'm putting it in the Hall of Fame while the show is still running. This show has already given me enough to know exactly where it stands.

Here's my confession though. I went in expecting a fun D&D adaptation, something silly to put on in the background. What I got instead was a story with characters I actually care about, animation that keeps getting more ambitious with every season, and a plot that somehow manages to top itself every single time it comes back. Shows usually peak and coast. This one just keeps climbing.

The Plot (In a Nutshell)

Vox Machina is a band of misfits, mercenaries, and full time bar tab dodgers who stumble into becoming the people who actually save the world. What starts as a group taking odd jobs for coin turns into a fight against a vengeful undead lord, a coalition of ancient chromatic dragons burning entire cities to the ground, and now, in the current season, something even older stirring in the dark. It's set in Exandria, the fantasy world built by Matthew Mercer, and every arc raises the stakes without losing the characters in the noise.

The premise works because of how unglamorous the group's starting point is. These aren't chosen ones or prophecy driven heroes. They're broke adventurers who take a mercenary job because they need the coin, and the story lets the stakes grow organically from there instead of announcing on day one that these seven people are destined to save the world. That grounded starting point is part of why the eventual scale of what they take on hits as hard as it does.

My Take

What actually gets me about this show is how it never treats "funny" and "devastating" as opposites. One episode has Grog getting into a drinking contest, and two episodes later someone's dead and the whole group is quietly falling apart from grief. That whiplash should feel jarring. Instead it feels like how people actually process loss, one minute laughing to survive it, the next minute completely gutted.

And the thing that keeps me coming back season after season is that nothing here feels like filler. Season one sets up the group and the Briarwood revenge arc. Season two throws the Chroma Conclave at them, an entire coalition of dragons burning Emon to the ground and forcing the group to scatter and regroup from nothing. Season three brings that fight to its actual conclusion, closing out Thordak and the rest of the Conclave while still finding room to deepen what everyone's carrying emotionally after all that loss. Season four splits the group up to deal with the fallout on their own terms, which sounds like it could drag, but instead turns into some of the most character focused writing the show has done. Every season picks up exactly where the last one left the characters emotionally, not just where the plot left off.

The animation itself has quietly leveled up every single time too. Season one already looked sharp for a show funded off Kickstarter money, but by season three the fight choreography got noticeably more ambitious, camera work started doing things you'd expect from a much bigger budget, and the character designs picked up small details that reward people paying close attention. Most shows either lock in a visual style and stay there or slowly get lazier as the seasons pile up. This one keeps spending more effort exactly where you'd expect a show to start coasting.

The Characters

Vax'ildan: The one who carries the weight nobody asked him to. Vax spends most of the show quietly deciding he's the one who has to make the sacrifice, the one who has to take the hit, and watching him wrestle with his own mortality while falling for someone he's terrified to lose is some of the most affecting material in the whole series.

Vex'ahlia: Sharp, guarded, and constantly doing the math on what everything costs, literally and emotionally. Vex starts out as the twin who keeps score and slowly turns into the one holding the entire group's emotional accounting together.

Percival de Rolo: Percy is what happens when revenge actually works. He gets his vengeance on the Briarwoods and it hollows him out instead of healing him. Watching him try to figure out who he is once the thing he's been building toward for years is actually done is some of the best character writing in the series.

Grog Strongjaw: The muscle, the comic relief, and somehow also one of the most quietly moving arcs in the show. Grog spends seasons wrestling with whether being strong is the same thing as being good, and the show never treats his intelligence, or lack of it, as a punchline without also giving him real depth underneath it.

Pike Trickfoot: The moral center of the group, and one of the only people in Vox Machina who actually seems to know who she is from episode one. Pike's faith gets tested constantly, and instead of that being a weakness, it becomes one of the show's steadiest emotional anchors. Even when the group scatters or falls apart around her, Pike is usually the one holding the thread that pulls everyone back together, not through force, but through the quiet certainty of who she's chosen to be.

Scanlan Shorthalt: The bard whose ego is only matched by how much he actually needs this group, even when he pretends otherwise. His arc around fatherhood and abandonment sneaks up on you after seasons of dick jokes and increasingly unhinged songs, and by the time it actually hits you realize how much groundwork was quietly laid under all the comedy.

Keyleth: The druid figuring out what leadership actually costs, torn between duty to her people and loyalty to the group that's become her real family. Her slow burn arc with Vax is handled with more patience than most live action shows manage.

Why It Works

Part of the magic here is where this show actually came from. This wasn't a studio pitch. Critical Role, the tabletop group behind all of this, launched a Kickstarter in March 2019 asking for $750,000 to fund a single 22 minute animated special. Within an hour they'd cleared their goal. By the time the campaign closed 45 days later, fans had pledged over $11.3 million, making it one of the most funded film or television projects Kickstarter had ever seen. Amazon took notice, picked up the distribution rights before the season even finished production, and turned what was supposed to be one short episode into a full series.

That origin story matters because it shows up in the finished product. This is a show built by people who actually played these characters at a table for years before any of it hit a screen, voiced by the same cast who lived through every dice roll and improvised joke in the original campaign. You can feel that lived in quality in every performance. Nobody's reading lines cold, they're revisiting people they already know intimately. Laura Bailey isn't just voicing Vex, she's replaying years of choices she personally made as that character live on stream, and that history bleeds into every line delivery in a way you can't fake with a normal casting process.

Critically, the show has backed up the hype too. All three completed seasons hold a perfect 100 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes, with critics consistently pointing to the animation, the humor, the voice work, and the fight choreography as reasons it stands apart from most adult animation. The show keeps figuring out how to get better instead of just coasting on goodwill.

Final Thoughts

I'm putting an unfinished show in the Hall of Fame, and I'm not apologizing for it. Some things don't need a finished story to prove they're great, they just need to keep giving you a reason to trust them every time they come back. Vox Machina has done that four seasons running, and I have zero doubt season five closes it out exactly the way this cast and crew have built it up to.

If you love fantasy with actual heart, characters who feel like people instead of archetypes, and animation that never stops getting more ambitious, this is for you. If you think D&D is just nerds rolling dice in a basement, this is also for you, because it'll change your mind by episode three.

Are you caught up on season four, or are you still working through the Briarwoods arc?

Tell me who your favorite member of Vox Machina is, and don't be shy about defending them in the comments if I didn't give them enough love up there.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Incredible animation, characters you actually care about, and a show that somehow tops itself every season. Why Vox Machina earns the Hall of Fame now

entry.title: Gay Romance In Media Has A Suffering Problem
entry.content:
I am so tired. I am deeply, spiritually tired of watching gay people suffer on screen and being told that's a love story.

At this point I actively avoid queer stories in media because I already know how it's going to go. Someone is going to die, or cheat, or get sick, or lose everything, or all of the above. The suffering is basically a given. And what kills me is that it doesn't have to be this way. We have proof. We have examples of queer stories that are actually good, that don't treat gay love like it comes with a mandatory tragedy attached. So why is the default still misery? Let me get into it.

This post contains spoilers for some of the films and series mentioned.

The Film That Broke Me (And Not In A Good Way)

I recently watched The Paradise of Thorns, a 2024 Thai film about Thongkam and Sek, a gay couple who pour everything they have into building a life together on a durian orchard. They buy back the land. They build a home. They have a whole future planned. And then Sek dies in an accident before you've even had a chance to breathe. What follows is Thongkam spending the rest of the film fighting Sek's family for their shared home, because same-sex marriage had no legal recognition in Thailand at the time, meaning he has zero rights to any of it.

Look, the premise is rooted in a real injustice and I get what the film is trying to say. But the execution just buries Thongkam under suffering, humiliation, and grief for the entire runtime. By the time the credits rolled I felt like I needed to sit in a dark room and rethink my life choices. I should not have had to recover from finishing a film. The argument about marriage inequality was strong enough on its own without the film also needing to throw everything else at this poor man.

Compare that to Matthias and Maxime, a 2019 Canadian-French film about two childhood best friends who are forced to confront buried feelings after an on-screen kiss unravels everything between them. It's not a perfect film by all means. The pacing is slow and the open-ended conclusion will frustrate some people. But it doesn't leave you feeling like you need therapy. Matthias showing up at the airport as Maxime is about to leave for Australia was a small, quiet moment, and it meant something. 

The Side Character Problem

And it's not just the main couples either. Even when queer characters are side characters, they get done dirty. It's like writers feel entitled to use gay relationships as a dramatic device without actually caring about what happens to those characters. The relationship exists to create chaos, to shake up the plot, to give the main story something to react to. And once it's served that purpose? Disposable.

Elite is the most infuriating example I can think of. Omar and Ander had one of the best build-ups in the show's early seasons. A slow, careful story about a young man (Omar) terrified to be himself, hiding his sexuality from his conservative Muslim family, falling in love with someone patient enough to wait him out (Ander). By season three, Ander had cancer, Omar cheats on him during treatment, and the writers seemed determined to dismantle every good thing they had built between them, episode by episode. There was no narrative reason for it. It was chaos for the sake of chaos. They technically survived that season, but the relationship was already dead. They broke up not long after, and honestly it felt inevitable given what the writers put them through. I will never forgive them for that.

When They Actually Get It Right

Young Royals is my go-to example that it doesn't have to be this way, and the last BL series I watched and actually loved. A Swedish prince falls for a working-class student at his boarding school, and yes, there are real obstacles. The weight of the monarchy, the class gap, the very public nature of Wilhelm's life, a leaked private video used against them. None of it is easy. But the show never uses their queerness as the reason things have to fall apart. It uses their circumstances, their fears, their different relationships with identity and what it means to live publicly. When Wilhelm gives up the crown and runs to find Simon in the season three finale, it's the payoff for everything you watched those two go through. I watched the whole show twice and I would do it again.

The Handmaiden is a different case because it's not a romance in the traditional sense, but it belongs here. Park Chan-wook's 2016 Korean thriller puts Sook-hee and Hideko through genuine danger, betrayal, and manipulation. The difference is that they are never passive victims of their story. They outsmart every person who tried to use them, claim the inheritance, and leave together on their own terms. Their love is not a source of tragedy. It's the thing that gets them both out.

Red, White and Royal Blue (2023) is the lightest thing on this list but it deserves a mention. Alex, the son of the US president, and Prince Henry of England go from enemies to secret lovers to publicly out and happy, all in one film. It's fun, the chemistry is there, and it ends with both of them on a balcony in front of crowds celebrating their relationship. Kinda cute. It doesn't reinvent anything, but it exists as a queer romcom where nobody dies and nobody gets destroyed, and sometimes that's exactly what you need.

I'll also mention Heated Rivalry briefly, even though I came into the show having already read the Game Changer book series. It follows Shane and Ilya, rival hockey players whose brutal on-ice competition hides a secret relationship spanning nearly a decade. The show takes seriously just how terrifying it is to be a gay man inside professional hockey culture, and the ending actually delivers. No tragedy required.

So Why Is Suffering Still The Default?

Here's what I keep coming back to: queer relationships in media are almost always written with an expiry date on their happiness. The joy is loudest during the forbidden, secret, stolen-moment phase, when being gay is still a source of tension and drama in itself. But the second the characters come out, the second they settle into actually being together? Writers lose the plot. They reach for an affair, a tragedy, an illness, a cheating arc, because apparently two people being gay and in love and doing fine is not a compelling enough story on its own. But it is, and we have seen it done. The excuses are running out.

I'm tired of bracing myself every time I sit down to watch something. I'm tired of treating hope as a risk. Queer love stories don't need suffering to feel real. They just need writers who actually believe that queer love is worth something beyond the pain it causes.

What queer love stories have you watched that actually got it right?

Drop them in the comments. I'm building a list and I need recommendations that won't leave me needing recovery time afterward.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Queer stories deserve more than mandatory tragedy. I break down the "suffering problem" in media and look at titles that actually get it right.

entry.title: In Defense of Jason Statham
entry.content:
Jason Statham has made the same movie at least twelve times, and I have watched every single one. I don't have a good explanation for this.

Neither does he, probably.

There was a version of this man who could have had a genuinely strange and interesting career. Early Guy Ritchie films, a real comedic breakout, solid franchise work. The range was there. And then something happened. A switch flipped. And now every new Jason Statham film comes with a checklist: mysterious past, small town or remote island, a government conspiracy, at least one scene where he stares at something for slightly too long. We keep showing up anyway. This Spotlight is for him, and also for us. Mostly for us. Consider this the case for the defense.

The origin story nobody talks about

Before any of this, Statham was a diver. Not a "did a few cannonballs at the local pool" diver. A real one. He saw a man do a high dive on a family holiday in Florida when he was around eleven or twelve, came home, joined a club, and within a year he was on the British team. He stuck with it for a decade. By 1985 he'd been inducted into the British National Diving School, and in 1990 he represented England at the Commonwealth Games in Auckland, competing in the 1 metre springboard, 3 metre springboard, and 10 metre platform. He didn't medal. Eighth in one event, eleventh in the other two. He tried out for the Olympics twice, Seoul in 1988 and Barcelona in 1992, and missed the cut both times. At one point he was ranked twelfth in the world for platform diving.

He's talked about it being a sore spot, missing the Olympics, watching divers now pull in serious money for the same sport he trained in for ten years of his life. But here's what nobody mentions enough: that decade of getting his body to do precise, dangerous things on command is the actual foundation of everything that works about him on screen. The control. The total lack of panic in his face when something violent is happening to or around him. That's not acting school. That's a decade of standing on a platform knowing exactly what your body needs to do next.

The magnetism

Statham doesn't act intense. He just is. That's the whole trick. Most action stars telegraph danger, they flex, they raise their voice, they do something to remind you they're threatening. Statham just walks into frame and you already believe him. No warm-up required.

It shows in the way he moves through every fight scene, like it's a Tuesday for him, because for years it actually was. But the real weapon is the stillness. Statham at rest is somehow more unsettling than most actors mid-explosion. You can't teach that. You either have it or you don't, and he has it in embarrassing amounts.

The project selection

Early Statham actually had taste, and a bit of luck too. He was modelling for French Connection when the brand became an investor in Guy Ritchie's debut film, and that's how he ended up in front of Ritchie at all. The story goes that Ritchie made him audition by acting out one of his old street-hustling routines, selling fake jewellery to a stranger, and that became his way into Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels. From there it was Snatch, which needed real comic timing in a chaotic ensemble and got it. Then The Transporter handed him a character that fit like a glove, precise, quiet, physical, no unnecessary emotion. Smart choice.

Crank followed in 2006, a film with a premise so thin it's almost a dare: Statham's hitman gets poisoned with a synthetic drug that kills him the moment his adrenaline drops, so he spends ninety minutes picking fights, robbing strangers, and generally causing chaos just to stay alive. It's stupid. It's also exactly the kind of stupid that works because he commits to it without a flicker of irony.

The Bank Job in 2008 is where things actually got interesting. He played Terry Leather, a small-time car dealer dragged into the real 1971 Baker Street robbery, where a gang tunnelled into a Lloyds branch and made off with safe deposit boxes worth somewhere between one and three million pounds. The film leans into the rumour that the British government quietly shut down press coverage because some of those boxes allegedly held compromising material tied to a member of the royal family. Whether that part is true or not, Terry Leather is a man with actual financial stress and actual stakes, not a man with a mysterious past. It's one of his best, most overlooked performances

Then came Deckard Shaw in the Fast and Furious franchise, a character he's now played across four films that have collectively pulled in over four billion dollars, and Wrath of Man in 2021, his fourth collaboration with Guy Ritchie, where he played H, a new armoured truck guard at a Los Angeles security firm who is very obviously not a new armoured truck guard. His coworkers find out the hard way during a robbery, and from there the film slowly reveals he joined the company specifically to track down the men who killed his son. These projects varied enough to keep things interesting.

Then somewhere in the last two years the selection process changed, and by "changed" I mean it stopped. The Beekeeper made him a retired government operative avenging his elderly neighbour after she gets scammed. A Working Man made him an ex-black-ops construction foreman whose boss's daughter gets kidnapped by the Russian mob. Shelter made him a former MI6 assassin hiding on a remote Scottish island who has to protect a young girl from his old agency. These are not three different movies. These are one movie with different location scouts.

The formula is so locked in now that his next film, Mutiny, is already fully plotted online before I've even seen a trailer worth trusting, and I called the shape of it before I even checked: he plays Cole Reed, a former special forces operative turned head of security, framed for murdering his billionaire boss, who ends up on a cargo ship uncovering an international conspiracy. Man with a past. Someone pushes too far. Carnage follows. I knew the whole plot before I confirmed a single detail, and that should worry me more than it does. I'm going to watch it anyway.

The range vs. the commitment

Whatever you think of his recent choices, Statham does not phone it in. That's the maddening part. He shows up to every single one of these mid-budget action thrillers and treats the script like it's prestige cinema. Full commitment, every time. No visible boredom, no coasting, no "I just need to make rent" energy even when the movie clearly doesn't deserve that level of dedication. And that commitment is exactly what keeps his films watchable even when everything around him is falling apart.

But commitment is not the same as range. He's shown real range before. Snatch proved he could do comedy without losing his edge. Spy proved he could be the funniest person on screen in a full ensemble comedy. He just decided, at some point, to put all of that in a box and leave it in storage somewhere.

The underrate factor

The conversation around Statham has always been "guilty pleasure", like enjoying his films is something you have to confess. That framing is doing him dirty.

Watch The Bank Job, where he plays a real person dragged into an actual criminal conspiracy, and you'll find a performance that's grounded and quietly compelling. Watch Wrath of Man, where Ritchie keeps H's backstory close to his chest for the first half of the film and Statham barely speaks. He doesn't need to. His presence carries the mystery on its own. Critics weren't sold, the film sits at 68% on Rotten Tomatoes, but regular audiences gave it 90%, and it went on to gross over a hundred million dollars worldwide against a forty million dollar budget.

These aren't just guilty pleasures. These are good films with a lead performance that doesn't get enough credit because the man chose to spend the second half of his career playing Discount Liam Neeson. He was better than that. He still is, when he wants to be.

The scene stealer

Spy (2015). Rick Ford's first big monologue, where he runs through a list of impossible things he's apparently survived in the field. Reattaching his own arm after it was severed. Walking away from a car crash while the car was on fire. Jumping off a high-rise with nothing but a raincoat acting as a parachute and breaking both legs on landing, then carrying on like nothing happened. All of it delivered straight at Melissa McCarthy with the complete sincerity of a man who has never once doubted himself.

The joke only works because Statham doesn't blink. Rick Ford isn't in on the joke. Paul Feig wrote and directed him to play it exactly like he'd play any of his action roles, fully committed, completely straight, and because of that the comedy turns into something else entirely. It's not a funny-because-it's-Jason-Statham situation. It's a funny-because-this-is-actually-a-great-comedic-performance situation. Every scene he's in during that film is gold, and it remains the clearest proof that there was a whole other career sitting right there for him. He chose not to take it. I'm still grieving.

A small glimmer of hope

There's one thing that's actually keeping me hopeful. Guy Ritchie and Statham have reunited for Viva La Madness, their sixth film together, based on J.J. Connolly's novel and pitched as a standalone follow-up to the world of Layer Cake. Ritchie has said he and Statham had been trying to make this one for over ten years, and they finally wrapped filming in May 2026 with a cast that includes Vinnie Jones and Jason Isaacs. There's no release date yet, sometime in 2027 is the rumour, but the fact that it exists at all means something. This isn't another job-with-a-secret-past thriller. This is the same director who got real comic chaos out of him in the late nineties, coming back for round six.

I'm not saying it'll be a return to form. I'm saying the man clearly still has the appetite for something different. Let me hope small. It's all I've got.

TWC recommends

  • The entry point: The Transporter (2002). It's still the clearest picture of what Statham actually is and why it works. Tight, focused, and built entirely around his strengths. No bloat, no overcomplicated plot trying to justify itself. Just a precise physical lead performance in a film that knows exactly what it is. Start here.
  • The deep cut: Wrath of Man (2021). This is Statham at his most stripped back, a man running almost entirely on presence and barely concealed fury. Ritchie directs it like a cold, methodical revenge machine, and Statham matches the energy. H barely speaks, barely explains himself, and you don't need him to. If you want proof that Statham doesn't need dialogue to hold a film together, this is your exhibit A. Also, Spy (2015) deserves a mention here. It's not a deep cut in the traditional sense, but as a Statham performance it's wildly underappreciated. Rick Ford is one of the funniest characters he's ever played, and he does it all with a completely straight face. Watch that one too. Watch both of them.

If Statham did one proper comedy tomorrow, would you actually watch it, or are you already too comfortable in the brooding-man-with-a-past era to want anything different?

Drop your answer in the comments. And if there's a Statham film I'm sleeping on, I want to hear that too.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: I dive into the career of Jason Statham. The best action star who chose the same role every time.

entry.title: RECAP: Elite Season 7
entry.content:
No cold open dropping you into a crime scene this time. The story just starts and moves forward. That decision alone signals that the writers were trying to do something different.

This was the first season to drop the flash-forward interrogation structure the show had used since the beginning.

I went into Season 7 expecting absolutely nothing. After what Seasons 4 through 6 put me through I had basically written this show off and was just watching out of stubbornness. But here is the thing: Season 7 actually has consequences. People carry their baggage from one episode to the next, the decisions they make actually cost them something, the new characters come with real drama attached instead of just taking up screen time. Is it a full comeback? No. But it is enough to make me sit up and pay attention again, and after the last few seasons, that counts for a lot.

This post contains spoilers for Season 7 of Netflix's Elite.

How it kicks off

The season opens with Omar(yes, he's back) in therapy, his counselor Mateo pushing him to actually process his grief over Samuel instead of running from it, the nightmares still very much alive.

Back at Las Encinas, panic's spreading over Didac. His family's mafia ties put him at the center of suspicion for the shooting that closed out last season, and worried parents push for a vote on whether he even gets to stay. The new school director, Luis, tries to smooth things over, but Didac ends up suspended while the vote plays out. His own brother, Pau, tells him to stay out of it entirely when he asks about the shooting, though he promises Didac isn't going anywhere. At school, Nico wants to help him, though Rocio isn't so sure it's worth the trouble.

A new student named Chloe becomes the school's latest gossip target when her sex tape leaks. She doesn't seem to care much, brushing off Sonia's concern, and it later comes out that she's the one who leaked it herself, telling her mother, Carmen, that everyone's always going to try to use people like them, so she might as well control the game rather than let it control her. Carmen's got her own complicated dynamic going with a man named Jose Luis, who turns out to be Cruz's lawyer, and it's later revealed Carmen once signed away access to her own son in exchange for a payout from Cruz, something she's now trying to reopen.

Ivan finally gets discharged from the hospital, and the group throws him a surprise party. Sara's eaten up with guilt the whole time, and Raul quietly tries planting the idea that Patrick might've been the one who hit him. Ivan doesn't buy it. Just as Sara's on the verge of confessing the truth, Raul stops her cold by hurting her hand, then, once they're alone, offers to take the blame for the accident himself, a gesture that looks kind on the surface and manipulative underneath, especially once he's the one comforting her over the guilt of him "sacrificing" himself for her.

Elsewhere, Luis tries guilting Nico's parents, Maria and Alfonso, into letting Didac stay, pointing out how close he and Nico actually are. In the middle of that conversation, they learn Maria's nephew, Eric, has been arrested at a protest that turned into a riot, and they bail him out and invite him to stay with them, despite Alfonso's worry that Eric's activism will be a bad influence, pointedly bringing up Didac as the kind of friend Nico actually needs instead.

At Ivan's, the group tries lightening the mood with a small get-together. Ivan comforts Isadora, who's avoiding Didac entirely, telling her not to mourn what's lost but to make the most of the time she still has with people. Patrick leaves Ivan an emotional voicemail before officially leaving, promising it isn't goodbye forever and that he still loves him. Once everyone clears out, Ivan breaks down crying, only for the arrival of a pizza delivery guy, Joel, to interrupt. Ivan trips on his way to answer the door, and Joel catches him, ending up staying for dinner out of simple kindness.

Sara tries heading out to see Isadora, but Raul locks the doors on her, blaming her for provoking the earlier fight that left her bruised. They end up watching a movie together instead, Sara miserable the whole time as Raul dozes off beside her.

At the club, Eric's activism talk bores Chloe enough to split the group up. Nico apologizes to Sonia over how things went with Ari, and she tells him she accepts him exactly as he is. Chloe, dancing nearby, lets Eric try to comfort her about the leaked tape, unbothered enough to show it to him outright. She kisses him, he tells her he'd rather actually get to know her first, and she talks him into sleeping with her anyway, secretly recording the encounter without his knowledge.

Back at Ivan's, Joel comforts him through the loneliness and the two share a kiss, though Joel immediately pulls back, unsure it's the right move. Meanwhile Isadora invites Didac up to her suite, catching her mother Roberta's attention, while Pau grabs Isadora separately, wanting to talk. Isadora and Didac end up having an honest, emotional moment together over the uncertainty hanging over him, and it turns physical, until partway through Isadora dissociates and asks him to stop. He stays with her anyway, worried, rather than leaving. Elsewhere, Nico tries to kiss Sonia, but she deflects, wanting to just dance instead.

Ivan apologizes to Joel for the kiss, and the two clear the air, agreeing to just be friends, Ivan even offering to use part of his inheritance to help Joel's future. At the club, Eric tries getting Chloe to have a real conversation, and she just walks off. She later watches the secret recording with him, and when Sonia warns her to be careful with it, Chloe admits that she's the one who leaked her own tape in the first place before walking away. At home, Carmen tells her to have more self-respect, and Chloe pushes back, insisting everyone takes advantage of people like them, so she's simply playing the same game her own mother taught her.

Jose Luis and Carmen meet again, and it comes out that she's demanding access to Cruz's pension, the money tied to a contract she signed agreeing to stay away from her own son. If Jose Luis won't pay up, she's threatening to break that agreement and reach out to Ivan directly. It cuts straight to Ivan quietly looking over an old photo of his father.

At home, Joel receives a package from Ivan: a full scholarship offer to Las Encinas. Omar wakes up beside him and is stunned to see it, upset in a way Joel doesn't immediately understand, since Omar had told him he'd studied in the US rather than admit the truth. Omar finally comes clean about everything the school actually did to him and the people he loves. Joel argues it's not fair to deny him the chance regardless, and Omar, scared but supportive, agrees to back him.

When Joel shows up to register, Ivan's thrilled to show him around, and Omar turns up too, finally accepting the internship offer to help run the school's app. Maria and Roberta agree to let Didac stay, which Luis calls the right call. The episode ends on a gut punch: Luis, revealed to be an undercover cop, pinning Didac's photo up on an investigation board.

The twists and the escalation

The school's anonymous app becomes a weapon almost immediately, students piling onto Didac while Omar quietly spirals, unsettled by how close Ivan and Joel have gotten and increasingly convinced therapy isn't helping. He has a panic attack reliving the night Samuel died. Ivan, oblivious to any of that tension, buys Joel a suit for an upcoming race, and their flirtation deepens fast enough that when Omar finally meets Joel in person, Ivan introduces him as his boyfriend, and the moment was a little awkward for everyone.

Isadora's mother, Roberta, turns out to be the one behind the shooting that closed out last season, a secret Pau lets slip in a flashback, and she makes her disapproval of Isadora and Didac's relationship clear from the start. When Didac tries comforting Isadora through her ongoing struggles with intimacy, Roberta interrupts to pressure Isadora into entering their family's horse into an upcoming race, over Isadora's objections. The horse ends up poisoned not long after, and Roberta immediately points the finger at Pau.

Sara's unraveling under Raul's control becomes impossible to hide, breaking out in stress rashes she scratches raw and claims are just allergies. Her PE teacher, Jessica, notices and starts pushing her toward a self-defense class, planting the first real seed of resistance. Meanwhile Chloe, unaware Ivan is actually her half brother, starts eyeing him as her next conquest, until Carmen finally steps in and reveals the truth to stop things before they go further.

Sara, playing a longer game than anyone realizes yet, convinces Raul that getting Ivan to move in with them would help control the narrative around the hit and run and bring in rent money. Around the same time, anonymous cries for help start appearing on the school app, and it's eventually revealed Omar has his own history with suicidal ideation, a moment from his past where Joel talked him back from a ledge, one he still hasn't fully processed.

Sara's birthday party becomes the backdrop for Ivan officially moving in. Luis secretly hacks into Didac's phone under the guise of a hug, laying more groundwork for whatever he's actually building toward. Rocio, Nico, and Eric join a protest at a homeless shelter that turns violent, ending in a gunshot and Rocio's arrest while Eric panics and runs. Sonia, still hurt over Ari, gives Nico another chance after a mixtape gesture wins her over, while Chloe, chasing Sonia's attention out of spite, sleeps with Nico and gets caught in the act, earning herself a furious callout from Sonia for using people as pawns. Raul, riding high off the party, proposes to Sara live on stream. She doesn't answer. She shows up to Jessica's self-defense class instead.

Eric's mental health spirals harder in the episodes that follow, self-harming and swinging unpredictably between warmth and shutdown, a semicolon tattoo hinting at a history nobody's fully addressed yet. At a school exchange event, Ivan, still grieving his father, decides to apply for the program himself just to get away from everything, while Chloe and Eric's own connection keeps short-circuiting, undone every time either of them gets too close to being honest. Martin, Isadora's father, resurfaces to bribe Judge Duran over an eviction, with Luis quietly listening in the whole time. Drug dealers get raided at the club not long after, and it comes out that Pau orchestrated the whole thing.

Omar, trying to do right by everyone but himself, tells Joel to stop holding back and go be with Ivan, insisting he'll be fine alone. He isn't. Dalmar finds him passed out afterward surrounded by pills and empty bottles, a devastating low point that forces Joel to move in and keep watch over him instead.

As Omar recovers, Sara pulls Chloe further into her scheme, using her to help stage a threesome with Raul purely to catch him on camera and finally have real leverage against him. In the middle of all that, Ivan and Joel get caught sleeping together in Omar's own bed, gutting him completely, and Ivan, guilt-ridden, offers to end things if that's what Omar needs. Meanwhile, high on cocaine with Carmen while sorting through Cruz's old belongings, Ivan watches her hallucinate Cruz mid-conversation, and in her disoriented state, she kisses him before realizing what's actually happening and fleeing in horror, a moment made far more disturbing by a truth Ivan doesn't know yet. Isadora, pulled deeper into her father's orbit, gets offered ownership of the family club, and Luis quietly moves her from a background figure to a central name on his investigation board.

Sara turns on Chloe publicly not long after, throwing her under the bus to protect her own image, and it fractures whatever fragile trust they'd built. Isadora, manipulated by her father into signing off on an eviction she doesn't realize targets her own friends' building, is eventually talked back from it by Didac, who pushes her to see through the scam before real damage is done. Sara, cornered by Raul, finally turns the tables and threatens mutual destruction if he goes to the police, forcing an uneasy standoff between them. Eric's spiral bottoms out in an incident that ends with an ultimatum from Nico's family, therapy or nothing, while Carmen quietly begs Ivan to keep what happened between them secret, unaware Chloe's already overheard everything.

By the final stretch of this run, everything's converging. Omar, finally choosing himself, moves out and back in with his own parents, leaving Joel behind in tears over an empty room. Ivan and Joel commit to each other for real. Isadora, growing suspicious of Didac, secretly installs cameras and catches him photographing documents meant to expose her family, the exact betrayal Luis had quietly been engineering all along. And Ivan, done being used, finally confronts Carmen directly, coldly negotiating a two million euro payout in exchange for cutting all ties for good, unaware of just how much more complicated the truth of who she really is to him might still become.

How it all wraps up

The finale opens grim: police find a body and rule it a suicide before the show even tells you whose. Elsewhere, Nico's family panics when Eric goes missing, and when he finally comes home high, a frustrated Nico snaps and throws him out, a decision that's going to weigh heavily by the episode's end.

Isadora confronts Didac over Luis, and the two end up at the police station together, where Luis finally admits he went undercover after last season's shooting. Isadora, furious, tells him she won't betray the people she loves for his investigation, no matter what he's uncovered.

Sara watches Raul and Chloe together in the halls, and Jessica tells her exactly what's happening: Raul knows Sara's still hooked on him, and he'll keep dangling that control for as long as she lets him, the only real way out being to leave the school entirely. Sara, instead of leaving, lures Raul into sleeping with her one more time and secretly records it. Meanwhile Carmen, having finally gotten Ivan's payout, tries reaching out to Chloe for a fresh start, only to find Raul's blocked her number "for Chloe's own good." Sara catches Carmen in the hallway and warns her outright about Raul's history, how he isolates and invalidates before the abuse even starts, insisting even someone as sharp as Chloe isn't immune to it. Then she sends Chloe the tape.

Eric, meanwhile, is spiraling badly. Convinced everyone's given up on him after Nico's outburst, he ends up alone at the squat house, climbs to the roof, and posts on the self-help app that he wants to talk before he ends his life. Sonia's the one who answers.

Isadora, still wrestling with what to do about her family, gets pushed by Rocio's blunt insistence that people who do wrong should face consequences regardless of who they are. It's enough to make Isadora finally confront her parents directly, only to learn they already know about Luis's investigation and aren't worried, since the police don't have real evidence yet. Piecing it together, Isadora realizes the shooting and her horse's death were both her own family's doing, part of a power play against Didac's. She hands the trafficking documents over to Judge Duran, enraging her father, while Roberta, oddly sympathetic, tells her this is exactly why she wanted her daughter kept out of the family business in the first place.

Ivan asks Joel to come with him to South Africa, encouraging him to take the good moments life offers. Joel, torn, turns to Omar and Dalmar for advice. Omar tells him to go if he loves Ivan. Dalmar pushes back hard, telling Joel to stop letting men run his life and to actually live for himself for once.

Chloe notices Ivan's bags packed and gets pulled away by Raul before she can process it, right as Sara's tape lands in her inbox. Furious, she slaps him and tries to leave, and he responds by throwing her phone and hitting her. Carmen shows up outside, refusing to leave until the door opens, and Raul warns Chloe to keep it together or he'll lose control completely. She fakes calm, but Carmen clocks the fear on her face and the phone lying broken on the floor. As Ivan arrives to grab his things before heading to the airport, Carmen quietly tells Chloe to leave with him, then turns to Raul and invites him up to the rooftop for a drink instead.

Isadora sets her own trap in motion, telling Roberta not to come to the meeting with Martin and lying to her father that her mother's simply lost trust in her. Martin, thinking his plan's working, cruelly tells Isadora she'll never be cut out for the family business the way Roberta always said, since his real business with Duran is already finished and she's no longer useful to him. Right as Duran texts that she's arrived at the meeting location, Isadora quietly forwards her location to the police, then tells her father he's right, that she should prioritize the business over her own doubts, right before revealing she's been wearing a wire the entire time. The police, having heard everything, arrest Martin and race toward Duran.

Sonia realizes it's Eric on the other end of the app conversation and rushes to tell Nico, who runs to the squat house roof and finally reaches him, admitting his earlier anger was really at himself for not knowing how to help. He tells Eric how much he's changed his life for the better and how much he'd lose without him, and the two embrace as Eric agrees to come home.

At the airport, Ivan waits on Joel, who shows up bag in hand, uncertain until the moment actually arrives. Back home, Dalmar looks visibly anxious about something as Omar wonders what's wrong. In the end, Joel doesn't get on the plane, returning home heartbroken but resolved, and Omar, gentle but firm, tells him staying apart for now really is for the best, then goes back to therapy himself.

On the rooftop, Duran waits alone until Rocio joins her, and just as Duran senses something's wrong, Martin's men arrive with guns, dragging both women toward the edge. Police storm in just in time, arresting the men and taking Duran into custody for her own corruption, leaving Rocio devastated by the fallout.

Then the season delivers its real gut punch. On the rooftop with Raul, Carmen confronts him over hitting Chloe, needling him until he snaps and chokes her. She asks, almost calmly, for ice for her whiskey. Confused enough to loosen his grip, he lets her go, scoffing at how unhinged she seems, and she asks again what a man's supposed to do when a woman wants ice in her drink. While he's still processing the question, she shoves him off the roof, telling him to go get it himself. She looks down and finds him dead below.

The season closes on the fallout. Nico brings Eric home to his parents' relief. Roberta is stunned by everything that's come out, and Isadora pretends total ignorance about her father's arrest to Didac, telling him to stay away from her instead of explaining anything. Chloe and Carmen are both questioned by police once Raul's body is discovered, Carmen calmly telling officers he was a troubled abuser and that Chloe was with her the entire time. In the final scene, a flashback reveals Dalmar was standing near the building when Raul fell, and the footage on his phone clearly shows Carmen watching from the rooftop right after. He stares at the video, terrified of what he's just found.

Where we left everyone:

  • Raul: Dead. Pushed off a rooftop by Carmen. The police are calling it suicide for now.

  • Carmen: Covered by Chloe's alibi. Has Ivan's two million and also has Dalmar's video hanging over her whether she knows it or not.

  • Sara: Free. It took recording him, baiting him, and watching someone else finish the job, but she got out.

  • Chloe: Shaken but standing. She lied to the police for her mother. That relationship is unresolved in a way that feels very intentional.

  • Ivan: On a plane to South Africa. Moving forward the way Patrick asked him to. The Joel chapter is open-ended.

  • Joel: Stayed. He chose himself over Ivan's cab and went home to people who actually know him. Hurting, but finally making decisions on his own terms.

  • Omar: Back in therapy and out of Joel's space. A small step in the right direction.

  • Eric: Home and safe, thanks to Nico. The road ahead is still uncertain but he's on it.

  • Nico: Stumbled a lot this season but showed up when it counted most.

  • Isa: Father's under arrest. Corruption shut down. Steps out of her family's shadow for the first time. She and Didac part ways.

  • Didac: Still in love with Isa. His cooperation with Luis paid off but cost him everything else.

  • Rocio: Her mother was arrested for corruption. She deserved better from the writing this season and I'm still annoyed about it.

  • Luis: Case closed. Martin and Duran are both in custody. He got what he came for.

  • Dalmar: Sitting on video evidence of the night Raul died. He hasn't decided what to do with it yet. This will absolutely matter in Season 8.

What worked

Eric stole the show this season. His mental health arc gets more room to breathe than almost anything else here, and it hits because the writing treats it seriously rather than as a shock beat. Ivan handled himself with real maturity this season too, especially given everything he's been carrying since Cruz died. And Carmen pushing Raul off that roof works well as more than just a shocking finale twist, it's a woman finally acting on years of watching men like him get away with it, and the show earns that catharsis by the time it happens. Dalmar was a quiet highlight too, steady in a season full of people barely holding it together.

Overall thoughts

Season 7 is not bad. Actually, better than not bad, and I didn't think I'd be saying that after the last few seasons.

This is the best this show has been since Season 3. It's not a full return to form, but a real, visible step back toward what made the early seasons work. The drama hits harder because it's grounded in who these people actually are rather than just what scandalous thing happens next. The abuse storyline, Eric's mental health arc, Omar's grief, the toxic family loyalty threading through the corruption plot: all of it works because the writing gives it room to breathe.

The weak spots are still there. The dialogue is kind of cheesy, Isa and Didac go in circles for too long, and the organized crime subplot never ignites the way it clearly wants to. Rocio gets sidelined despite one of the more compelling setups this season. And the show completely drops Omar's role running the student app after using it to build the Eric storyline in the first place, a frustrating loose end for a character who didn't need to come back just to be forgotten again.

My Rating: 7.1

One season left. The show set up the right questions to answer. Here's hoping Season 8 actually crosses the finish line properly, because after seven seasons of watching these people hurt each other in increasingly creative ways, they all deserve a clean exit.
