entry.blogger:metaDescription: Elite Season 7 is finally a step back in the right direction.

entry.title: About The Boys.
entry.content:
The actual finale episode was not that bad. I kind of liked it. My real issue is with the season as a whole.

The story, the power scaling, the budget, the character decisions, all of it. Because when you go back and look at where this show started and compare it to where it ended, the distance between those two points is painful to sit with.

The Boys is an Amazon Prime Video series created by Eric Kripke, who also created Supernatural, and it is based on the comic book series of the same name by Garth Ennis and Darick Robertson. It premiered on July 26, 2019, and became the most watched series Prime Video had ever released at the time of its launch. Five seasons. Forty episodes. A premise that was sharp, specific, and genuinely dangerous in a way that superhero content rarely is: what if the most powerful beings on earth were not heroes at all, but brand assets managed by a corporation, and what if the only people trying to stop them were a bunch of deeply broken, barely functional civilians with no powers and no leverage and nothing left to lose?

That premise is extraordinary. And for two seasons it was executed with a precision and a nastiness that made it feel like nothing else on television. Then something shifted. And by the time Season 5 wrapped up, the show that had once felt revolutionary had become the thing it spent its entire run mocking: bloated, unfocused, and more interested in its own mythology than in the story that made people care in the first place.

This post contains spoilers for The Boys on Amazon Prime.

What This Show Was at Its Best

Seasons 1 and 2 worked because they had a clear architecture. Hughie Campbell loses his girlfriend Robin in Episode 1 when A-Train runs through her at full speed while fleeing a crime scene. He does not even stop. She just ceases to exist mid-sentence. That moment is the entire thesis of the show in four seconds: to a superhero operating at that speed and that level of power, a human life is not even an obstacle. It is an inconvenience they do not register.

From that opening, the show builds outward with complete control. Billy Butcher pulls Hughie into a team of vigilantes called The Boys whose entire purpose is to hold supes accountable in a world where Vought International, the corporation that manages and markets them, has made accountability structurally impossible. Vought is the ultimate villain. Not just because of what the supes do under its protection, but because of how it functions: a media empire that transforms public relations into impunity, wrapping atrocities in branding and calling it heroism. Every corrupt thing that happens in Seasons 1 and 2 traces back to that corporate machinery. The show understood that the scariest thing about power is not the individual who wields it but the system that makes them untouchable.

Homelander worked in those early seasons because he was contained by the system even as he controlled it. He was dangerous but he was also constrained: by Vought's PR concerns, by the need to maintain public approval, by the fact that he needed the performance of heroism to sustain his actual power. The tension between what he was and what he had to pretend to be was the engine of everything. Antony Starr played that role with such precision that every scene he was in felt like watching a loaded gun that had not quite decided whether to go off yet.

The Identity Crisis: Who Is This Show Even About?

At some point, The Boys completely forgot that Hughie and Annie were the main characters and Vought was the ultimate villain. That is literally what the show was built on. Hughie and Annie (Starlight) are the emotional center: two people navigating a world that is trying to crush them from opposite sides. Their relationship is the human thread running through all the noise. When the writers lose track of it, the whole structure loosens.

Somewhere around Season 3, the show quietly became the Butcher and Homelander show. And because the writers became so fixated on that dynamic, everyone else got shortchanged. Starlight especially. By the final season she felt completely stagnant, like the writers had no idea what to do with her and decided the answer was just fewer scenes and more standing in the background looking concerned. This is one of the show's two protagonists. A character who spent four seasons fighting to carve out an identity inside a machine designed to erase it. She deserved a final season that matched that arc. She did not get one.

The deeper problem is that too many characters overstayed their welcome because the writers were too cautious to commit to actually killing anyone who mattered until the very end. Frenchie is the clearest example. His storylines had been running on diminishing returns since Season 3 and the show kept manufacturing new emotional arcs for him rather than letting him go when the story had finished with him.

And then there is Victoria Neuman. A head-popping congresswoman operating inside the system, using Vought's own methods against everyone around her, building toward what felt like the most interesting endgame the show had constructed since Season 2. Seasons of setup. Multiple storylines converging around her. And then at the end of Season 4, Butcher uses his new tentacle powers to tear her apart in a scene that should have been cathartic and instead just felt abrupt. A major political threat with real remaining potential, killed to clear the board for a final season that used that cleared board to set up spinoffs rather than deliver the payoff Neuman's arc had been building toward. What a waste.

The Budget and the Pacing Problem

The budget in Season 5 went completely off a cliff and I refuse to be talked out of this observation.

Go back and watch Season 3 Episode 6. Soldier Boy, Butcher, and Hughie going up against Homelander for the first time with actual combined force is the moment that entire season was building toward, and it delivered completely. The choreography, the stakes, the character beats embedded inside the action. That is what a big action set piece looks like when the writing and the production are working together properly. This is what Season 5's final confrontation should have been reaching for: that same integration of character and spectacle. By multiple accounts the finale delivered the deaths and the gore but not the emotional catharsis. The action felt under-resourced and the staging was constrained in ways that made the whole thing feel like it was filmed under limitations the show could not fully overcome. This was THE FINAL SEASON. The last eight episodes of a show that became a cultural phenomenon. The production scale should have matched that moment. It did not feel like it did.

The pacing collapsed in the same direction. Characters switching sides, major deaths, revelations that should have been given room, all of it piled on top of each other in the final episodes with no space between any of it. Butcher killing Homelander by driving a crowbar into his skull and pulling it out with enough force to destroy him entirely is exactly the ending that story deserved. But the sequence around it needed to breathe, and it did not get the room.

And while we are at it: Butcher's tentacle powers in Season 4. An eyesore from start to finish. The visual was wrong, the power set contradicted everything the show had built around the distinction between supes and humans, and it was clearly a creative choice made to give Butcher a way to kill Neuman rather than something that emerged organically from the story. It looked bad and it felt bad and using it to kill one of the show's most interesting secondary characters made both things worse simultaneously.

The Rare Wins: What Actually Worked.

To be fair, a couple of things actually landed.

A-Train had the best individual story of the final season and it ended in the most devastating way the show could have chosen. He started this show as the supe who killed Hughie's girlfriend without breaking stride. Literally the inciting incident of the entire series. His arc across five seasons is the long slow process of a man who chose power over conscience, then chose power over humanity, and then finally, too late to save himself, chose to become something worth remembering. He spent his last episode helping The Boys escape the Freedom Camps. Then Homelander killed him for it. He had finally, in his own eyes, become a hero again. And it cost him everything.

Firecracker had one of the most unsettling arcs of the final season, and it landed exactly where the show needed it to. She entered the series as the ultimate true believer, a woman who weaponized her own trauma and manufactured outrage to build a platform for Homelander. Her journey across the season is the slow, agonizing process of a woman who traded her soul for proximity to power, only to realize that the god she worshiped views her as nothing more than a disposable prop. She spent her final moments desperately trying to maintain her relevance while the walls closed in, tethered to a man who didn't care if she lived or died.

The Power Scaling Problem

This has been quietly unraveling since Season 3 and nobody on the writing staff seemed to notice or care enough to fix it.

Homelander is established across the first two seasons as someone with hearing so acute he can pick up a heartbeat from across a building. He clocks A-Train muttering under his breath. He registers Frenchie tapping a finger on a surface from another room. His powers are positioned as nearly absolute: super strength, flight, laser vision, near-total physical invulnerability, and sensory perception that makes hiding from him essentially impossible. The show establishes them clearly and repeatedly because they are the foundation of why he is so terrifying. He cannot be snuck up on. He cannot be lied to by someone whose heartbeat gives them away. He sees and hears everything.

And then, whenever the plot needs characters to have a private conversation or execute a plan without him knowing, those abilities simply cease to exist. Characters discuss things in rooms they should not be able to discuss privately. Plans are executed in proximity to him that should have been impossible to execute. The show switches his powers on and off based entirely on what the current scene requires rather than what the established rules of his character would permit. This is lazy writing and it is disrespectful to an audience that paid attention. If you build a villain whose powers make him almost omniscient, you need to write around those powers consistently, not ignore them whenever they become inconvenient.

The Gen V Crossover: A Lot of Setup, Very Little Payoff

Marie Moreau was built up across an entire spinoff series as this absolute powerhouse with the potential to fundamentally shift the balance between supes and humans. The show spent a full season establishing her abilities, her growth, her specific place in the larger war against Vought. The crossover into The Boys was supposed to be the payoff for all of that investment: the moment the Gen V world and the main show's world collided with real consequence.

She crossed over into Season 5 and brought a notebook and escorted some people to Canada. That is it. That is the complete summary of Marie Moreau's contribution to the final season of the show her spinoff was designed to connect to.

If you can skip an entire spinoff series, watch those characters appear on the main show, and still not miss a single thing that matters to the plot, then that spinoff should not have been positioned as essential viewing. The whole point of building out a connected universe is that the connections pay off. The Gen V crossover did not pay off. It was a waste of the audience's goodwill and a waste of a genuinely interesting character the spinoff had done real work to develop.

Did The Boys Stick The Landing?

The finale episode itself was okay. Butcher killing Homelander with a crowbar to the skull while saying "this is for Becca" is the right ending to that story. The epilogue earned some of its sentiment: Hughie and Annie expecting a child named Robin. Mother's Milk becoming Ryan's legal guardian. Kimiko moving to Marseille to honor Frenchie's memory. Those details feel right. The show remembering who these people are when the violence stops is always where it does its best character work.

But the season as a whole? Not even close to what this show was capable of at its peak. It is so frustrating to watch something that started this sharp and this grounded in its own rules slowly lose its identity over five seasons. The writing prioritized setting up future franchise content over delivering a satisfying conclusion to the story it had been telling. It let down characters that made people fall in love with it in the first place. It ran out of road for some characters two seasons too late and ran out of ideas for others two seasons too early.

The Boys at its best, Seasons 1 and 2, is some of the smartest, nastiest, most genuinely unsettling television of the 2020s. You can still go back and watch it. The finale does not erase that. But a show this good deserved a final season that matched what it was capable of. It did not get one.

It is what it is.

But enough of my rant. How did you actually feel about the finale?

Did it work for you or are you sitting there just as disappointed? What else pissed you off this season that I did not mention? Drop it in the comments, let us talk about it.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A sharp premise lost to its own mythology. I explore why the final season of The Boys felt like a hollow shell of its former self.

entry.title: RECAP: Primal Season 2
entry.content:
Season one was about two grieving creatures finding each other in the wreckage of everything they lost. Season two takes that and throws it across oceans and centuries.

This was a wild ride from start to finish, full of surprises I did not see coming.

This post contains spoilers for Primal Season 2.

Lost at sea, and then lost from each other

Season two picks up right where season one left off. Mira has just been taken away on a ship, and Spear is not about to let that be the end of it. He tries to swim after the boat and fails, washing right back up on the same beach he started from. So he does the only other thing he can: he builds a raft. Fang is not thrilled about getting on it, and only does once Spear bribes her with bugs.

The two of them ride the open ocean together, fishing for food, watching shooting stars and a lunar eclipse pass overhead, and surviving entirely on each other. A massive shark destroys their raft in a storm, Spear ends up inside its mouth before stabbing his way out, and by the time the seas calm down, Fang has washed up alone on an unfamiliar beach with no idea where Spear is.

The split sets up the next two episodes. Fang, stranded and searching, runs into a red Tyrannosaurus who keeps his distance at first before the two start hunting and bonding together. Spear, meanwhile, gets dragged inland by a group of strangers and wakes up with a broken arm in the middle of what is basically a Celtic village. He fights his way out before their leader steps in and proves they mean him no harm.

The collision between these two storylines is brutal. Red and Fang, now bonded, end up raiding the same village that just took Spear in. Spear sees Fang with a body in her mouth and has no idea what to think. A three way standoff turns into a full battle between Spear, Red, and the entire village, and it ends with Fang killing Red to protect Spear, something she clearly does not want to do. She comforts Red as he dies, and that single moment says more about who Fang has become than anything else in the two episode arc. Spear watches all of it happen, wounded and shaken, and the two of them walk back into the forest together, both carrying something heavier than before.

New faces, old ghosts, and a war with the Vikings

Still shaken by what happened with Red, Spear and Fang take shelter in a cave during a storm, where Spear finds a wall of old paintings showing humans, dinosaurs, and creatures from long before either of them. It is a quiet stretch. Spear even copies Mira's nightly moon ritual at one point, without really understanding why he is doing it.

A bear carrying a Viking warrior crashes into their cave, and Spear spots the scorpion symbol on the warrior's shield, the same one branded on Mira. From there it is a straight line of violence: Spear and Fang track the Viking back to his village, free Mira and a group of other captives, and immediately find themselves at war with the whole settlement.

The fight that follows is one of the most savage in the whole series. Fang kills a Viking woman named Rikka by slamming her into the ground, and in the chaos, Spear accidentally kills her child after the boy latches onto his back. He throws the kid off without realizing what he has done until it is already too late. Spear, Fang, and Mira escape on a stolen boat while the village burns behind them, and the surviving Viking Chieftain and his remaining son set out for revenge with nothing left to lose.

A side episode steps away from the main story to follow a group of Victorian era scientists in 1890s England, one of whom ends up living out Spear's entire journey almost beat for beat after being attacked by an escaped, feral inmate. It almost feels like a what if: what would happen if a regular man got pushed back to the same primal instinct Spear has been running on this whole time.

Back with the main cast, the Viking Chieftain and his son catch up to Spear, Mira, and Fang at sea, and the fight ends in tragedy on both sides. Fang throws Eldar overboard and Spear knocks his father off a flying bird mount mid-battle, but Spear ends up accidentally killing Eldar in the fall while trying to save his own father. The Chieftain, having lost everything now, simply gives up and lets the river carry him away.

What he finds downstream is worse than death. Dragged into an actual underworld of fire and lava, he is offered a deal by a massive, horned demon: power and revenge, in exchange for whatever is left of his soul. He takes it without blinking, and the season's real villain is born.

Back with Spear, Fang, and Mira, life gets gentler for a moment. Fang lays a clutch of eggs, and Spear is clearly thrilled about it, fishing nonstop to keep her fed and giddily helping build her nest. The Chieftain, now a fire demon, attacks, and though Spear and Mira manage to fend him off, the bigger threat turns out to be the next group that finds them: a massive Egyptian war ship that takes the whole group prisoner, smashing one of Fang's unborn eggs in the process.

Slavery, empires, and a giant named Kamau

The middle stretch of the season is where Primal goes the biggest it has ever gone. Spear, Mira, and Fang are dragged aboard the Colossaeus, a literal floating city run by a ruthless Egyptian Queen who forces captives into endless war campaigns across the ancient world. They are not alone. A massive, enslaved giant named Kamau, the one who accidentally smashed Fang's egg, ends up locked up right alongside them, and despite the obvious tension, the four of them are forced into an uneasy team just to survive.

What follows is basically a tour through history's worst battles, with Spear, Fang, and Kamau forced to fight in invasion after invasion: a Babylonian kingdom, a Qing Dynasty city, an early Slavic settlement, a Greco-Roman city. Every win just means another battle waiting right behind it, over and over, with no end in sight for any of them. Mira, meanwhile, is forced to dance for the Queen's entertainment, which is honestly one of the more painful threads of the whole season to watch.

Kamau's backstory finally gets told. He was a peaceful farmer before the Queen's army ambushed his village, killed his people, and forced him into servitude using his daughter as leverage. It changes how you see everything he has done up to that point, including the egg he destroyed by accident, and it sets up the rebellion that closes out this stretch of the season.

That rebellion is huge. Spear, Mira, Fang, and Kamau finally turn on the Queen and her entire fleet, freeing the enslaved rowers below deck along the way. Kamau gets the most satisfying moment of payback in the whole season, throwing the Queen overboard to her death after she spends three episodes holding his daughter hostage. The group escapes with Fang's two surviving eggs intact, but the celebration does not stretch on for long. In the distance, the Viking Chieftain, now a literal demon of fire, has finally caught up to them.

Spear's ending

The final episode pulls all the way back to Spear's childhood for the first time in the whole series, showing his father leading their tribe before dying defending it from a pack of smilodons, with young Spear forced to finish the fight and take his father's place as leader. Looking back at it now, you can see exactly why Spear became who he is: a man who has been losing family and stepping into the role of protector since before the show even started.

From there, the group makes landfall, and Mira finally reunites with a friend from her old life, Amara, leading Spear, Fang, and her two surviving offspring into Mira's actual village. Spear struggles to find his place among other humans for the first time since losing his own family, eventually retreating into his new home to paint his entire life story on the walls using his own blood. Mira finds the mural the next morning and sees that Spear painted everyone else surrounded by family, while he drew himself standing alone off to the side.

The Viking Chieftain catches up to them one last time, now fully transformed by the fire demon's power. Spear and Fang fight him together, and Fang manages to put herself out after being set on fire, but Spear charges in anyway, tackling the Chieftain down a mountainside and taking fatal burns in the process. The Chieftain survives and gloats over his win before getting dragged back into the underworld by the same demon that gave him his power in the first place.

Spear is brought home unconscious, and the village shaman makes it clear there is nothing more to be done. In his final moments, Mira looks at his mural and finally understands what he wanted all along: a family, and a place to belong. She climbs onto him, and the two spend his last moments together before he dies.

The season closes years later, with Fang and her now grown offspring still living in Mira's village, and a teenage girl, Spear and Mira's daughter, riding one of Fang's children and letting out a roar of her own as the screen cuts to black.

Where we left everyone

  • Spear: Died defending Mira's village from the Viking Chieftain, after finally finding the sense of family and belonging he had been chasing since losing his first family in season one.

  • Fang: Survived the Chieftain's attack, raised her surviving offspring to adulthood, and remains in Mira's village years after Spear's death.

  • Mira: Lost Spear but carried on his legacy, raising their daughter within her own community alongside Fang and her offspring.

  • The Viking Chieftain: Survived his final fight with Spear, dragged back into the fiery underworld by the demon that gave him his powers in the first place.

  • Kamau: Freed himself and his daughter from the Egyptian Queen's enslavement, last seen sailing toward an unknown future after years of servitude.

Final verdict and overall thoughts

I went into this season already knowing Mira was Spear's love interest. That was never in question for me. What I did not expect was how big the show would go to get there: new tribes, new civilizations, an entire ancient world I had no idea was coming. That is the real strength of this season, it kept widening the map without ever losing the two characters at the center of it.

Where it lost me a little was the ending. It felt rushed, and from what I have heard, that comes down to the show not knowing if it would even get a third season while this one was being made. You can feel that uncertainty in how fast everything wraps up. Still, even with that stumble, the story this season told was a great one, and it lands as bittersweet in the best and worst ways.

My Rating: 8.7

Did this season hit you as hard as it hit me?

Season 3 is already out, so I am watching that next and dropping my recap with my thoughts as usual once I am done.

← Prev: Season 1 Next: Season 3 →

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: A full spoiler recap of Primal Season 2, following Spear and Fang from a raft lost at sea to Vikings, empires, and a finale that changes everything.

entry.title: RECAP: Elite Season 8
entry.content:
Eight seasons of secrets, sex scandals, murder, and filthy rich teenagers making the worst decisions imaginable, and this is how we go out.

Look, I've been on this Elite journey longer than I care to admit and the final season had a lot to live up to. Did it deliver? Sort of. Was it frustrating? Absolutely. Was I still glued to my screen? Every single episode.

This post contains spoilers for Season 8 of Netflix's Elite.

How it kicks off

The season opens right where the story ends: graduation night, two drunk girls stumbling across Joel's dead body. Then it rewinds to give us the whole picture.

In the present, Omar's reunited with Nadia, back home for a short stay. At Las Encinas, siblings Hector and Emilia Krawietz have taken over the Alumni club, much to Principal Virginia's displeasure, though there's not much she can do about it given the Krawietzs are one of the wealthiest families in Spain with a hand in nearly everything, legal and otherwise. The siblings frame Alumni as an exclusive club now, sponsorship required to join, and the payoff is real enough that Nadia credits her UN internship entirely to Alumni connections.

Hector's instantly drawn to Joel, hitting on him despite Joel's clear disinterest, still trying and failing to reach Ivan, who's ignoring his calls from South Africa. The rest of the group has its own shifts: Chloe and Eric are happy together, which needles Nico, while Sonia's now with Dalmar. Sara wastes no time publicly accusing Chloe of killing Raul, and she's not entirely off base, since the actual killer, Chloe's mother Carmen, is one of the real suspects. With no money for a lawyer, Carmen pushes Chloe toward Hector for his wealth. Isa's in a similar bind financially, her mother nudging her toward getting in good with the Krawietzs too. Isa's already hired Omar to help rebuild the club's image and attract investors, all while dodging Detective Luis, who keeps pushing for a friendship she clearly doesn't want.

Dalmar's facing deportation, though the notice comes with a loophole: cooperate with police or the government in some way, and documentation becomes possible. Conveniently, he happens to be sitting on a recording of Carmen pushing Raul off that rooftop.

Home life isn't any calmer. Omar comes back to find Joel crashing in his room and throws a fit, not without reason given Joel's history of cheating on him with Ivan. Dalmar tries to smooth things over, but Joel lies about staying at Ivan's instead and sneaks off to crash at the Alumni club, where Hector finds him and makes a move, offering to sponsor him for the club under the guise of just wanting him happy. Joel isn't buying it.

Chloe and Isa both angle for Emilia's sponsorship, hoping to leverage her connections for their own gain, and Isa has the stronger pitch, offering her own club up in service to the Alumni. The group dynamics keep fraying: Nico blames Chloe for being a bad influence on Eric, and when Chloe ends up distraught over it, Sonia tries cheering her up with gossip, revealing that Omar told Dalmar, who told Sonia, that Isa's broke. Chloe uses that information immediately, manipulating Omar and leaking Isa's finances straight to Emilia, winning the sponsorship for herself. Emilia toys with Chloe the whole time, insisting she'd never betray a friend while clearly relishing the chaos she's stirring.

Guilt-ridden, Omar tries checking in on Joel, who brushes him off the moment Ivan returns to Spain. Their reunion doesn't stay happy for long, Ivan still stinging over Joel not joining him abroad. Joel calls him out for being entitled about it and accepts Hector's invitation out of spite. Emilia warns her brother that Alumni's exclusivity depends on every candidate passing a test designed to push them past their limits, and Hector agrees to it without hesitation.

The episode ends back at the graduation party, cutting to a bloodied Ivan and Dalmar being arrested for Joel's murder.

The twists and the escalation

Ivan and Joel wrestle in gym class, Emilia teasing her brother for being visibly jealous watching them, while a flash forward jumps straight to graduation night, Hector waking up next to Joel's body, throat already slit.

Back in the present, Carmen assures a cornered Chloe she'll handle the police herself. Emilia's first real test for Chloe is cruel: she swaps Eric's BPD medication for drugs, sending him into a panic everyone mistakes for a breakdown. Chloe stays behind to take care of him, and Emilia tells her that her priorities disqualify her from sponsorship. Isa, meanwhile, has Omar running errands nonstop, which Nadia calls out, pushing her brother to stand up for himself. Luis keeps circling Isa too, and overhears her and Omar planning a party while worrying about money.

Joel's own first trial is worse. Hector tells him to secretly record girls in the locker room shower, and when Principal Virginia catches him, Hector saves him by threatening to leak the footage if she expels him, then coerces Joel into a sexual act, framing it as simply part of the trial. Elsewhere, Nico helps Sara see clearly for the first time that she's been romanticizing an abusive relationship, taking her to Raul's old place to force the reality of it.

Joel works as a bartender now at Isa's club, Ivan can't stop watching him, and Dalmar nudges Joel to actually give Ivan a chance. Emboldened, Joel blows Hector off entirely, until Ivan ruins the moment by paying Isa to let him take Joel home like a transaction, Joel feels humiliated. On the dance floor, Eric shows up insisting he's fine, but the group blames Chloe for his earlier episode anyway, and she breaks down, ending things with Eric over a voice message out of fear she's bad for him before telling Emilia she's ready to join Alumni. In the chaos, Luis has someone secretly sabotage the party decor, injuring several people including Joel, and uses the resulting liability to extort Isa over her lack of permits. Omar has a panic attack amid it all, and Nadia, planning to leave, decides to stay and look after him instead.

Dalmar's bike gets stolen, and reporting it gets him arrested for lacking ID, forcing Sonia to bail him out. Furious and desperate with his citizenship on the line, he anonymously blackmails Carmen using the footage of her killing Raul, demanding the two million Ivan gave her. Meanwhile, an angry Joel goes straight to Hector and agrees to whatever it takes to get into Alumni, and they hook up.

By episode three, both Chloe and Joel are officially accepted into Alumni. A flash forward shows Joel apologizing to Isa at graduation, her fury barely contained as she warns him he'll regret whatever he's done. In the present, Luis forces Isa into dinner with him in exchange for a visit with her imprisoned father. Hector demands a two thousand euro fee from Joel to stay in the club, and when Joel can't pay, refuses to let Hector cover it for him, insisting he won't be anyone's charity case. Instead, Hector rigs a solution: a race he always wins, letting Joel bet on him and use the winnings to pay off Ivan and fund his own way. Omar warns him it all sounds like a cult. Joel insists he can handle it.

Dalmar's extortion attempt on Carmen backfires badly. She hands over a bag stuffed mostly with paper, tracks him home with a hidden device, and threatens to frame him unless he returns what little real money she gave him, though pity gets him a spare thousand anyway. His deportation notice tightens to just one month left. Isa's own visit to her imprisoned father goes just as poorly, Martin insisting she sell the club to a loan shark named Cibran to clear his debts and bail him out. Furious at his selfishness, she relapses back into drugs. Omar suggests borrowing from Ivan instead, but his doubt over whether they can actually save the club offends her. With no other option, her mother Roberta forces her to approach Cibran anyway, and his offer isn't nearly enough to cover the debt.

At school, Isa overhears Joel and Nico discussing the Alumni race and impulsively bets her own club on it. Chloe, worried, tells Ivan, who arrives just in time to catch Joel and Hector making out and can't stop Isa from entering the race regardless. Mid-race, Isa crashes and Ivan rushes to her, while Joel, heading toward Hector, gets struck by Emilia's car. He calls out for Ivan as Hector and Chloe pull him away instead. Emilia wins the race and gloats to Isa that the club is now hers by forfeit, until Ivan reveals he quietly bought the club the night before, protecting Isa from losing it entirely. Emilia warns that Isa still owes her. That same day, Isa learns her father's been killed by Cibran, and a devastated Roberta blames her daughter for all of it, leaving Luis to comfort a shocked Isa. The episode's graduation-night thread closes with Joel confronting Luis directly, threatening to expose him before dropping a beer bottle on his foot and walking off.

Episode four opens on a wealthy Alumni couple, Pier and Guillermina, offering a huge donation to the club in exchange for time with Joel, something Emilia's thrilled to arrange and Hector flatly refuses. Isa keeps apologizing to Ivan for the chaos with her club, and he stays supportive, promising to help with its reopening. When Ivan runs into Joel and asks directly if he's with Hector, the moment turns awkward fast, interrupted by Hector himself inviting Joel over. Ivan warns him and walks away. Chloe tries reconciling with a heartbroken Eric, who swears to cut her off entirely, a conversation Emilia overhears and uses to invite Eric to a pool party of her own. There, Joel and Hector hook up on one end of the pool while Emilia and Eric do the same on the other, the siblings watching each other the entire time in a way that feels less like coincidence than design.

Carmen and Chloe scheme to isolate Dalmar and then swoop in as his saviors so he won't leak the Raul footage, starting by getting him fired. Chloe, meanwhile, sets Sonia up with a guy and secretly photographs it, visibly conflicted about what she's doing. Sara invites Nico over, and after they sleep together while she's high, she spirals into believing he took advantage of her, hurting him badly before kicking him out. Back at the club, Eric grows friendly with Chloe again now that he's moved on with Emilia, and a furious Chloe retaliates by leaking Sonia's photo online, then seduces and secretly films Dalmar, posting that too. Sonia sees it and is devastated.

Emilia, jealous of how obsessed her brother's become with Joel, secretly arranges the meeting between Joel and Pier and Guillermina herself. Hector rushes to stop it and clashes with a completely oblivious Omar, who ends up throwing him out. Joel initially refuses the couple's advances, until the amount of money on offer changes his mind. A flash forward shows the resulting orgy, Joel occupied with Pier and Guillermina while Chloe pulls Eric into another room, where he produces a knife. In the present, Omar's jumped and beaten badly by a group of Alumni members led by Hector, left bleeding in an alley.

Episode five opens with Omar in a coma, Nico's father treating him and warning the family he needs specialized care they can't afford, until Joel quietly pays for it himself, also bailing Dalmar out of a bad deal with Carmen by covering his rent. Ivan takes over Isadora House and rebrands it Cruz9, and things briefly look up as he and Joel reconcile, even talking about moving in together ahead of a keg party celebrating their early graduation. But the Alumni schedule an orgy for the same night, naming Joel the planner, and Hector, furious watching Joel effectively turn into a sex worker for the club, threatens to tell Ivan himself before Joel beats him to it. Ivan's upset once he learns exactly how Joel's been earning money.

The wider group gives Chloe the cold shoulder over what she did to Sonia, until Eric, pointing out Omar would want everyone united right now, reconciles with her, upsetting Nico further. Dalmar learns of Carmen's plan to buy his silence by taking care of his family financially, and reluctantly agrees to work the orgy for the pay. Behind his back, Joel blackmails Carmen directly for a quarter million euros, giving her two days before he leaks the footage himself. Chloe, panicked, tells Eric, who offers to help scare Joel into backing down.

At the club's reopening, Isa helps broker a real conversation between Ivan and Joel, who admits he needs independence but wants only Ivan's love, promising the blackmail scheme is just temporary. At the hospital, Omar wakes to the Alumni threatening Nadia's internship if he reports his own assault. Luis, meanwhile, gathers evidence of hookups at Isa's club to threaten her with running an unlicensed brothel, and when she refuses whatever deal he's offering, he assaults her. Shaken, Isa turns to Joel, who apologizes and confronts Luis himself, threatening exposure.

At the orgy, Chloe sneaks Eric in and corners Joel alone, Eric pulling the knife on him. Joel fights back, and Dalmar, hearing the struggle, intervenes, forcing Chloe and Eric to flee, Eric dropping the knife in the scramble. Back at the keg party, Sara opens up to Nico about being unable to process feelings for someone who isn't Raul, apologizing for her earlier accusation, and Nico forgives her, right before she notices Carmen, Chloe, and Eric acting suspiciously and starts following them. Hector, still pursuing Joel, gets him to agree to sleep with him one more time in exchange for using his connections to protect Isa from Luis. Outside, a devastated Ivan gets a breakup text from Joel and gets drunk, and while Dalmar helps him wait, someone knocks Dalmar out cold. Inside, after Hector falls asleep, Joel gets up to send Ivan one last message when someone slits his throat.

Episode six picks up with Omar, healed and home, texting a Joel who's already dead. Emilia comforts a distraught Hector, who has no memory of the night and is convinced he killed Joel out of jealousy. Police detain the group, and as accounts get pieced together, suspicion lands on Eric once his knife turns up as the murder weapon, prompting a panicked Nico to backtrack and blame Chloe for manipulating his cousin instead, which only wounds Eric further. Under formal questioning, Dalmar mentions the orgy and Ivan corroborates it. Omar, devastated, confronts Emilia directly, and she deflects everything onto Dalmar, dismissing Joel and the others as simply sex workers, a lie Omar seems to believe in his shock.

The group rallies around Ivan's public popularity to try clearing his name, while Chloe searches for her missing phone, unaware it's still hidden in the Alumni room where she'd left it planning to blackmail Joel herself. The Alumni lean into painting Dalmar as the culprit using overtly racial framing, and Omar's fury only deepens when Principal Virginia, herself Black, stays silent through it. Carmen offers to bail Ivan out but claims she can't afford to do the same for Dalmar, instead pressuring him to sign a false confession in exchange for taking care of his family, using the wave of racist online hate against him as leverage. Dalmar refuses and instead puts the pieces together himself, telling police about Joel's blackmail scheme against Carmen as the real motive, though Detective Luena needs a corroborating witness before she can act on it.

Elsewhere, Sonia recalls drone footage from the keg party and tracks down its owner, finding two figures near the Alumni club carrying a large bag the night of the murder. Hector's doubts about his sister's sudden gentleness deepen into suspicion that she framed him out of jealousy over Joel. Omar and Sonia bring the drone footage to police, convinced it shows Hector and Emilia moving Joel's body, but it's overshadowed entirely when the police reveal Dalmar has already confessed.

By episode seven, Omar and Sonia visit Dalmar to understand why he took the fall, and he explains the online hate campaign and Carmen's deal, while also revealing what he knows about Raul's murder, convinced Carmen killed Joel to protect that secret rather than Eric doing it. Theories splinter across the group: Omar and Sonia suspect the Krawietz siblings, while Ivan and Isa still suspect Chloe and Eric. Nadia, helping Omar move out, learns her father's health is failing and gives up her flight back to New York to stay, and Omar finally admits the real reason he stayed silent about his own assault, the Alumni's threat against her internship. She tells him she doesn't care about losing it, and the two agree to report the Krawietzs together.

At school, Sara and Nico fight over her suspicion that Chloe manipulated Eric into murder, and when Eric overhears, worried Nico told her the truth, Nico gaslights him, denying it and turning the blame back onto Eric for not trusting him. Sara, eavesdropping on Isa and Ivan working through their own theory about Chloe and Eric, fills in gaps for them without them realizing where the information's coming from. Chloe finally finds her dead phone in the Alumni room, unable to see what it recorded until it charges.

Hector, furious with his sister, keeps his distance from her, and the two arrive separately to an Alumni party at Cruz9. Ivan, Sara, and Isa use the opportunity to steal Chloe's phone, Ivan distracting her with a selfie while Sara sends her off checking on Eric, giving Ivan the window to grab it and rush to Isa's suite. Upstairs, Omar tips off Luis and Luena, who confront Hector and Emilia together. Hector accuses his sister outright of killing Joel, and hurt, she admits everything, revealed in flashback cleaning up the crime scene, drugging Ivan and texting from Joel's phone to frame him, knocking out Dalmar when he unexpectedly tags along. Facing arrest, she insists she's only an accomplice, that the real killer is Hector, driven by jealousy over Joel and Ivan. Both siblings are taken into custody, Emilia reminding her brother coldly that he owes her now.

Chloe, finding Eric safe, realizes her phone is missing and that Ivan tricked her, rushing with Eric to the suite only to find Ivan and Isa blocking their way. Behind them, Sara's already found the real footage from the night of the orgy, and together they finally see who actually killed Joel.

How it all wraps up

The finale opens with the truth finally shown in full: Inspector Luis picking up Eric's forgotten knife and slitting Joel's throat, the whole thing caught on Chloe's phone. In the present, Omar's already working an angle to bring down both Luis and the Krawietzs at once.

He first tries striking a deal with Hector and Emilia, offering them the real footage in exchange for a signed confession admitting they assaulted him and left him for dead. Emilia doesn't believe he actually has the video. Hector counters with his own offer instead, promising to shut the Alumni club down completely if Omar hands it over. Torn, since that would let Hector walk away scot-free, Omar hesitates, and Hector doesn't wait for an answer, going straight to Luis and telling him Omar has the footage. Luis tears Omar's apartment apart looking for it, and Nadia, shaken, tells her brother to stop playing games with people this dangerous, insisting the only real move is going straight to the police.

Omar takes her advice and heads to the station, but Luis intercepts him before he can reach Detective Luena and tries to assault him, only stopped when Luena walks in. Omar flees and tells the others what happened. Furious, Isa decides to take matters into her own hands, inviting Luis over that night with a plan to seduce and kill him herself.

Ivan objects to the plan, so Isa drugs him too, just enough to keep him from stopping her. Meanwhile, Nadia plants a different idea in Omar's head, that maybe the only real solution is tearing out the root of the problem entirely. Omar pulls Sara into it and asks her to go live with him. On camera, he lays out everything Las Encinas has buried over the years, from Samuel and Marina's deaths all the way through the accidents that nearly killed him and Ivan, furious that nobody's ever actually been held accountable. Then he has Sara upload the footage of Luis killing Joel, live, for everyone to see.

At the same time, Isa's upstairs flirting with Luis, waiting for her moment to inject him with drugs, but he catches on before she can and a struggle breaks out. Luena, having just watched Omar and Sara's livestream, arrives in time to find a drugged Ivan trying desperately to reach Isa. Police storm in and arrest Luis before he can seriously hurt her. As Ivan and Omar help her up, Isa tells Luis exactly what she thinks of him, that his jealousy over lives he could never have drove him to force his way into theirs by violence. Then, as he's being led out in handcuffs, she quietly injects him one more time. He seizes trying to call for help, and dies before anyone can reach him.

Hector and Emilia are released and decide to leave together, though Hector keeps a cold distance from his sister the whole way out.

With Joel's case resolved, Dalmar's finally set free. Carmen, terrified he'll still release the footage of her killing Raul, plans to flee the country with Chloe, though Chloe wants to stay. Carmen makes one last attempt to buy Dalmar's silence, offering a hundred thousand euros and legal help with his citizenship in exchange for deleting the video. Sara, meanwhile, tries livestreaming the last days of high school but can't push through her own grief over Raul's death, until Nico reminds her plainly that he was abusive and got exactly what he deserved, encouraging her to livestream everyone else preparing to leave instead. Nico himself finally reconciles with Eric, admitting he loves him despite everything between them, while a still-drugged Ivan rambles emotionally about how precious life is during all of it.

After Luis is finally caught, Dalmar hands the footage of Raul's murder over to Sara directly, telling her it's her call what happens with it, and that he doesn't care if it costs him his own citizenship to do the right thing. Sara, in turn, warns Eric that she's coming for Carmen and Chloe no matter what. Eric rushes to stop Chloe from leaving, offering to go with her, but Carmen tells him he belongs with his own family, adding that if it's meant to happen, he and Chloe will find their way back to each other eventually. After a quiet, bittersweet goodbye, Chloe and Carmen leave together.

In the fallout from Omar's livestream, worried parents start protesting outside the school, and Principal Virginia, emboldened rather than defensive, makes the call to shut Las Encinas down for good. The graduating seniors finish their final exams at a public school instead, and the series ends on Ivan, Isa, Eric, Sonia, Nico, and Sara walking through its doors, overdressed and completely out of place, while the other students just stare.

How the show ended

  • Joel: Dead. Murdered by Luis in the Alumni room on graduation night with Eric's forgotten knife.

  • Omar: Alive and finally the one who brings everything down. He goes live with Sara, exposes eight seasons' worth of covered-up crimes, and ends the show with Nadia choosing to stay.

  • Ivan: Cleared of Joel's murder. Still grieving.

  • Dalmar: Released from custody once Luis is unmasked.

  • Chloe: Leaves Madrid with Carmen after Sara signals she is not done with them.

  • Eric: Stays behind. Reconciles with Nico. Heads to the public school with the rest of the group.

  • Isa: Alive. She killed Luis herself, quietly, as he was being led away by police. Cruz9 is still hers.

  • Nico and Sara: They find their way to each other. I don't care for them.

  • Hector and Emilia Krawietz: Arrested, then freed. They vanish. The ending clearly left a door open for something else.

  • Luis: Dead. Isa injected him mid-arrest. He had a seizure, threw up, and died.

  • Las Encinas: Shut down permanently, eight seasons of secrets finally catching up to the school itself.

What worked

Nadia showing up again, even briefly, was nice, though it did feel more like a cameo than a real return. Isa and Ivan carried their share of the season fine. And if I'm honest, nothing this season quite matched the emotional weight Eric brought to Season 7, which says something about where the priorities landed this time around.

What didn't

Joel gets treated like the season's real main character, and everyone else pays for it. Sara, Nico, and Eric all get pushed to the background to make room for him, which leaves the ensemble feeling lopsided in a season that should've been giving everyone a proper sendoff instead.

The Krawietz siblings vanish without a trace by the end, it's just another unanswered question dressed up as an ending. The Alumni prostitution ring gets introduced with maximum shock value and then dropped just as fast, like the show forgot it needed to actually do something with it. And then there's the incest angle with Hector and Emilia at the pool, which didn't need to exist in the first place, and matters even less once it turns out Emilia wasn't even the killer. If that storyline isn't building toward her being the culprit, what was the point of making the Krawietzs weirder than they already were?

Speaking of which, Luis as Joel's killer just doesn't work for me. The reasoning behind it isn't strong enough to justify the reveal. The whole season builds Hector's obsessive jealousy and Emilia's cold, calculating streak specifically so one of them can be the answer, and swapping in Luis at the last second feels like a shortcut rather than a real twist. Emilia had the motive, the ruthlessness, and the opportunity sitting right there. She would've been the stronger choice by a mile.

Sara accusing Chloe of killing Raul also felt off, especially coming from the one person who knew exactly what kind of abuser he was. It's one thing to want answers, but going after Chloe with that accusation while sitting on her own history with him feels less like grief and more like deflection. Sara's all over the place this season, and that inconsistency is part of why. There's also the small matter of Sara hitting Ivan with her car back in Season 6 never getting addressed again, not once, not even in passing. I haven't forgotten and I'm not planning to.

And can we talk about how many grown adults are chasing after teenagers this season? Luis pursuing Isa is deeply uncomfortable, and it's not the first time this show has leaned on that exact dynamic. It didn't work then and still doesn't now.

The first half of the season is pretty scattered too, juggling too many threads without much sense of where it's actually headed. And once Luis gets exposed, Isa killing him in full view of arresting officers makes zero sense when you think about it for even a second. No autopsy, no follow-up questions, nothing. Dalmar's arc doesn't hold together either: the same guy who blackmailed Carmen to avoid deportation somehow turns down her payout later, meaning he had two real shots at securing his citizenship and managed to blow both of them.

PS: Nico was completely wasted this season.

My Rating: 6.5

What did you think of the finale?

Did Luis as the killer work for you, or were you also convinced it had to be Emilia? And while we're at it, where do you think the show jumped the shark?

← Prev: Season 7

entry.title: Privacy Policy
entry.content:
Last updated: May 2026

Your privacy matters. This page explains what data is collected when you visit The Watchlist Chronicles and how it is used.

What This Blog Collects

This blog does not directly collect personal information from visitors. I do not run sign-up forms, collect emails, or store any data about you on my end. However, third-party services used on this blog may collect data automatically, including your IP address, browser type, device information, and pages visited.

Advertising

This blog uses Google AdSense to display advertisements. Google may use cookies to serve ads based on your prior visits to this or other websites. If you prefer not to see personalised ads, you can opt out at www.google.com/settings/ads.

Cookies

This blog uses cookies through Google services including Blogger and AdSense. Cookies are small files stored on your device that help these services function properly. You can control or disable cookie settings through your browser at any time.

External Links

Posts on this blog may contain links to external websites. Once you leave this blog, I have no control over how those sites handle your data. I recommend checking the privacy policy of any external site you visit.

Changes to This Policy

This policy may be updated occasionally. Any changes will be posted on this page.

If you have any questions, feel free to reach out.

entry.title: About
entry.content:
No fancy film degrees here. Just someone who watches a lot of things and has too many thoughts about them.

This blog started because I kept finishing shows and movies with something to say, and nowhere to say it. So now I write it down. Sometimes it is a full review. Sometimes it is just a quick take highlighting the good and bad. Either way, it is honest.

I cover everything: Korean dramas, anime, Hollywood blockbusters, prestige TV, and the occasional thing I probably should have skipped. If I watched it, it is fair game.

I am not a critic. My only rating system is whether I actually enjoyed it. That is it.

If you are looking for someone to tell you what is worth your time, or what to avoid, you are in the right place.

What You Will Find Here

Quick Takes: Short, no-fluff thoughts on something I just finished. No spoilers unless I say so.

The Chronicles: Longer posts when something gave me a lot to think about.

Spotlight: When a specific actor, director, or detail deserves its own conversation.

Extras: Everything else. Recommendations, lists, random thoughts.

entry.title: REVIEW: Sneaky Pete
entry.content:
Sneaky Pete is a 2017 crime comedy drama on Amazon Prime. A con man steals his cellmate's identity to escape a dangerous gangster.

The show follows Marius, a con man fresh out of prison who steals the identity of his former cellmate Pete to escape a very dangerous gangster he owes money to.

The plan? Track down Pete's estranged family, a loud, messy, lovable crew of bail bondsmen, and convince them he's their long-lost Pete. What follows is a wild juggling act of con jobs, family drama, and increasingly high stakes that is genuinely so fun to watch. At least for the first two seasons.

The Highlights

  • Marius carries this whole show on his back. He's played with this perfect mix of charm and barely-contained panic, and you're always aware that the whole thing is one wrong move from collapsing. The show doesn't work without him.
  • Seasons 1 and 2 are sharp. The writing is tight, the twists actually pay off because they've been properly set up, and Season 2 manages to raise the stakes even higher while keeping the characters feeling real.
  • Audrey is everything. She's this incredible combination of warmth and absolute steel, and you love her and lowkey fear her at the same time. Every scene she's in is better because she's in it. Full stop.
  • The tone is a nice balance. It's dark without being suffocating. There's real humor threaded through the tension in a way that keeps the energy up without making the danger feel fake.

Fair Warnings

  • Season 3 is bad. Like, disappointing bad. The plot gets bloated, the character work feels rushed and inconsistent, and the tight focus that made the first two seasons so good just disappears. The acting is still solid but the writing isn't there, and at some point I just tapped out.
  • It got cancelled and I found out too late. Already struggling to care and when I found out the show got axed in 2019, that sealed it for me. Closed the tab and never looked back.
  • Some plot points ask a lot of you. This is a con man show so a certain amount of "okay I'll buy it" is part of the deal. But there are moments, especially later on, where the writing leans a little too hard on convenient coincidences to keep things moving.

Final Verdict

My Rating: 7.1

Seasons 1 and 2 are great, just stop there. You'll know when Season 3 starts losing you, and when it does, just leave it. Trust me.

Did anyone actually push through Season 3 or did you bail too?

Drop it in the comments. I want to know if I'm alone in this or if we all made the same call.

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: I loved the first two seasons of Sneaky Pete, but Season 3 killed it for me. Here’s why I recommend watching this show, but knowing when to walk away.

entry.title: Am I Tired of Anime, or Just Older Now?
entry.content:
People keep asking me if I've fallen out of love with anime, and the answer is no. Also, this is not a "quitting anime" post.

I can throw on Attack on Titan right now and still lose my entire evening to it like it's the first time. I am also counting down to Haikyuu and Vinland Saga like a kid waiting for Christmas. So no, this is not a "I'm quitting anime" post. If I were truly done, none of that would move me. So whatever this feeling is, it's not burnout on the medium itself. It's something else.

It's not that I hate what's airing. It's that I sit down to start a new show, scroll through my list, and just... close the app. Nothing pulls me in anymore. And when I do force myself to commit to something and it turns out to be average, I don't just shrug it off like I used to. I feel drained, like I wasted something I can't get back. So let's actually dig into this, because I don't think it's as simple as "anime bad now."

So what's actually going on then?

I think it's two things happening at once, and they're feeding into each other.

The first is just how much is out there now. Anime isn't the niche thing you had to dig for anymore, it's a full blown industry pumping out shows nonstop. Netflix alone logged 4.4 billion anime viewing hours in the first half of 2025, and that's just one platform. That's not counting Crunchyroll, HIDIVE, or whatever else is fighting for your watch time. One single season right now can drop sequels for Jujutsu Kaisen, Frieren, Vigilantes, Hell's Paradise, Oshi no Ko, Golden Kamuy, a new Fate, and Fire Force's ending, all in the same three months. Add in the smaller isekai and slice of life shows nobody's even talking about and it's just noise. Too much noise.

When there's this much to choose from, picking wrong feels expensive. You commit six episodes to something, it goes nowhere, and now you've lost time you can't get back. So instead of picking anything, I just... don't pick. I scroll and close the app. It feels like decision paralysis dressed up as fatigue.

The second thing, and this is the one I'm less comfortable admitting, is that I think I've just gotten pickier with age. Not old in a sad way, just old in a "I know what I like and I don't have patience for filler anymore" way. When I was younger I'd sit through a slow first ten episodes because everyone said it gets good later. Now I don't have that patience, and when a show turns out average after I gave it my time, it stings more than it used to.

The solo leveling gut check

Solo Leveling is the clearest example of what I mean. The hype for this show was massive, I went in expecting to be floored, and what I got was a lot of flashy power up moments stapled onto a story I've basically seen a hundred times. Weak guy gets secret power, becomes strongest hunter, and everyone who doubted him regrets it. The animation is gorgeous by the way, I'm not taking that away from it. But gorgeous animation around a plot I could predict from episode two just isn't enough for me right now.

Isekai is not helping matters

Then there's isekai, which has gotten so saturated that shows now use the entire title as the plot summary. 

Ever heard of Reborn as a Vending Machine, I Now Wander the Dungeon? I'm not kidding. It's a real show where a man dies and comes back as a sentient vending machine in a fantasy dungeon. It ran three whole seasons from 2023 to 2026 and people liked it for how weird it is. I'm not even mad it exists, I'm mad that this is a normal Tuesday now and nobody blinks.

And it's not just the weird ones. Even the standard power fantasy shows have caught the same disease. The Strongest Tank's Labyrinth Raids: A Tank with a Rare 9999 Resistance Skill Got Kicked from the Hero's Party is basically a full sentence, not a title. Same with Even Given the Worthless [Appraiser] Class, I'm Actually the Strongest, which tells you the entire twist before you've even pressed play. Nobody scrolling past these needs to read a synopsis, the title already spoiled it for them.

I found out that this actually started because readers stopped reading descriptions, so the title had to do the summarizing instead, and it worked well enough that every studio copied it. Now it's an endless line of "I Got Reincarnated As X And Now I'm Overpowered In This Specific Way" shows, just with the specific way swapped out each show. The titles keep getting longer because the ideas keep getting thinner. When a title needs fifteen words to explain the premise, the story inside usually doesn't have fifteen words worth of anything new to say.

Standing in front of that wall of near identical shows every year is exhausting on its own, separate from whether any individual show is good or bad. It's just a lot to wade through to find the one thing that might actually be worth my time.

Maybe I'm just older now

I keep circling back to this because I think it might just be the real answer. When I was younger, average was fine. I had time to burn, I could sit through a mediocre show without a care in the world. Now, time feels tighter, and when I actually clear space to sit down and watch something, I want it to be worth it. An average show doesn't just feel average anymore, it feels like a loss. Like I could've used those hours on a rewatch that I know would've delivered, or on one of the handful of upcoming shows I'm actually excited about. Honestly, I could've just taken a nap and gotten more out of it.

That's probably the grumpy old lady talking, but I think there's something honest in it too. I'm not less interested in anime. I'm less interested in gambling my limited time on things that might not pay off.

So am I tired of anime or not?

No. I keep coming back to that answer every time I think this through. What I'm actually tired of is the noise, and I'm less patient than I used to be when a show doesn't earn my time quickly. Those two things together can look like burnout from the outside, but they're not the same as losing interest in the medium.

The fix isn't quitting anime. It's probably getting more selective, leaning harder on recommendations I trust instead of chasing whatever's trending, and giving myself permission to drop something the moment it stops working for me instead of finishing it out of obligation.

Anyone else feel like this, where it's less "I hate anime now" and more "nothing's grabbing me"?

Tell me in the comments, what's the last show that actually pulled you in, no forcing required?

More reviews and takes at The Watchlist Chronicles.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: Am I tired of anime, or just older and pickier? Breaking down why nothing's grabbing me lately, even with a packed watchlist waiting.
